bullets: The newly released V³AST-Bench evaluates coding-agent safety through 212 risk tasks in 18 categories. Its runtime environments inspect resulting states, records, and artifacts, while paired capability tests distinguish harm avoidance from simple inability to complete a task. Why it matters: If you are selecting a safety suite for agents that execute code, this design measures what the agent actually changes rather than judging its written response. It can also prevent an incapable model from receiving the same safety credit as one that could act but correctly abstains. Evidence: E004. High confidence.

Δτ-Bench is the strongest example of a recurring pressure in this feed to test agents under changing environments. Its 1,588 validated multi-turn tasks alter tool ecosystems as services disappear, replacements emerge, and documentation becomes noisy; SkillShift-Bench independently applies controlled context, perception, and execution changes to web agents. Why it matters: If an agent will operate against changing services or websites, a static test cannot determine whether it discovers new tool paths and revises outdated procedures. These benchmarks let buyers and developers include adaptation—not only initial task completion—in model selection. Evidence: E010, E012. High confidence.

NumTrace is a new benchmark that audits the provenance of numerical claims from financial analyst agents. Its 540 questions over 2,163 regulatory filings check whether each number has the correct source, entity, concept, period, unit, and scope rather than merely matching a reference value. Why it matters: If you are evaluating financial research agents, answer accuracy alone can hide a number copied from the wrong context. NumTrace supports a product decision based on whether an agent can provide evidence with the financial meaning needed for review and audit. Evidence: E034. High confidence.

SentryBench introduces two-sided, cost-sensitive safety evaluation for tool-using agents in public-safety scenarios. It jointly scores successful attacks, missed legitimate emergencies caused by excessive refusal, and unwarranted actions caused by over-reaction. Why it matters: If you are choosing an agent for alerting or dispatch workflows, ranking systems only by attack resistance can reward models that refuse useful work. This benchmark makes the operational costs of both unsafe action and unsafe inaction visible in the same evaluation. Evidence: E033. High confidence.

A newly released PlantSeg audit tests whether visually related image families crossed the benchmark’s training and evaluation partitions. It reports that verified cross-split families involved about 10.7% of the benchmark and includes contamination-aware reevaluation and a reconstruction that keeps related groups in separate partitions. Why it matters: If you maintain or use an image benchmark, random image-level splitting may overstate transfer when near-related samples appear on both sides. This audit provides a concrete reason to split by related image family and rerun comparisons before using scores for model selection. Evidence: E044. High confidence.

IntentDelta is a new human-constructed benchmark for agents facing revised user requirements. Its 638 trajectories and 3,766 turns track the cumulative intention state and reference actions as constraints and priorities change; FeatureLoop independently tests coding agents in persistent workspaces as users clarify requirements. Why it matters: If you are evaluating assistants for multi-step work, final completion alone can conceal whether the agent forgot an earlier requirement after a later revision. These artifacts support testing the preservation and correct replacement of constraints across the full interaction. Evidence: E023, E110. High confidence.

iPrefBench evaluates how personal mobile agents handle underspecified requests in an executable mobile environment. It separates information an agent should infer from activity history from information it should ask the user to supply, while accounting for unsupported assumptions and unnecessary questions. Why it matters: If you are choosing a personal-assistant model, task success does not reveal whether it guessed private preferences or repeatedly interrupted the user. This benchmark makes the trade-off between personalization and clarification burden part of the selection decision. Evidence: E018. High confidence.
bullets_zh: 新发布的 V³AST-Bench 通过 18 个类别中的 212 项风险任务评估编码智能体的安全性。其运行时环境会检查任务执行后产生的状态、记录和制品，而配套的能力测试则用于区分规避危害与仅仅无力完成任务。Why it matters: 如果你正在为可执行代码的智能体选择安全评测套件，这种设计衡量的是智能体实际改变了什么，而不是评判其书面回答。它还可以避免让无能力执行任务的模型获得与有能力行动但正确选择不行动的模型相同的安全评分。Evidence: E004. High confidence.

Δτ-Bench 是本信息流中反复出现的趋势——在变化的环境中测试智能体——最有力的例证。它包含 1,588 项经过验证的多轮任务，会随着服务消失、替代方案出现以及文档噪声增加而改变工具生态；SkillShift-Bench 则独立地对网页智能体施加可控的上下文、感知和执行变化。Why it matters: 如果智能体将在不断变化的服务或网站中运行，静态测试无法判断它是否能发现新的工具路径并修订过时的流程。这些基准让采购方和开发者能够在模型选择中纳入适应能力，而不仅仅是初始任务完成情况。Evidence: E010, E012. High confidence.

NumTrace 是一个新基准，用于审计金融分析师智能体所提出数值主张的来源可追溯性。它针对 2,163 份监管申报文件设置了 540 个问题，检查每个数字的来源、实体、概念、期间、单位和范围是否正确，而不只是看其是否与参考值一致。Why it matters: 如果你正在评估金融研究智能体，仅看答案准确性可能会掩盖数字是从错误上下文中复制而来的问题。NumTrace 有助于根据智能体能否提供具备审查和审计所需金融含义的证据来作出产品决策。Evidence: E034. High confidence.

SentryBench 针对公共安全场景中的工具调用智能体，引入了双向、成本敏感的安全评估。它联合评估攻击成功、因过度拒绝而错过合理紧急事件，以及因反应过度而采取不当行动的情况。Why it matters: 如果你正在为警报或调度工作流选择智能体，仅按攻击抵抗能力对系统排名，可能会让拒绝执行有用工作的模型得到更高评价。该基准在同一评估中同时呈现不安全行动和不安全不行动的运营成本。Evidence: E033. High confidence.

一项新发布的 PlantSeg 审计检验了视觉上相关的图像族是否跨越了该基准的训练分区和评估分区。报告指出，经核实的跨分区图像族约涉及该基准的 10.7%，并提供了污染感知的重新评估，以及一种将相关图像组保留在不同分区中的重构方案。Why it matters: 如果你维护或使用图像基准，当近似相关的样本同时出现在分区两侧时，图像级随机划分可能会夸大迁移能力。这项审计给出了按相关图像族划分数据的具体理由，并说明在使用分数进行模型选择前应重新运行比较。Evidence: E044. High confidence.

IntentDelta 是一个由人工构建的新基准，面向需要应对用户需求修订的智能体。它通过 638 条轨迹和 3,766 个轮次，在约束与优先级发生变化时跟踪累积意图状态和参考动作；FeatureLoop 则独立测试编码智能体在持久化工作区中应对用户逐步澄清需求的能力。Why it matters: 如果你正在评估用于多步骤工作的助手，仅看最终完成情况可能会掩盖智能体在后续修订后忘记较早需求的问题。这些评测资源支持测试智能体能否在完整交互过程中保留约束，并正确替换约束。Evidence: E023, E110. High confidence.

iPrefBench 评估个人移动智能体如何在可执行的移动环境中处理规定不充分的请求。它区分智能体应从活动历史中推断的信息与应询问用户提供的信息，同时将缺乏依据的假设和不必要的提问纳入考量。Why it matters: 如果你正在选择个人助理模型，任务成功并不能揭示它是否擅自猜测了私人偏好，或是否反复打断用户。该基准将个性化与澄清负担之间的权衡纳入选择决策。Evidence: E018. High confidence.

Brave and OpenReview were unavailable, and several attention collectors had partial failures, so the briefing does not imply full-field coverage or use attention metrics as corroboration.

evidence_items.summary: PURPOSE: Accurate dose calculation is a fundamental component of modern radiotherapy, enabling precise tumor irradiation while sparing surrounding healthy tissue. With the increasing adoption of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-guided radiotherapy and growing interest in real-time adaptive radiotherapy, there is a demand for fast and accurate dose calculation techniques on both computed tomography (CT) and MRI. To facilitate research in this area, the DoseRAD2026 dataset and accompanying challenge introduce a publicly available benchmark dataset comprising paired CT and MRI data with corresponding beam-level photon and proton Monte Carlo (MC) dose distributions, enabling the development and systematic evaluation of advanced dose calculation and prediction methods. ACQUISITION AND VALIDATION METHODS: The DoseRAD2026 dataset comprises paired CT and MRI data from 115 patients (75 training, 40 testing) treated on a hybrid MRI-linear accelerator (MRI-linac) for thoracic or abdominal lesions and is derived from the SynthRAD2025 dataset. Image pre-processing included deformable image registration, air-cavity correction and resampling. Ground-truth photon (6 MV) and proton dose distributions were generated using open-source MC dose calculation algorithms and resulted in a training dataset of 40,500 photon beams and 81,000 proton beamlets. DATA FORMAT AND USAGE NOTES: The dataset is organized into photon and proton subsets, each comprising paired CT-MRI images, beam-level dose distributions, and JSON files specifying patient-specific beam configurations. Data are provided in compressed MetaImage (.mha) format with standardized naming linking dose files to beam parameters in the JSON files. The dataset is released under a CC BY-NC 4.0 license, with the training set available from April 2026 and the test set withheld until March 2030.
evidence_items.title: DoseRAD2026: A benchmark dataset for AI-accelerated photon and proton dose calculation in radiotherapy.

evidence_items.summary: As frontier language models grow increasingly capable and autonomous, independent third-party evaluations are critical for characterizing their systemic safety risks. While closed-source releases are routinely accompanied by comprehensive system cards, open-weight models receive less scrutiny regarding frontier risks. To address this gap, we present an independent safety evaluation of DeepSeek V4.1 Flash-1017, the latest version of V4.1 Flash that departs from V4 with a new architecture, scaled-up training, and strong agentic capabilities. Drawing on the EU General-Purpose AI Code of Practice, we evaluate the model across 34 benchmarks, including 5 in-house suites, spanning evaluation integrity, loss of control, and harmful manipulation. Conforming to the AEF-1 standard, we compare V4.1 Flash-1017 against V4.1 Flash, earlier DeepSeek V4 models, and leading closed-source systems (GPT-6 Astra, GPT-5.6 Sol, and Gemini 3.8 Flash). Overall, V4.1 Flash-1017 shows substantial safety improvements over the V4 generation and approaches or matches leading closed-source baselines on several dimensions, while still exhibiting notable behaviors that warrant continued attention. Building on our findings, we highlight three key observations and recommendations. First, because safety can shift and even regress across minor updates, developers should integrate safety evaluation into incremental releases. Second, as final-turn outputs and end-state checks alone cannot reliably detect loss-of-control behaviors, deployments require process-level observability across both reasoning traces and action logs. Third, because public benchmarks elicit strong evaluation awareness and face data contamination risks, developing private benchmarks is essential for trustworthy frontier evaluation.
evidence_items.title: Evaluating DeepSeek V4.1 Flash-1017 for loss of control and harmful manipulation risks

evidence_items.summary: Although Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated potential in clinical documentation, generating the rigorous, evidence-based reasoning required for unprecedented, atypical, and rare disease case reports remains a significant challenge. We present MedCaseAgent, an end-to-end agentic reasoning paradigm that bridges this gap by synthesizing publication-quality reports from unstructured clinical notes. MedCaseAgent leverages a hierarchical structure, integrating patient-level data mining with iterative, tool-integrated reasoning. By dynamically querying medical literature and knowledge bases, the agent maintains high clinical fidelity and assesses case novelty. The framework is inherently modular, supporting various backbone LLMs in a plug-and-play fashion. To facilitate this research, we release MedCase-150K, a large-scale multimodal clinical case-report corpus, and MedCase-Bench, a robust temporally held-out evaluation suite. We also introduce an open-source model post-trained from Qwen3.5-9B and optimized specifically for this task. Under both LLM-judged and rule-based evaluation, MedCaseAgent outperforms existing general-purpose and specialized medical LLMs and agents. Blinded expert reviews and ablations further support the system's clinical relevance and evidence grounding.
evidence_items.title: MedCaseAgent: From Multimodal Clinical Evidence to Rare Disease Case Reports

evidence_items.summary: OpenDUck is an open source implementation of Dynamic Undocking (DUck). OpenDUck can be found at https://github.com/CBDD/openduck. DUck is a particular application of steered molecular dynamics where the work needed to bring the main hydrogen bond in a protein-ligand complex to the quasi-bound state is evaluated 1. The quasi-bound work (WQB) is a measure of the structural stability of the complex and relates with the first dissociation barrier. DUck was designed as a filtering step in virtual screening campaigns and shows enrichment of docking results up to 40% for completely novel chemotypes. Due to its fast and cheap nature, it has been used in various screening pipelines like DUckCov2 for covalent docking or in fragment-based drug discovery3. Recently, new applications of structural stability have emerged. Maciej & Barril4 showed good binding mode prediction results and Miñarro et al.5 have deepened the understanding of modulation of protein-protein interactions by molecular glues. With the success of structural stability and the prospect of new applications, a push towards an open source, flexible and accessible implementation of Dynamic Undocking became imperative. OpenDUck has been developed as a python library to capitalize on big open source initiatives in computational chemistry such as OpenMM and OpenForcefield. While minimizing the external dependencies, we have been able to harness the development effort from those initiatives to provide as much flexibility as possible. We also aim to ease the maintenance and future updating of the code and protocol, by compartmentalizing the different DUck steps and parameters. OpenDUck comes with an executable openduck with all the necessary utilities and parameters to launch and evaluate Dynamic Undocking both in AMBER or in OpenMM. In addition to that, the openduck library can also be used to develop custom protocols with just a few lines of code.
evidence_items.title: Benchmark dataset for OpenDuck: an open source implementation of Dynamic Undocking

organizations: Department of Computer Science, Norwegian University of Science and Technology, Gjøvik, Norway
evidence_items.summary: Hundreds of degraded textile fragments from the Viking Age Oseberg ship burial (834 CE) still await reconstruction. Deep puzzle solvers perform well on clean natural images, but no historical textile dataset existed to train or test them. We present TEXMET, a curated dataset of 18,644 CC0-licensed historical textile images from the Metropolitan Museum of Art and, to our knowledge, the first textile-specific benchmark for puzzle solving, and use it to evaluate three state-of-the-art solvers: JPDVT, FCViT and DiffAssemble. Our results show that domain data, not architecture alone, limits transfer. Transformer models trained on natural images lose up to 60 points of puzzle accuracy on textiles, while the graph-based DiffAssemble, fine-tuned on TEXMET, reaches 85.89% on textiles and improves from 26.67% to 64.44% on 45 photographs of real Oseberg fragments, each cut into a 3×3 grid and reassembled in isolation. This short paper summarizes our article in the ACM JOCCH Special Issue on Visual Heritage.
evidence_items.title: TEXMET: A Curated Dataset and Deep Learning Benchmark for Archaeological Textile Reconstruction

evidence_items.summary: Large language models increasingly act through code, modifying repositories, executing programs, and interacting with services in agent form. Their actions introduce risks that cannot be assessed from generated responses alone. Safety evaluation must verify actual consequences, distinguish harm avoidance from task incapability, and cover realistic workflows. We introduce V$^3$AST-Bench, a benchmark for Verifiable results, Valid interpretation, and Versatile risk coverage of Agent Safety. It comprises 212 risk tasks spanning 18 categories. Dedicated runtime environments verify harm and task outcomes through executable checks over states, records, and artifact behavior, while paired capability twin tasks verify workflow competence. Our experiments span 51 combinations of 11 models and five harnesses, spanning 86,496 trials and over 9 billion tokens of model interaction. Results show that V$^3$AST-Bench remains challenging even for frontier coding agents, as Claude Opus 4.8 with Claude Code still causes verified harm on 20.9% of tasks. Across model-harness combinations, agents with comparable competence exhibit markedly different safety outcomes, showing that task capability alone does not guarantee safe execution. More importantly, even explicit recognition of risks does not reliably prevent harmful actions, revealing a critical gap between risk awareness and safe execution. These findings highlight the need to move beyond risk recognition toward enforcing safety throughout execution.
evidence_items.title: V$^3$AST-Bench: Verifiable, Valid, and Versatile Safety Evaluation for Coding Agents

evidence_items.summary: Evaluating deformable 3D reconstruction requires ground truth linking camera motion, surface deformation, material correspondence and image appearance. We introduce the Synthetic Deformable Tubular Benchmark, generated with LumenMorph, an open-source toolkit for creating, annotating and evaluating tubular scenes. The release contains 5,580 RGB images. Its baseline crosses three surface-motion conditions with moving and stationary cameras in six scene families; matched appearance variants cover only moving-camera finite-element actions in four families. Documented public and evaluation interfaces expose camera poses, geometry, depth, deformation fields, persistent material correspondences and discrete finite-element records. Persistent triangle identities and material weights let users track the same surface location across frames and query its three-dimensional trajectory. Separately implemented geometric and mechanical checks assess annotation consistency with the generating models. Structure-from-motion, optical-flow and supplied-geometry displacement-interpolation studies demonstrate how the resource distinguishes registration coverage from geometric accuracy, exposes camera- and surface-motion effects, and tests the benefits and mismatch of mechanical priors. Public readers, evaluation contracts and the configurable generator support reuse and extension. Data integrity, fixed-environment repeatability and retained-prediction score replay have distinct verification scopes. The benchmark provides a controlled synthetic reference without claiming anatomical or clinical realism.
evidence_items.title: Synthetic Deformable Tubular Benchmark: A mechanically annotated dataset for evaluating deformable 3D reconstruction

evidence_items.summary: Retinal vessel segmentation is widely used in retinal image analysis, yet model selection based only on aggregate overlap scores can overlook structural fidelity, cross-dataset robustness, and application-specific error costs. We evaluated five executable binary vessel-segmentation pipelines (FSG-Net, SA-UNetv2, DCP-1024, GAVE, and FR-UNet) on 244 images from six public datasets using pixel-level agreement, cross-dataset stability, thin-vessel retention, structural metrics, error composition, and available computational evidence. Results were aggregated with equal weighting across datasets. No pipeline was optimal in every setting. FSG-Net achieved the highest equal-dataset mean Macro-F1 (0.77), IoU (0.63), clDice (0.83), and Skeleton F1 (0.78), whereas SA-UNetv2 achieved the highest mean sensitivity (0.85) and Thin-Vessel Sensitivity (0.63). Differences across datasets were often larger than those among the leading pipelines, and errors shared by all five methods were concentrated near annotated vessel boundaries and faint peripheral vessels. In an ancillary analysis on 45 HRF images, segmentation masks were converted into 11 ring-wise vascular features for leave-one-out classification. Controlled perturbations showed that local mask errors can be amplified in downstream features, while targeted stabilization reduced sensitivity for five features. The results support task-conditioned, benchmark-relative pipeline selection rather than a single universal ranking and highlight the need to validate the selected pipeline on the intended target domain.
evidence_items.title: Evidence-Guided Selection of Retinal Vessel Segmentation Pipelines: A Cross-Dataset Benchmark of Performance, Structure, Failure Modes, and Reproducibility

evidence_items.summary: Reproducible offline benchmarks for electric vehicle charging require explicit transition definitions and auditable data processing. We introduce IoEV-MARL, comprising 157,071 decision-level transitions from SUMO simulations of the road network of Tangier, Morocco, organized in a 62-column table. The corpus covers 700 collection episodes, seven seeds, four traffic regimes, and five behavioral arms: NEAREST, WEIGHTED, tabular Independent Q-Learning, and two QMIX checkpoint/exploration configurations. Learned collection policies originate from 120-episode training campaigns. A three-layer contract distinguishes decision-time observations, inter-decision elapsed time, and outcome/evaluation fields. Elapsed time is missing when no subsequent decision is recorded. The ETL protocol documents horizon censoring, missing successors, dimensional grain, and file-level provenance. Seven-fold leave-one-seed-out evaluations benchmark Behavior Cloning and offline Implicit Q-Learning on accept/reject decisions conditional on the selected station. Mean Behavior Cloning balanced accuracy ranges from 0.758 to 0.928 across tiers and feature sets, measuring imitation rather than operational performance. In matched greedy evaluation, QMIX has lower station-load dispersion in 7/7 seeds under Normal traffic, versus 2/7, 4/7, and 4/7 under Light, Peak, and Surge. Discrete-state audits characterize coverage gaps and structural reachability constraints. IoEV-MARL supports offline decision-learning research without establishing closed-loop performance gains.
evidence_items.title: IoEV-MARL: A Reproducible Offline Dataset and Benchmark for Electric Vehicle Charging Coordination Under Centralized and Decentralized Training

evidence_items.summary: In this paper, we introduce $\Delta\tau$-Bench, an executable agent benchmark that models the structural evolution of large tool ecosystems. In $\Delta\tau$-Bench, independently evolving services continually reshape how tasks can be accomplished: familiar tools may disappear or be replaced, while more efficient alternatives emerge amid overlapping functionality and noisy documentation. Against this moving capability frontier, we evaluate whether agents can proactively discover efficient tool-use paths and promptly revise their accumulated procedural knowledge, bringing together demands that existing benchmarks fail to examine. $\Delta\tau$-Bench comprises 1,588 validated multi-turn tasks across 42 domains and six successive ecosystem states generated through capability-preserving transformations. Our evaluation shows that even the strongest evaluated model or harness achieves only 42.3% task success, while initial gains from existing skill-learning methods can not consistently translate into better adaptation as the ecosystem evolves. These findings motivate Steward, an ecosystem manager that jointly manages tools and procedural knowledge through incremental skill maintenance and dynamic provisioning during task execution. Experiments show that Steward sustains higher task success across ecosystem changes with lower skill-maintenance overhead, while improving both recovery from disrupted workflows and adoption of more efficient alternatives.
evidence_items.title: $\Delta\tau$-Bench: Pushing Agents Toward a Moving Capability

evidence_items.summary: This record contains the THReD Agent Benchmark: the tasks, code and results used to evaluate the AI agent in THReD, a system that turns electronic health record (EHR) extracts into AI-ready datasets through a chat assistant that proposes preprocessing steps for the user to confirm. The benchmark comprises 141 preprocessing tasks in seven categories: single-tool, multi-step, goal-level, failure and recovery, requests where the agent should not act, robustness to schema variation, and prompt injection through the data. Each task has an expert reference pipeline and outcome checks evaluated on synthetic EHR tables; no patient data is used or sent to a model. Four configurations, from no context to the full deployed context, were each run five times with Claude Haiku 5.5 (2,550 episodes), with 95% confidence intervals from a cluster bootstrap over task templates. With the deployed configuration, the agent completed 92.7% of tasks on the first answer (95% CI 88.1–96.4%) and 95.6% within three turns, with tool-selection F1 0.926, argument accuracy 0.905, outcome agreement with the expert pipelines of 0.913 (row F1) and 3.3% invalid tool calls. It abstained correctly on every should-not-act request, recovered from every injected tool fault, handled every schema variation, and never followed an instruction planted in the data. Without a data profile, first-attempt completion fell to 58.0%. Contents: BENCHMARK REPORT.md: design, results, failure analysis, observations and limitations benchmark/results/: all metrics with confidence intervals, one row per episode, and the failed episodes benchmark/: the harness, scoring, outcome checks, task definitions, synthetic-data generator and privacy audit The scripts drive THReD's own agent and run from within the THReD source tree.

evidence_items.summary: Skill learning enables web agents to reuse prior experience for long-horizon interactive tasks. However, learned skills are typically evaluated in closed environments, overlooking the fact that real-world web deployment involves continuous shifts in invocation context, perceptual grounding, and execution feasibility. To this end, we introduce SkillShift-Bench, the first benchmark for evaluating skill learning with controlled open-environment shifts. SkillShift-Bench simulates Contextual Shift, Perceptual Shift, and Execution Shift across three self-hosted web systems, and evaluates agents with diagnostics covering task success, interaction cost, skill use, and skill failure. Comprehensive experiments reveal systematic robustness degradation under controlled shifts, characterized by lower success rates, higher interaction costs, and more frequent skill failures, with Execution Shift exerting the strongest pressure. We further formulate shifted skill execution as a nonstationary local executability problem and provide both a dynamic-regret analysis and a practical test-time adaptation method, demonstrating the feasibility of improving learned-skill execution without relearning the skill library. Code, tasks, environments, documentation, and the leaderboard are available at https://skillshift-bench.github.io/.
evidence_items.title: SkillShift-Bench: Benchmarking Skill Learning under Environment Evolution for Web Agents

evidence_items.summary: We introduce WorldOracle, a benchmark specifically designed to evaluate action-conditioned world models (ACWMs) against paired real-world executions. Given the same initial observation and low-level action sequence, WorldOracle asks whether a predicted rollout reproduces what happens in the real world, including physical consequences and task-state transitions. We evaluate models along four complementary dimensions: physical state correctness, interaction spatial alignment, key interaction area fidelity, and multi-view action coherence. To support this evaluation, we curate real-world training and evaluation suites that cover different interaction dynamics and embodiments. The evaluation suite contains long, multi-segment episodes with both successful and failed executions, enabling evaluation across varied action outcomes and behavior distributions. Experiments on seven representative ACWMs reveal distinct model strengths and failure modes. WorldOracle provides a systematic foundation for measuring and advancing action-conditioned world modeling for manipulation. We release the datasets, evaluation code, and leaderboard: https://worldoracle-benchmark.github.io/.
evidence_items.title: WorldOracle: Benchmarking Action-Conditioned World Models against Real-World Executions

evidence_items.summary: Real conversations between fraudsters and their targets are among the most informative artifacts for studying telephone scams, yet also the scarcest: passive honeypots overwhelmingly capture automated messages and hang-ups, large-scale studies characterize call metadata rather than dialogue, and manual scam-baiting does not scale. We present a dataset of real scam-call conversations collected by an active voice-agent honeypot. Dedicated numbers are seeded into the lead-generation channels fraud operations harvest; inbound callers are answered by a low-latency conversational agent that adopts a plausible target persona and sustains the interaction while every call is recorded, transcribed, and automatically labeled. Over an initial 53-day window we captured 10,015 inbound scam and spam calls (6,601 with two or more turns): roughly 895 hours of audio and 328,869 transcribed turns from 5,665 distinct originating numbers. Under a holistic classifier the substantive calls are predominantly predatory-but-legal lead generation ("spam", about three in five), while about one in seven is an outright "scam" (949 in this snapshot). Each call carries a turn-level transcript, three-channel audio, per-turn latency telemetry, and layers of automatic labels, including a holistic scam/spam/legitimate judgment corroborated by independent human review (75% agreement on the binary decision). We describe the collection system, the record structure, and technical validation of the corpus's realism and label quality, including that the agent is recognized as non-human in only about 5% of engaged calls. We also benchmark established scam-detection methods, where detectors trained on published synthetic dialogue collapse in precision on real traffic.
evidence_items.title: A Corpus of Real Scam- and Spam-Call Conversations from an Active Voice-Agent Honeypot

evidence_items.summary: Recent AI systems have achieved strong results on a wide range of benchmarks, yet these gains have not translated into economically meaningful deployment across many professional domains. We argue that this gap is largely an evaluation problem: widely used benchmarks lack sustained performance measurement on real and economically valuable workflows. This paper introduces Agents' Last Exam (ALE), a benchmark designed to evaluate AI agents on long horizon, economically valuable, real world tasks with verifiable outcomes. Developed in collaboration with 250+ industry experts, ALE covers non-physical industries defined with reference to O*NET / SOC 2018 (the U.S. federal occupational taxonomy). It is organized around a task taxonomy with 55 sub fields grouped into 13 industry clusters covering 1K+ tasks. Current results show that the hardest tier remains far from saturated: across mainstream harness and backbone configurations, the average full pass rate is below 1%. ALE is designed as a living benchmark: its task pool grows continuously as new workflows and industries are onboarded. More broadly, ALE is intended not merely as another leaderboard, but as an instrument for closing the gap between benchmark success and GDP relevant impact.
evidence_items.title: Agents' Last Exam

evidence_items.summary: Drone communication networks increasingly support surveillance, logistics, disaster response, and tactical coordination, where a compromised link can quickly affect mission safety. Intrusion detection systems (IDSs) in such settings are challenging because attack evidence is distributed across drones and edge nodes, while centralizing raw data adds delay, bandwidth cost, and privacy exposure. Federated learning (FL) offers a natural way to train IDS models without moving raw data; however, conventional FL still gives limited attention to mobility-sensitive link quality, resource heterogeneity, trust, and security-rule consistency when deciding which client updates should influence the global detector. This paper proposes CMA-FL, a cognitive multi-agent assisted FL framework for resource-aware intrusion detection in drone communication networks. Each selected drone-edge client trains a long short-term memory (LSTM)-based temporal detector, while task-specific client-side agents evaluate signal/data quality, security-rule consistency, resource state, local training behavior, and update utility. Server-side trust, client-selection, weighting, aggregation, and explanation agents then govern participation and reliability-weighted aggregation. On the evaluated public drone-communication benchmark, CMA-FL achieves 99.6% accuracy with 0.99 precision, recall, and F1-score and reduces response time by more than 80% relative to the evaluated FL, edge-cloud, and cloud-only alternatives. These results characterize the controlled benchmark setting, generalization to independently collected flight traces, stronger non-IID partitions, and adversarial clients remains to be established.
evidence_items.title: Poster: CMA-FL: Cognitive Multi-Agent Federated Learning for Resource-Aware Drone Communication Attack Detection

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly support science, but they can also convert hazardous scientific knowledge into actionable misuse guidance. Existing benchmarks often rely on templated queries disconnected from real-world hazards, and employ LLM-as-a-Judge paradigms without domain grounding. To address this, we introduce SciHazard, a real-world-grounded benchmark for scientific risks and a dataset agnostic evaluation framework for measuring harmfulness. SciHazard contains 2400 hazardous questions and 600 oversafety questions across 12 disciplines, with both queries grounded in regulated entities and documented failure scenarios. To compute \textsc{DeHarm-Score} , we develop a decomposed evaluating procedure that combines query hazard severity, refusal behavior, and response-level risk. For non-refused responses, it further decomposes response-level harm into \textsc{Executability}, quantified via dynamic checklists with importance weighting, and \textsc{Net-new risk}, assessed through retrieval-augmented claim extraction and synthesis-barrier verification. An expert-validation study shows that \textsc{DeHarm-Score} improves agreement with expert annotations by 90.17\% over the strongest baseline. We benchmark 31 frontier LLMs and deep research agents in an extensive scientific safety evaluation. Notably, deep research agents yield 32.3\% higher mean \textsc{DeHarm-Score} than standard LLMs, exposing autonomous agents as a critical blind spot in current safety defenses. Code and dataset are available at https://github.com/AI45Lab/DeepSafe-Sci.
evidence_items.title: DeepSafe-SciHazard: A Benchmark for Measuring Scientific Safety Risks with Decomposed Harm Scoring

evidence_items.summary: Diffusion video models produce striking clips, but they cannot reliably render an exact formula, a correct chart, a ruleconsistent game or narration synchronized to on-screen events. A different route is emerging: multimodal agents that write code to render every frame and synthesize every sound. We introduce VibeVideoBench, a benchmark for evaluating agents on code-driven video generation. Its 239 self-contained tasks in English and Chinese span 12 categories, from data stories and music-driven pieces to classroom lessons and paper explainers; each asks an agent, running in its native harness inside a sandbox, to deliver a finished MP4 with sound within one hour. Evaluation is hierarchical and evidence-based: program checks of the delivery spec, about 13k task-specific rubric checks traced to the requirements they enforce, and five quality dimensions anchored per task, judged by three VLM judge panels and validated with blind human preferences. Across nine frontier agent systems and 2,151 scored rollouts, the benchmark is far from solved: GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 lead clearly, yet even the best system fails a core requirement on about a quarter of tasks. Whether a video arrives at all matters as much as its quality, and three quarters of the lost videos are final renders started too late, run too slowly or never started. The judges agree with each other and with human preferences on system rankings, but only moderately on individual videos.
evidence_items.title: VibeVideoBench:Evaluating Multimodal Agents on Code-Driven Video Generation

evidence_items.summary: Visual Place Recognition (VPR) is an important means for loop closure detection in visual Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM). While state-of-the-art VPR and SLAM approaches excel in urban and feature-rich natural environments, the vast and feature-poor environments of extraterrestrial surfaces like on the Moon or Mars pose severe challenges for existing approaches. This paper presents a novel benchmark, VPR-Space, to evaluate VPR capabilities on extraterrestrial surfaces. There are three contributions: (1) We collected sixteen VPR database-query datasets based on existing data from Space Analog Domains (SAD), terrestrial environments that resemble properties of the Moon or Mars. The collection includes a range of challenges regarding environment, viewpoint change, and illumination conditions. (2) To address the ill-posed nature of VPR, we propose a novel approach to generate the ground-truth information in VPR benchmarks. Instead of defining that a query and datbase image show the same place if and only if their camera poses are within fixed position and viewing direction thresholds, we propose to make the decision dependent on whether the match would be valuable in the downstream SLAM task. To avoid the overhead and restrictions of evaluating VPR in-the-loop within SLAM systems, we provide VPR ground-truth (GT) matrices based on the performance of an ensemble of state-of-the-art Relative Pose Estimators (RPE). Under this GT we require a VPR method to identify exactly those image pairs for which a subsequently applied RPE is expected to provide a valuable pose estimate in a SLAM context. (3) We evaluated nine state-of-the-art VPR approaches. The results show considerable room for improvement and indicate directions for future research. We provide a pre-release version of the dataset on github: $\texttt{https://github.com/rfechner/VPR-Space}$
evidence_items.title: VPR-Space: A Benchmark for Visual Place Recognition in Space Analog Domains

evidence_items.summary: In high-stakes domains such as finance, critical information evolves through multi-party interaction. Recovering these changes and their sources is fundamental to reliable speech understanding. Existing speech benchmarks focus on transcription, local understanding, and turn-level state prediction, leaving joint decision evolution across speakers insufficiently evaluated. We introduce DecisionTraceBench, a speech state-tracking benchmark for Decision-Critical Information State Tracking (DCIST). It jointly evaluates decision event sequences, speaker attribution, scope, and temporal evidence, using trajectory-level F1 to measure complete event-chain recovery. Our dataset comprises Chinese financial dialogues involving two to four speakers, with 100.39 hours of synthetic audio and 8.61 hours of human-performed recordings. On a fixed cohort of human-performed recordings, five cascaded systems and two direct-audio models achieve DCIST scores of 5.73% to 21.35%. Ablations with speaker-labeled reference scripts and no temporal localization requirements yield a maximum score of only 38.72%. Audio perturbation experiments further show that overall transcription error rates do not adequately reflect complete trajectory recovery. These findings reveal limitations in jointly understanding information provenance and state evolution, providing a benchmark for evaluating decision-process understanding and decision traceability in high-stakes speech applications.
evidence_items.title: DecisionTraceBench: Tracking Decision-Critical Information in Multi-Party Spoken Conversations

evidence_items.summary: An agent that truly knows and acts on behalf of its user has been a long-standing promise of AI assistants. Computer-use agents bring this promise within reach by capably executing fully specified tasks across apps. However, real-world user requests are often underspecified. To act correctly for the particular user, an agent must infer some missing information from the user's activity history and ask for other information that only the user can provide, without making unsupported assumptions or burdening the user with unnecessary questions. We present iPrefBench, a benchmark for evaluating the infer and ask capabilities of personal mobile-use agents in an executable iOS environment with an interactive simulated user. Grounded in a coherent persona with 3,051 past activity events, iPrefBench comprises 130 underspecified user tasks across 26 apps. Each omitted user-dependent requirement is, by construction, either history-inferable or ask-only. iPrefBench evaluates personalized mobile agents on both whether agents complete tasks correctly for the user (i.e., personalized task completion) and whether they seek user input when necessary (i.e., user-agent interaction). Evaluation of 7 frontier agents reveals a substantial gap between execution and personalization. Agents achieve high action completion scores (up to 91.6%) but low full task success (up to 47.7%) because personalization lags behind. They especially struggle with ask-only information, failing to request enough necessary information. Our findings highlight a challenge for personalized agents in knowing what to infer and when to ask. We hope that iPrefBench can serve as a valuable testbed for building agents that know their user and work with them.
evidence_items.title: iPrefBench: A User-Centric Benchmark for Personalized Mobile Use Agents

evidence_items.summary: Driving video captured through a windshield violates the world-space consistency assumed by 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS): the road scene exhibits parallax while cabin reflections remain attached to the camera, causing standard 3DGS to embed reflected content into the reconstructed scene. We introduce RIDE-Splat, a pipeline for reflection-free 3D reconstruction from posed driving video without clean images, reflection masks, or pretrained networks. RIDE-Splat assigns world-consistent transmission through the windshield to a 3DGS scene and the dominant camera-attached reflection to one shared, signed RGB image. It builds the clean reconstruction in two passes. First, it learns the 3D geometry and the signed reflection image, representing both added radiance and transmission attenuation. Then, it uses the reflection-removed training images to fit a clean 3DGS model. At inference, the reflection image is discarded, preserving the standard 3DGS rendering path. We also introduce the RIDE-Splat Dataset, the first 3D reconstruction benchmark for reflection removal from driving video -- with real driving scenes, physical windshield reflections in training views, and separately captured non-reflective evaluation images. Across the RIDE-Splat Dataset, XLD, and Wayve, RIDE-Splat outperforms 3DGS, DC-Gaussian, and RobustSplat on all nine aggregate metrics, improving PSNR by up to 3.59 dB and reducing LPIPS by up to 0.0876. We achieve the highest metrics in 38 out of 42 per-scene comparisons and removes windshield reflections that remain visible in the baselines while preserving the transmitted scene.
evidence_items.title: RIDE-Splat: Reflection Removal for In-the-Wild Driving Environments

evidence_items.summary: Broken access control (BAC) ranks among the most severe web-application vulnerability classes, yet its automated repair remains largely unexplored. Unlike memory-safety vulnerabilities, BAC is a logic vulnerability whose repair demands a deep understanding of an application's access-control model and business semantics, which traditional automated vulnerability repair techniques handle poorly. Large language models (LLMs) open a promising avenue for this problem, but no standard benchmark exists for studying how well they repair BAC vulnerabilities. We construct BAC-Bench, the first benchmark for BAC repair, consisting of 46 real-world BAC vulnerabilities drawn from six widely used web applications spanning four programming languages. Each vulnerability is equipped with a sandboxed runtime environment, a PoC validation program and a functional test program. We further propose a BAC repair-strategy framework that characterizes any BAC patch along four dimensions, Position, Coverage, Mechanism, and Content. Evaluating eight base LLMs and two commercial LLM agents on BAC-Bench, we find that single-turn base LLMs repair 37.68% of the vulnerabilities on average, while two minimal scaffolds, Apply-Feedback and Navigate-and-Locate, raise this average to 66.03%, with the best base LLM reaching 75.36%, close to the 78.99% of the best agent. Notably, some LLM-generated patches surpass the official patches, and one incidentally closed a zero-day vulnerability that had lain dormant for three years. Our findings delineate the current capability boundary of LLM-based BAC repair and offer guidance toward its practical adoption.
evidence_items.title: Repairing Broken Access Control in Web Applications with LLMs: An Empirical Benchmark Study

evidence_items.summary: We propose a novel method for robust point cloud registration with only one tunable parameter. Our method, dubbed TLP, uses truncated $L_p$ functions with different values of $p$ to assign priority scores to correspondences, select the hypothesis, and refine the final model. By leveraging the robustness of truncated functions, TLP effectively handles the high outlier rates commonly encountered in real-world 3D feature matching. We also exploit GPU parallelization to evaluate hypotheses efficiently, enabling registration from thousands of correspondences in under a second on average. With only one tunable parameter, our method offers greater practicality than multi-parameter methods that require dataset-specific tuning of several parameters. Evaluations on public benchmark datasets demonstrate that TLP achieves higher accuracy than state-of-the-art single-parameter methods. Furthermore, it outperforms two widely used multi-parameter methods on three of the four evaluated datasets while maintaining competitive runtime.
evidence_items.title: Robust Single-Parameter Point Cloud Registration using Truncated Lp Functions

evidence_items.summary: Modern surgical AI increasingly requires multimodal understanding rather than isolated perception, yet existing datasets remain largely limited to single-task supervision such as recognition or templated question answering. Current medical VQA resources often rely on synthetic templates, lack natural descriptive supervision, or provide sparse annotations that hinder reasoning about spatial relations and procedural context. We introduce MIS-VQA, a surgical vision-language dataset generated through an annotation-driven pipeline that converts heterogeneous surgical annotations into structured textual scene representations. Using EndoVis18 and CholecT50, we transform phase, instrument, interaction, triplet, and segmentation labels into unified contexts that guide large language models to generate clinically coherent question-answer pairs. MIS-VQA supports four response types-concise and detailed descriptions, perception-level grounding, and multi-step reasoning-enabling hierarchical evaluation from atomic visual grounding to compositional reasoning. To address annotation sparsity, we incorporate confidence-filtered segmentation and cross-annotation consistency checks, enabling spatially grounded supervision at scale. MIS-VQA establishes a unified benchmark for surgical vision-language understanding with spatial supervision and multi-tier reasoning evaluation. To demonstrate its utility, we introduce LLaVA-SurgXpert, a family of surgical vision-language models with visual encoders to analyze how visual representations influence multimodal reasoning. Experiments show consistent improvements over existing surgical VQA baselines while revealing capability gaps between perceptual grounding and higher-level reasoning hidden in prior benchmarks.
evidence_items.title: MIS-VQA: An Annotation-Driven Surgical Vision-Language Dataset for Complex Surgical Understanding

evidence_items.summary: Language-model agents must adapt as users revise their requirements and priorities during complex tasks. We introduce IntentDelta, a human-constructed multi-turn benchmark with 638 trajectories and 3,766 turns across WebShop and TravelPlanner. Each turn pairs a user utterance with a cumulative intention state and human reference actions. The trajectories are cross-verified and cover feasibility- and preference-driven changes in constraints and priorities. We evaluate eleven agents on intention recovery and action quality. Average Intention Recovery is 33.1\% in TravelPlanner and 44.7\% in WebShop, while average Action Score is 31.6% and 41.0%, respectively. Agents struggle to preserve earlier requirements and distinguish soft preferences from must-have constraints. Correct intention recovery also does not guarantee successful execution, highlighting challenges in translating evolving user intentions into actions.
evidence_items.title: IntentDelta: A Human-Constructed Benchmark for Evolving User Intent

evidence_items.summary: LLM agents have been increasingly adopted for security-focused code review, but existing benchmarks mostly derive the reviewed changes from their later fixes instead of the real-world bug-introducing commits. In this paper, we present SecPRBench, the first comprehensive benchmark for evaluating agentic security review on validated real-world code changes. More specifically, we have built an automated agentic pipeline to autonomously harvest, build, and validate massive real-world bug-introducing commits for popular software systems. To ensure precise evaluation, we also adopt LLM-as-a-judge to credit the findings matching ground-truth vulnerabilities. To date, we have collected 265 tasks from nine critical systems, including Firefox, V8, and OpenSSL with millions of lines of code. Across eight frontier models, recall ranges from 32.5% to 78.1%, with Grok 4.6 and GPT-6 sol ranking at the top. Our study also shows that most misses are not simply oversights: in 68% of them, the agent reports on a file that holds the flaw but argues for a different mechanism. Security-focused harnesses also behave differently: OpenAI's Codex Security lowers recall by 8.3 points, mostly by abstaining, while Anthropic's Defending Code harness raises it by 7.7 points, at a higher cost.
evidence_items.title: Can Agentic Code Review Catch Vulnerabilities Before They Are Merged?

evidence_items.summary: Speaking-style captioning (SSC) aims to generate natural language descriptions of how speech is delivered, capturing paralinguistic attributes such as vocal timbre, prosody, and expressivity. Many downstream applications, including conversational AI agents, controllable speech generation, and large-scale audio annotation, require dimension-specific style captions that describe targeted aspects of speech (e.g., speaker traits, emotion, or delivery style), rather than a single undifferentiated description. However, existing work lacks a unified formulation for controllable speaking-style captioning. We address this gap by formulating SSC as an instruction-following audio-language task, where explicit instructions specify the speaking-style dimensions to be described. We introduce StyleInstructCaps, the first standardized benchmark for controllable speaking-style captioning in audio-language models. StyleInstructCaps provides a dataset and evaluation framework that measures metadata groundedness, hallucination, instruction-following ability, generalization to unseen instructions and audio datasets, and speaker-style consistency. Across nine state-of-the-art audio-language models, we find that strong instruction-following ability does not necessarily imply grounded speaking-style understanding, and that SSC-specific instruction-diverse training substantially improves groundedness, controllability, and speaker consistency.
evidence_items.title: A Benchmark for Controllable Speaking-Style Captioning in Audio-Language Models

evidence_items.summary: GUI grounding benchmarks ask whether an agent can localize a target that is already visible in a static screenshot. Real interfaces often violate this assumption: a target may be off-screen, appear only after a state change or hover, remain occluded, or become actionable after a delay. This leaves the ability to recover target visibility unevaluated. To measure this reveal step, we introduce Interactive GUI Grounding (IGG), a benchmark in which an agent must first make the target visible through interaction and then click it. IGG contains 601 tasks across 16 controllable GUI environments and seven visibility-constraint sub-types, with a compact action space of scrolling, moving, dragging, waiting, and clicking. In our human study, participants achieve 94.6% accuracy, while GPT-5.5 reaches 79.4% and the strongest evaluated open-source VLM reaches only 31.6%. To identify the source of this gap, we conduct two controlled interventions. Telling Qwen3-VL which interaction to perform raises its accuracy only from 30.8% to 33.9%, whereas performing the interaction for the model raises it to 81.9%. The bottleneck is executing the reveal interaction, not recognizing the target once it is exposed. We further show that this capability is learnable, demonstrating that visibility recovery can be strengthened consistently across model families.
evidence_items.title: IGG: A Benchmark for Interactive GUI Grounding under Visibility Constraints

evidence_items.summary: LLM agents combine models with execution harnesses, so agentic benchmark performance reflects their joint behavior. We argue that harnesses should therefore be evaluated through their interactions with underlying models. We develop a framework combining five complementary measures: (i) Valid Completion Rate (VCR), how reliably agents finish normally and deliver evaluable results, irrespective of task correctness; (ii) Model-Harness Fit, how well a harness supports task achievement through valid completion for a given model; (iii) Cross-Model Fit, a harness's overall suitability across evaluated models; (iv) Interaction Residuals, pairing-specific execution strengths and weaknesses hidden by component-level summaries; and (v) Token Load, the token demands of agent execution, including failed attempts. We evaluate four general-purpose harnesses (OpenCode, Codex CLI, Pi CLI, and DeepAgents) with four core models, plus two fixed native model-harness systems, on six benchmarks covering context management, tool use, long-context planning, multimodal interaction, and artifact handoff. Including native references and stress conditions, 111 evaluation settings yield 52,168 trajectories. Harness rankings vary across models and benchmarks; task performance and valid completion can favor different pairings, and similar task scores can accompany distinct execution profiles. OpenCode ranks first in cross-model performance, while DeepSeek V4 Flash Preview maintains consistently high Mean VCR across harnesses on the shared four-benchmark panel. These findings support evaluating model-harness interactions, training transferable harness-use capabilities in models, and harness designs adapted to the model and task.
evidence_items.title: When Agents Fail: Model or Harness--Who's to Blame?

evidence_items.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly execute tasks asynchronously: a main agent continues working while its subagents run, and the task state may change before their results arrive. The main agent must decide which work to update or preserve and which checks to repeat, while avoiding prohibited changes. Final task success alone does not reveal whether these results were handled correctly, and natural asynchronous arrivals are hard to reproduce. We introduce Async-RBench, a benchmark for asynchronous task execution in LLM agents, with 200 executable tasks covering eight scenarios. A scenario controller regulates result delivery using predefined task-state conditions, while an Event Response Contract (ERC) specifies what each response must change, preserve, avoid, and re-verify. The Dynamic Replanning Score (DRS) weights the response process and outcome equally and is reported separately from task success. We evaluate nine agents and find DRS scores of 19.2 to 45.1, with the lowest scores on duplicate reports and subagent failures. Under our execution protocol, all nine agents obtain lower task success with asynchronous than with batched delivery (26.0% vs. 29.7% on average). For three agents, prompting the main agent to rebuild its plan after every result improves DRS by only 2.6 to 3.5 points. Together, these findings highlight the challenges of reliable asynchronous task execution and the need to evaluate how agents handle incoming results alongside end-to-end task success.
evidence_items.title: Async-RBench: Benchmarking Asynchronous Task Execution in LLM Agents

evidence_items.summary: In unsupervised multivariate time series anomaly detection (MTSAD), local variation can inflate reconstruction and forecasting errors, making observation-space discrepancy an unreliable indicator of abnormal system behavior. Since latent-space scoring can mitigate this limitation, we reframe one-class MTSAD as current-point system-state compatibility estimation and propose TENET, the Time-point Encoding Network for Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection. We define the current-point system state as a latent representation of the target time point, constructed from variable-level temporal context in the input window. TENET constructs this state through a temporal layer that retrieves window context relative to the current point, encodes time with current-point-centered embeddings, and adaptively mixes the retrieved context with the current representation. With this design, TENET treats the input window not as the object to reconstruct, forecast, summarize, or score, but as context for constructing a latent representation evaluated with a fixed standard-normal negative log-likelihood score. Across benchmark datasets, TENET achieves state-of-the-art performance. Additional experiments further show that TENET remains effective under alternative one-class objectives and outperforms substitutions based on generic sequence encoders, suggesting that its advantage comes from decision-aligned representation construction rather than from a specialized scoring rule. These results indicate that one-class MTSAD can be strong when the latent representation is designed around the current time point.
evidence_items.title: TENET: Time-point Encoding Network for Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection

evidence_items.summary: Multi-stage analytical tasks require LLM agents to use intermediate evidence to decide whether to continue, redirect or stop. Self-reflection, in which an agent critiques its output, is widely studied, yet a critique does not show whether evidence changed the next action. We call that capability self-restraint. Existing agent benchmarks largely measure task completion or output quality and leave it untested. DMAIC-Bench evaluates it with 97 seeded tasks across 15 industrial cases in four sectors, built around Lean Six Sigma's explicit statistical prerequisites. Paired counterfactual variants require opposite actions at the same workflow position, distinguishing warranted restraint from indiscriminate stopping. We assess execution traces with a private scorer and final claims through independent expert review. Across 13 models from six providers, execution-level routing accuracy averages 92% on matched GO decisions and 19% on NO-GO decisions, counting any forbidden downstream computation as a route error. Execution traces show agents reporting correct diagnostics before performing analyses that those results disallow. Separately, blinded expert review of the 11 audited agents estimates that reports act on invalid evidence at 47% of reached NO-GO decisions, with an interval from 31% to 61%. Explicit stopping permission helps some models without consistently restoring correct decisions at both GO and NO-GO forks. Sixteen life-sciences tasks in bulk ribonucleic acid sequencing (RNA-seq) and case-control genome-wide association studies (GWAS) show that the same framework can evaluate evidence-dependent decisions beyond industrial workflows. Project code and data are available at: https://github.com/psptpx/DMAIC-Bench-public.
evidence_items.title: DMAIC-Bench: From Self-Reflection to Self-Restraint for Agents in Multi-Stage Analytical Tasks

evidence_items.summary: Screen Tables and Substrate Scopes are information-dense figures widely used in synthetic chemistry literature, yet automated extraction of structured reaction data from them remains challenging. We introduce RxnExBench, a multimodal benchmark for fine-grained reaction-level evaluation. Built from high-impact chemistry journals, it contains 3,565 expert-annotated reactions and 2,361 molecular structures. The dataset adopts a unified schema with 15 reaction roles and 26 core fields, supporting downstream AI-for-Chemistry tasks such as retrosynthetic planning, yield prediction, and reaction condition recommendation. RxnExBench further provides a reasoning-driven difficulty taxonomy, a modular annotation pipeline, and the Oracle-MolRec protocol, which disentangles molecular recognition from higher-level reasoning. Evaluation of 9 state-of-the-art VLMs shows that performance degrades substantially as schema complexity and reasoning demands increase. Under the Oracle-MolRec setting, results further reveal that accurate molecular recognition alone is insufficient, with multimodal integration and chemistry-aware reasoning remaining the primary bottlenecks. We release all data and code to facilitate future research in chemistry-aware multimodal understanding and AI-for-Chemistry dataset construction. The dataset and code will be released at https://github.com/opendatalab/RxnExBench.
evidence_items.title: RxnExBench: Benchmarking Vision-Language Models for Structured Chemical Reaction Extraction from Scientific Literature

evidence_items.summary: Repository-level coding benchmarks largely assume that tasks and environments remain unchanged throughout execution. In software development, code, dependencies, runtime state, and requirements can change while an agent is still working. We introduce SWE-Shift, a benchmark for evaluating coding agents under such mid-execution changes. From the same saved history and workspace, a Clean continuation proceeds without intervention, while a matched Shifted continuation receives a task-relevant update. Success requires completing the current task, preserving still-valid work, and satisfying the applicable state and evidence checks. The benchmark contains 120 scenarios across 12 change families, each evaluated at nine scheduled intervention positions. We evaluate 17 coding-agent systems, all of which have lower Shifted than Clean success. GPT-6 Astra drops from 67.35% to 24.79%, with 20.34% paired success. Tool/session changes and stale evidence yield zero paired success across all systems. Late-position paired success is lower for some systems and higher for others. These results show that success on the unchanged task can coexist with failures to preserve work, recover state, or refresh evidence after an update.
evidence_items.title: SWE-Shift: Evaluating Coding Agents in Evolving Workspaces

evidence_items.summary: Vision language models (VLMs) have been increasingly adopted in consumer smart-home camera systems to interpret recorded videos and provide insights. However, video clips captured from smart-home cameras are different from curated web videos dominating existing VLM benchmarks. Smart-home video clips often do not contain subtitles or narration and are captured from different viewing angles, under various lighting conditions, and in diverse scenarios. However, the capabilities of the model in this domain, under sparse visual signals and limited context, are not fully assessed by existing VLM benchmarks. To close this gap, we introduce OpenHome, a visual-only, four-option multiple-choice benchmark for evaluating smart-home video understanding. It contains 2,254 questions on 1,118 real-world video clips and organizes 10 tasks into three capability levels. Perception evaluates visible content, Reasoning evaluates causal, spatial, and temporal relationships, and Insight evaluates subject intent, supporting evidence and appropriate homeowner responses. Based on the dataset, we describe the task design, data pipeline and evaluation protocol, and report results for 32 closed-source and open-weight VLMs. The best model, Gemini 4 Argon, reaches 81.2% overall accuracy. Frontier closed-source models outperform open-weight models on every level. The best closed-source model leads the best open-weight model by 16.3% on Perception, 22.4% on Reasoning and 37.4% on Insight.
evidence_items.title: OpenHome: From Perception to Insight in Smart-Home Camera Videos

evidence_items.summary: In complex embodied visual reasoning scenarios, an agent often has only a limited field of view, and the evidence needed to answer a question may be distributed across time, viewpoint, and interacting objects. A model may therefore give a plausible answer without ever observing the relevant object, time, or view that supports it. Current visual reasoning benchmarks largely evaluate passive observations and final answers, overlooking settings that require active reasoning and evidence acquisition. We introduce JRDB-AVR, a benchmark derived from existing real-world JRDB robotics data through a structured question-generation engine that turns this gap into an explicit evaluation: an embodied agentic system receives a visual reasoning question, requests bounded observations by timestamp and viewing angle, and is evaluated on both the final answer and the grounded visual evidence supporting it. The benchmark contains diverse questions over multiple real-world environments involving temporal search, viewpoint selection, and human-oriented compositional reasoning. We also introduce JRDB-AVR-Agent, a reference active reasoning agentic method that maintains an explicit observation-grounded graph-based world model and answers through solving. Experiments reveal a substantial gap between answer accuracy and evidence accuracy in current baselines, showing that current VLMs can produce unsupported correct answers and that active evidence-aware evaluation is necessary for embodied visual reasoning. Code and benchmark are available at https://github.com/ControlNet/JRDB-AVR.
evidence_items.title: JRDB-AVR: An Active Visual Reasoning Benchmark for Embodied Agents in Real-World Environments

evidence_items.summary: This article describes an open image dataset for developing and evaluating active-fire segmentation methods in satellite imagery. The dataset contains 2,148 image-mask pairs from 25 California wildfires, with acquisitions spanning July 2020 to August 2026. Each image is a 512x512-pixel, three-channel composite derived from Sentinel-2 Level-2A bands B12, B11 and B8A at 20 m spatial sampling. A fixed linear rendering is applied throughout the dataset. Corresponding masks distinguish background, SWIR-rule active fire and invalid observations. The masks were generated from shortwave-infrared brightness and near-infrared contrast, followed by constrained neighborhood growth. The release includes chip-level metadata and an incident-disjoint partition containing 18 training, three validation and four test fires. Among the image pairs, 841 contain active-fire labels; these labels occupy 0.0766% of all grid cells. A mask-blind analyst review covers 233 test chips and provides a separate assessment of the rule-generated labels at chip and connected-component levels. Reference training and evaluation code accompanies the data, including a ResNet-34 U-Net implementation with validation-based checkpoint and threshold selection. The archived images, masks, metadata and review annotations support research on rare-class segmentation, learning from algorithmic labels and transfer across fire incidents. The versioned dataset is deposited on Zenodo, with preparation and reuse software maintained in a public GitHub repository.
evidence_items.title: A Sentinel-2 benchmark dataset for deep-learning active-fire segmentation across 25 California wildfires, July 2020-August 2026

evidence_items.summary: As AI agents become increasingly capable of complex, long-horizon reasoning, rigorous evaluation is essential for measuring progress toward real-world healthcare applications. However, existing healthcare benchmarks are often static or narrow in clinical scope, motivating broader evaluation of agents acting on raw patient data. We introduce HealthAgentBench, a suite of 75 agentic healthcare tasks across 9 categories each with its unique environment. The benchmark suite spans diagnosis, specimen assessment, research, and data management workflows and a broad range of modalities. Each task is designed to replicate an end-to-end clinical workflow: given task instructions and supporting resources, an agent must explore raw healthcare data, operate within a complex environment, and execute multi-step solutions that go beyond naive prompting, such as querying large clinical databases or interpreting gigapixel pathology images. All tasks are scored using binary success criteria derived from reference labels, executable rules, or computational baselines. We evaluate six agents (three GPT models through Codex and three Claude models through Claude Code) with one scored attempt per task (450 evaluations). Overall success ranges from 32.0% to 57.3%; Claude Code Opus-5.5 leads with a 57.3% success rate, followed by GPT-6-astra and Sonnet-5.5 at 50.7% each. Performance varies substantially by category with specialized imaging modalities such as CT and MRI being especially difficult. HealthAgentBench provides a challenging and realistic benchmark with substantial room for future progress. We release our benchmark athttps://github.com/microsoft/HealthAgentBench.
evidence_items.title: HealthAgentBench: A Unified Benchmark Suite of Realistic Agentic Healthcare Environments for Challenging Frontier AI Agents

evidence_items.summary: 54 Python snippets covering nine cryptographic misuse classes (36 vulnerable, 18 matched secure controls), a self-contained harness that queries local Ollama models with a fixed verdict-only prompt, and 1,890 recorded trials across seven open code models (qwen2.5-coder 0.5B to 14B, deepseek-coder 6.7B, codellama 7B). Includes an analysis script that reproduces per-model and per-class detection rates with Wilson 95% confidence intervals. v1.0.1 corrects the documentation: the harness sets no decoding options, so models ran at Ollama default sampling (v1.0.0 README wrongly said temperature 0). Data and results are unchanged. Related work (added in v1.1.0). Cihan, İçöz, Haratian and Tüzün (arXiv 2505.20206, "Evaluating Large Language Models for Code Review") test GPT-4o and Gemini 2.0 Flash as code reviewers on correctness classification and report that performance depends on the type of code and that the outputs can be faulty. CryptoBench asks a related question for security review of cryptographic API use with local open models. It reports detection together with the matched secure controls, so a model that flags everything can be told apart from one that finds real misuse. v1.1.0 changes this description only. Data, harness and results are unchanged.

evidence_items.summary: We propose V-Droid, a mobile GUI task automation agent. Unlike previous mobile agents that utilize Large Language Models (LLMs) as generators to directly generate actions at each step, V-Droid employs LLMs as verifiers to evaluate candidate actions before making final decisions. To realize this novel paradigm, we introduce a comprehensive framework for constructing verifier-driven mobile agents: the discretized action space construction coupled with the prefilling-only workflow to accelerate the verification process, the pair-wise progress preference training to significantly enhance the verifier's decision-making capabilities, and the scalable human-agent joint annotation scheme to efficiently collect the necessary data at scale. V-Droid obtains a substantial task success rate across several public mobile task automation benchmarks: 59.5% on AndroidWorld, 38.3% on AndroidLab, and 49% on MobileAgent-Bench, surpassing existing agents by 5.2%, 2.1%, and 9%, respectively. Furthermore, V-Droid achieves a remarkably low latency of 4.3s per step and 0.7s per decision, which are 6.1× and 32.1× faster compared with existing mobile agents. The source code is available at https://github.com/V-Droid-Agent/V-Droid.
evidence_items.title: V-Droid: Advancing Mobile GUI Agent Through Generative Verifiers

evidence_items.summary: Indoor context deciphered by ambient sensing underpins many applications, from assisted living to smart buildings, yet remains weakly connected to the language-aligned paradigm of modern multimodal systems. Through billions of IoT devices, ambient WiFi Channel State Information (CSI) captures the indoor context of human activity and environmental dynamics passively via ubiquitous, always-on infrastructure. However, unlike vision or audio, CSI lacks naturally paired text like captions or transcripts, limiting its integration with language-driven AI systems. We present CSI-TextBench, a large-scale dataset and benchmark for aligning CSI data with natural language, unifying 3 sensing benchmarks into 285,790 samples across 7 tasks and pairing them with 2,291 hierarchically structured, label-derived descriptions via many-to-many assignment to construct 2.0 million CSI-text training tuples. Benchmarking 5 alignment methods from 4 paradigm families, we show that contrastive CSI-text alignment matches supervised classifiers without class labels, adapts to unseen classes with few samples, and responds to open-vocabulary natural-language prompts. A single unified model supports compositional scene understanding, answering joint queries over activity, proximity, and identity, achieving 86.9% top-1 accuracy on 140 composite scenes, outperforming task-specific classifier ensembles. CSI-TextBench enables ubiquitous ambient sensing as a language-indexed perception layer, enabling indoor contextual awareness in language-driven AI systems.
evidence_items.title: CSI-TextBench: A Dataset and Benchmark for Language-Grounded Ambient Sensing Perception

evidence_items.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly wired to consequential tools that send public alerts, dispatch responders, and query citizen records, where one erroneous tool call carries real-world cost. Existing agent-safety benchmarks measure generic harm or prompt-injection success and implicitly treat refusing as the safe default. In public-safety deployments that assumption breaks: an agent too cautious to dispatch help fails as surely as one that triggers a false alert. We present SentryBench, which scores agents on a two-sided, cost-sensitive frontier jointly measuring attack success, over-refusal (missing a real emergency), and over-reaction (unwarranted action) under adversarial tool use, with scenarios grounded in real emergency-call transcripts, disaster messages, and real injection/jailbreak payloads. We formalize deployment harm as an asymmetric cost functional, prove naive caution is harm-dominated whenever it refuses more genuine emergencies than the attack harm it averts, and prove a targeted trust gate adds zero over-refusal on clean input. Across 840 scored episodes over three frontier models and three defenses, refuse-more caution drives over-refusal to 100 percent on two of three models for at most a 3.7-point change in attack success and yields the worst harm everywhere, whereas our trust-gating wrapper dominates the frontier (lowest harm on every model, over-refusal at or below baseline, higher containment). Provider content filters also silently perform part of the defending and must be reported separately.
evidence_items.title: SentryBench: A Cost-Sensitive Benchmark for Adversarial Robustness of Tool-Using LLM Agents in Public-Safety Deployments

evidence_items.summary: Although LLMs demonstrate high success in logical tasks, it remains debated whether this stems from genuine reasoning or statistical memorization. This study presents a novel, multi-dimensional, perturbation- and session-based behavioral testing framework to assess LLMs’ arithmetic reasoning. To reduce the potential effect of data contamination, texts from the DROP, GSM8k, and MATH datasets were structurally manipulated. A comprehensive analysis was conducted on seven different models (DeepSeek-r1, DeepSeek-v2, Gemma, Llama 3.1, Llama 3.2, Mistral, Qwen) across 90 unique base questions evaluated under 2 distinct format constraints and 4 different presentation scenarios, analyzing a total of 5040 responses. The evaluation combined three quantitative metrics with six qualitative metrics examining session-based vulnerabilities. Results reveal that, within the tested contexts, models suffered performance degradation and logical disconnections when presentation conditions, formats, or constraints changed. Furthermore, models with thinking mechanisms often failed to complete challenging tasks within the time limit rather than gaining an advantage from their reasoning process. Ultimately, these findings indicate that benchmark accuracy alone may not reflect robust reasoning, underscoring the critical need for in-depth evaluation protocols that focus on cognitive consistency and error anatomy rather than mere accuracy rates.
evidence_items.title: Evaluating Arithmetic Reasoning Skills Beyond Benchmark Accuracy: A Session-Based Experimental Design for LLMs
