evidence_items.summary: A numerical claim generated by a financial analyst agent can match a number in a company filing but refer to the wrong entity, concept, period, unit or scope. A check based on reference answers can mark such an answer as wrong but does not explain why it fails. In this paper, we present NumTrace, a new benchmark that audits the provenance of each numerical claim made by financial analyst agents: its source and financial semantics. NumTrace currently has 540 questions over 2,163 SEC EDGAR documents. To the best of our knowledge, it is the first numerical benchmark about who holds a company's shares (Form 13F) and what its executives are owed (Item 402(i)). On a frozen snapshot of these documents, we build the reference answers according to accounting rules. NumTrace then gives each claim three separate verdicts: value, binding and support. By retaining separate value and binding verdicts, NumTrace detects right number, wrong account (RNWA) errors: a claim has an RNWA error when it passes the value check but fails the binding check. The RNWA rate quantifies the gap between value-only and joint value-and-binding pass rates. Finally, we audit three agents, Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6 Astra and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. RNWA errors make up 67.5-81.8% of each agent's failing claims. In particular, on 13F co-filing group questions, about 91% of claims pass the value check, but fewer than half pass the binding check.
evidence_items.title: NumTrace: Auditing the Number Provenance of Financial Analyst Agents

evidence_items.summary: Vision-language models are shifting from offline passive understanding toward online proactive interaction. However, prevailing methods largely rely on explicit requests while miss the implicit user intent (e.g., "where should I click next?" while a user navigate a website), meanwhile fail to update the state simultaneously as user requests might update continuously. These limitations make them less suited to intent-aware interaction in practical. To address these challenges, we introduce StreamVibe-Bench, a new benchmark serving as testbed for user intent interaction, with 4.1K evaluation samples and 85K training samples spanning explicit, implicit, and dynamic intents. Building on this benchmark, we develop StreamVibe-VL, a streaming proactive model that infers implicit user intents from continuous observations and dynamically tailors its interactions as these intents evolve. We further introduce StreamVibe-Harness, which maintains user intents as persistent states with a fleixble lifecycles via a hierarchical memory to track the latest user intent and environmental state. Our experiments reveal three key findings: (i) StreamVibe-VL preserves strong general video understanding while improving response timing and answer quality by 10.7% over other baselines; (ii) existing proactive models remain limited in understanding user intent and deciding when to respond, especially under implicit and dynamic intents; and (iii) StreamVibe-Harness further improves response consistency and adaptation over sustained interaction, resulting in a 12.3% gain in proactive interaction.
evidence_items.title: StreamVibe: Proactive Video Agents for Evolving User Intent

evidence_items.summary: Large language models increasingly collaborate with humans and peer AI agents whose contributions may be incomplete, inconsistent, or incorrect. Effective collaboration requires calibrated trust, whereby decisions to rely on, verify, or assist a partner adapt rationally as empirical evidence accumulates. We investigate whether models translate partner evidence into appropriate reliance policies. We introduce a benchmark of 324 scenarios across 23 collaboration categories. Each scenario involves three sequential decisions with explicit transition dynamics, feedback emissions, and cost schedules, permitting exact analytical evaluation of choices against their expected consequences over the remaining interaction. Evaluating seven models alongside 36 controlled-history probes, we dissociate evidence sensitivity from normatively appropriate action. While the strongest frontier model approaches near-optimal decisions, other models exhibit recurring pathologies: procuring excessive safeguards, purchasing verification tests with zero expected value of information, prioritizing immediate savings over cooperative learning, and misallocating assistance to suboptimal channels. Supplying explicit posterior distributions resolves certain errors while introducing new failure modes. Calibrated trust in autonomous agents critically demands coupling empirical evidence with forward-looking decision utility.
evidence_items.title: Can LLMs Trust Appropriately? Evaluating Calibrated Reliance on Imperfect Partners

rationale: Also found via Hugging Face Papers
evidence_items.summary: People have long dreamed of an assistant that is always there to guide them and remind what they forget, from new dishes to lost keys. Powered by multimodal large language models (MLLMs), egocentric AI assistants on wearable devices are bringing this dream within reach: they see what the user sees and give instructions for user's physical work when necessary. However, testing such assistance is challenging and usually requires real people. The expensive and rare real interaction data leaves a key question unanswered: Can today's MLLMs truly help people in physical world? To answer this question, we propose InteractiveWorld, the first verifiable environment for closed-loop interaction between human and AI assistant. Unlike existing robot-centric simulators, InteractiveWorld lets the assistant guide a human agent who observes the scene, understands instructions, and acts independently. It thus realistically simulates how AI assistant collaborates with human: the assistant instructs, the human acts, and the environment executes actions and updates what they see next. Building on it, we introduce InteractiveBench, the first dynamic benchmark for egocentric AI assistants, with 120 multi-turn tasks across six categories. In each task, the assistant guides the human in real time, and every instruction shapes the outcome, which is scored by verifiable, state-based rewards. Experiments with 12 frontier MLLMs show they are still far from reliable assistants. Even the strongest model, Claude Fable 5.1, achieves at most 20% and 25% on long-horizon Guidance and Planning tasks, respectively. Overall, our work offers a verifiable platform and a rigorous evaluation set, laying a solid foundation for research on interactive MLLM assistants that truly help people in the physical world.
evidence_items.title: InteractiveWorld: A Verifiable Human-Centric Environment for Building Better Interactive MLLM Assistants

rationale: Also found via Hugging Face Papers
evidence_items.summary: Localized AI manipulations in long-form videos often affect brief events within otherwise authentic content, making video-level classification insufficient for forensic analysis. Existing audio-visual deepfake benchmarks largely focus on short talking-head clips, while long-form temporal forensics remains predominantly visual. We introduce AV-FABLE, a dual-timeline benchmark for sparse manipulations in open-scene long-form audio-visual videos. AV-FABLE contains 16,650 pristine--manipulated twin pairs (998 hours) created with 27 editing configurations, with separate audio and visual timelines that enable modality-specific temporal localization and expose errors hidden by joint-timeline evaluation. On AV-FABLE, zero-shot prompting of audio-visual large language models (AV-LLMs) yields near-chance detection and poor temporal localization. In contrast, supervised readouts of their frozen perception features recover strong forensic signals, suggesting manipulation evidence is encoded in these representations but not effectively exposed through language outputs. Motivated by this observation, we propose NFSR(Native Forensics via Separated Readouts), which reads frozen AV-LLM features with separate audio and visual temporal decoders. NFSR achieves the best audio-visual localization performance in-domain and across all three out-of-distribution settings, including transfer to held-out videos from an external long-video forensic benchmark. AV-FABLE, code, and model weights will be publicly released.
evidence_items.title: AV-FABLE: Audio-Visual Manipulation Forensics in Long-Form Videos

evidence_items.summary: Production LLM agents increasingly run episodic memory pipelines and procedural skill modules (e.g., SKILL.md files) in tandem. Both are injected into the same context region with no defined precedence, so they can issue contradictory instructions that no instruction hierarchy resolves, a condition we term epistemic parity. We introduce a benchmark for measuring how LLM agents adjudicate such cross-source conflicts. We (i) develop a four-way taxonomy of memory-skill contradictions (factual, format, procedural, permission); (ii) instantiate 52 scenarios under a tripartite test-case anatomy (memory injection, skill injection, ambiguous user task), scored almost entirely by deterministic checkers over tool-call payloads and output structure; and (iii) run each scenario under three context conditions to isolate positional bias, measure the efficacy of an explicit precedence directive, and classify disclosure behavior, quantifying silent adjudication: resolving a conflict without telling the user. Across 1,383 runs on three open-weight models, neither source wins uniformly: resolution depends jointly on conflict type, model, and injection order. Moving the skill block nearer the task raises its win rate in all six factual and procedural cells (sign test, p = 0.031) but reverses for format conflicts, indicating that adjudication tracks token placement rather than source semantics. An explicit "skill takes absolute precedence" directive raises skill compliance on the two stronger models yet leaves 3-10% residual non-compliance, and moves the smallest model's factual and procedural resolution in the wrong direction. Most consequentially, in 98.8% of runs where the agent acted through a tool call it emitted no accompanying text at all, and 89% of all runs disclosed nothing about the contradiction: silent adjudication is the default. Code, scenarios, and raw outputs are public.
evidence_items.title: Navigating Epistemic Parity in LLM Agents: A Benchmark for Cross-Source Conflict Resolution Between Memory and Procedural Skills

organizations: University of the Cumberlands
evidence_items.summary: 30 vulnerable Python functions across 14 CWE categories, 12 adversarial comment strategies in four families (verification premise, context manipulation, credibility vocabulary, pressure and distraction), and 3,360 recorded trials from four studies run locally through Ollama at temperature 0: an attack ranking (780 trials), a comment-stripping defense (1,020), a cross-model comparison (600) and a transferability study (960), on qwen2.5-coder 7B, deepseek-coder 6.7B, codellama 7B and codegemma 7B. Includes the original harnesses and an analysis script that reproduces every headline number with Wilson 95% confidence intervals. Related work (added in v1.1.0). Moon et al. (arXiv 2505.16222, "Don't Judge Code by Its Cover") show that LLM judges of code correctness are biased by superficial variations such as comments and variable names. Alves and Henriques (SBSeg 2026, Workshop de Cibersegurança em IA, DOI 10.5753/sbseg estendido.2026.33836) test four LLMs on smart contract vulnerability detection with comments removed or identifiers renamed and report that semantically equivalent code can lead to different diagnoses. Heibel and Lowd (arXiv 2407.11072, "MaPPing Your Model") show that a small amount of added prompt text can make a programming assistant insert vulnerabilities. That is the code generation side, while CommentInject targets the review side, where the attacker controls the comments. Cihan, İçöz, Haratian and Tüzün (arXiv 2505.20206) evaluate GPT-4o and Gemini 2.0 Flash as code reviewers and report that their outputs can be faulty. Thornton (arXiv 2602.16741) tests eight models, mostly commercial, over 9,366 trials and reports small, non-significant effects of adversarial comments on detection, and that stripping comments lowers detection for weaker models. CommentInject uses four open models of about 7B parameters, so its results should not be read as holding for commercial models. v1.1.0 changes this description only. Data, harnesses and results are unchanged.
evidence_items.title: CommentInject: A benchmark of adversarial code-comment injection against LLM vulnerability detectors

evidence_items.summary: Logging statements are central to debugging, failure diagnosis, and production observability, yet writing them requires developers to decide where to place a logging statement, which API and severity level to use, and what runtime information to expose. Automated logging aims to reduce this burden, but existing evidence remains dominated by Java-centric repositorysnapshot datasets. Thus, Java-centered benchmarks do not show whether findings on model behavior and model selection generalize to other programming languages or to real-world maintenance changes that introduce logging statements. This paper presents MultiLogBench, a multilingual benchmark and empirical study spanning six programming language ecosystems. MultiLogBench contains 63,965 production-code repository-snapshot instances, 744 revision-history cases where developers introduce logging statements during maintenance, and a paired transformed revision-history branch for robustness analysis. Using seven contemporary large language models under a unified protocol, we evaluate logging-site localization, frameworkanchor matching, severity prediction, message generation, variable recovery, and cascaded overall quality. Results show that automated logging is sensitive to language-ecosystem conditions. On repository-snapshot data, absolute performance levels and component profiles vary across language-specific subsets, with position prediction exhibiting the largest average withinmodel component gap. The six language-specific CCS leaderboards are nevertheless highly correlated, with a mean pairwise Spearman correlation of 0.912, and identify the same top two models; reordering is concentrated among the middle- and lower-tier models. Among the primary structural buckets, loop and nested-callable sites are the hardest.
evidence_items.title: Automated Logging Is Language-Sensitive: A Multilingual Benchmark and Empirical Study of LLMs

evidence_items.summary: Agentic artificial intelligence systems combine language-model interaction with tools that perform operations beyond text generation. In data analytics, an integrated workspace must support dataset handling, analytical computation, visualization, and controlled tool execution while making the limits of each capability clear. This paper presents Fabric, a software project intended to bring conversational model access and data-oriented workflows into a common workspace. The paper documents its architecture and a preliminary local evaluation on Windows 11 using Node.js v24.15.0. JavaScript syntax validation passed, and a targeted evaluation suite reported seven passing tests. A synthetic local benchmark processed 10,000 rows and verified a sum of 505,000. The broader test suite reported 415 passing tests and four failures, including a Windows filesystem-permission verification failure and spreadsheet-processing failures. These observations support only narrow claims about selected components. They do not establish end-to-end model accuracy, secure execution isolation, production readiness, or performance under real-world workloads. The paper reports the methodology, results, limitations, and further validation required for a rigorous assessment of Fabric as an AI-assisted data-analysis workspace.
evidence_items.title: Fabric: An Agentic AI Workspace for Natural-Language Data Analysis and Multi-Tool Task Execution

organizations: Independent researcher
evidence_items.summary: Preprint with the routed circuits, verifier and search code. We revisit the qubit-routing benchmark of Li, Ding and Xie (SABRE, ASPLOS 2019): 26 circuits routed onto the 43-edge IBM Q20 Tokyo coupling graph, scored by the number of added gates (three per inserted SWAP). With the same circuits, graph and metric and an exact replay verifier, our routings need 12,087 added gates in total against SABRE's published 68,559 (82% fewer). On identical inputs, Qiskit 2.4.1 SABRE gives 64,137 (default) and 53,418 (heavy trials), and pytket 2.18.5 gives 35,685. On the 15 circuits reported in common by later routing papers on this device, the best published counts (HAIL, 2025) total 13,044 against our 9,312. Our count is lower on every circuit than every method we found (SAHS, MCTS, FiDLS, ILS, TWP, HAIL), with one tie. The routings come from a level-synchronous beam search over SWAP sequences, combined with SABRE-style forward-reverse passes to refine the initial mapping. The search code was written by a language-model agent inside an autonomous discovery loop (about three hours, about 21 USD of model usage). Beam search for routing is not new. The contribution is the measured gap on this widely cited suite, the exactly verifiable routed circuits, and an account of the discovery process. Caveats: far more compute per circuit than the baselines, a metric that ignores depth and fidelity, two regenerated QFT circuits, and the design graph rather than the physical device. Files: the preprint (PDF + LaTeX source, figures, bibliography); the 26 OpenQASM benchmark circuits with the QFT generator; qmap.py (QASM parser, coupling graph, exact replay verifier, SABRE reimplementation); routings/best combined.json (initial mapping and full operation sequence per circuit) with a per-circuit source map; the baseline script and its output; every proposer run's router code, drivers and notes; SHA-256 sums. Reproduce: python qmap.py verify routings/best combined.json (prints total g add 12087).
evidence_items.title: Beam search over SWAP sequences on the SABRE benchmark: 82% fewer added gates than SABRE and 29% fewer than the best published routings for IBM Q20 Tokyo, found by an autonomous agent

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Artificial intelligence is increasingly being applied to the assessment, monitoring and care of older adults, with potential benefits across both population health and individual clinical practice. This narrative review examines current and emerging applications of AI in common conditions and care needs associated with ageing, including hypertension, stroke, myocardial infarction, Parkinson’s disease, osteoporosis, sarcopenia and supportive care robotics. Across these domains, AI-enabled analysis of electronic health records, electrocardiograms, imaging, video, wearable-sensor data and home-monitoring measurements may support earlier disease detection, more objective functional assessment, personalised risk prediction and treatment, and greater independence. Computer-vision approaches may provide detailed measures of movement following stroke and in Parkinson’s disease, while opportunistic analysis of existing imaging may improve recognition of low bone mineral density, vertebral fractures and reduced muscle health. Care robots may additionally assist with companionship, medication management and falls detection. However, much of the evidence remains based on selected datasets, proof-of-concept studies or controlled settings. Algorithmic bias, limited representation of frail and multimorbid older adults, privacy, governance, interpretability, interoperability, user burden and workforce consequences remain important barriers. AI should therefore complement rather than replace clinical judgement. Equitable implementation will require representative datasets, rigorous external and prospective validation, transparent models, user-centred design and evaluation of clinically meaningful outcomes.
evidence_items.title: Artificial intelligence in an ageing population

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Reliable plant-disease segmentation depends on evaluation images being independent of the data used for training. We audited PlantSeg, a large in-the-wild semantic-segmentation benchmark, to determine whether visually related image families cross its released partitions and whether such exposure changes the evidence produced by standard segmentation models. The audit combined multiple similarity signals with human adjudication, followed by contamination-aware re-evaluation, class-count-matched Monte Carlo controls, a two-seed training-exposure experiment, long-tail analysis, and group-disjoint benchmark reconstruction. Verified cross-split visual families involved about 10.7% of the released images. Across four canonical architectures, released-split evaluation was consistently more favorable than contamination-aware evaluation, and the main shifts persisted after controlling for disease-class composition. The training side exposure had very limited effect in the independent clean test cases but was seen to have an estimated 11–15% advantage in related contaminated test cases in both seeds. Deletion of family ties improved independence at the cost of rare class support; while the group-disjoint reconstruction kept all 115 disease classes intact while removing known family ties. This illustrates that benchmark contamination can be overestimated and family-aware split construction is a viable solution.
evidence_items.title: Improving Reliability in Plant Disease Semantic Segmentation by Quantifying Benchmark Contamination and Duplicate Family Exposure

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Activation functions (AFs) play a pivotal role in defining the representational power and learning dynamics of deep neural networks (DNNs). However, their influence on medical image restoration (MIR) remains insufficiently explored. This empirical study presents a comprehensive, multi-phase investigation into how different AFs affect spatial and frequency characteristics across MIR tasks, such as image deblurring, image deblocking, and image super-resolution, in three medical imaging modalities: computed tomography (CT), digital mammography (DM), and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). The study integrates a theoretical taxonomy of AFs, a fixed-weight analysis, and a full-scale empirical evaluation involving 15 representative AFs spanning classical, rectified, exponential, and modern smooth families, benchmarked across 3,000 medical images. These functions are implemented within two widely used state-of-the-art MIR architectures: U-Net and Enhanced Deep Super-Resolution (EDSR). Model performance is evaluated using Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR), Structural Similarity Index Measure (SSIM), Edge Preservation Index (EPI), High-Frequency Energy Ratio (HFER), and Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity (LPIPS), with statistical validation performed using Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) and Tukey’s Honestly Significant Difference (HSD) tests. Results reveal that while the Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) and its variants remain strong baselines due to their stability and efficiency, smoother and adaptive functions such as the Gaussian Error Linear Unit (GELU), Mish, and Funnel ReLU (FReLU) achieved superior performance in preserving fine spatial and frequency details.
evidence_items.title: An empirical benchmark of activation functions for medical image restoration networks

evidence_items.summary: Purpose This viewpoint examines organizational implications of agentic AI systems in planning, selecting tools, executing multistep actions, and evaluating their own outputs with limited human intervention. Design/methodology/approach This viewpoint synthesizes academic and practitioner insights to identify key organizational challenges associated with agentic AI drawing on organizational learning theory and recent research on human–AI collaboration, and propose practical directions for HR and learning and development. Findings As agentic AI becomes more autonomous, it is reshaping organizational learning, human oversight, and accountability. Organizations will need to redesign learning practices and governance mechanisms to ensure that people and AI work together effectively. Research limitations/implications This conceptual viewpoint does not include empirical validation. Future research should examine the proposed ideas across different organizational settings. Practical implications Organizations should assess workforce readiness, redesign learning around human–AI collaboration, and establish feedback mechanisms that strengthen learning, oversight, and accountability. Originality/value This viewpoint shifts the discussion from technological capabilities of agentic AI to its organizational implications, offering practical guidance for organizations adapting to increasingly autonomous forms of work.
evidence_items.title: Agentic AI in organizations: reimagining learning, autonomy, and human oversight

evidence_items.summary: Recent advances in 3D semantic segmentation have significantly improved scene understanding in autonomous driving. However, existing methods are typically developed under a closed-set assumption and evaluated under standard driving conditions, where all categories are known in advance. In real-world driving, autonomous vehicles inevitably encounter previously unseen objects, making closed-set perception insufficient for safe deployment. To address this challenge, we introduce DriveOSS, which, to the best of our knowledge, is the first real-world multimodal dataset and benchmark specifically designed for 3D anomaly segmentation and open-set semantic segmentation. It contains 12,661 synchronized and annotated frames captured using six surround-view RGB cameras, a 128-beam LiDAR, and a GPS/IMU unit. The dataset comprises 52 real-world driving scenes collected under clear, nighttime, cloudy, rainy, and snowy conditions and is organized into ID (in-distribution) and OOD (out-of-distribution) subsets. The ID scenes contain only known classes and are used for training, whereas the OOD scenes additionally contain unknown objects annotated as the outlier class and are used for validation and testing. Extensive experiments show that unseen objects remain a major challenge for current 3D perception systems. The dataset, benchmark protocols, and code are available at https://github.com/chrisyan/DriveOSS.
evidence_items.title: DriveOSS: Dataset and Benchmark for 3D Anomaly Segmentation and Open-set Semantic Segmentation in Autonomous Driving

evidence_items.summary: As LLM-based agents are deployed with increasing autonomy in real-world environments, a critical failure mode emerges: agentic misalignment, where agents choose harmful actions over failure. However, existing safety benchmarks primarily evaluate whether agents comply with explicitly harmful instructions, leaving the conditions that cause agents to choose harmful actions poorly understood. To address this limitation, we propose AM-Bench, a unified taxonomy and 35 scenario evaluation benchmark spanning seven industries for agentic misalignment grounded in the fraud triangle, a well-established criminological framework explaining goal-directed misconduct. We adapt this framework to agentic environments and construct our evaluation suite and detection systems along three dimensions: perceived threat, perceived opportunity, and reasoning. We operationalize each dimension into structured subcategories rooted in prior theory: five threat categories derived from the instrumental convergence thesis, seven opportunity categories drawn from the Emergent Strategic Reasoning Risks (ESRR) taxonomy, and a novel four-question binary reasoning framework synthesized from prior literature. Our evaluation of 10 frontier models reveals a 62-percentage-point gap in misalignment across scenarios, with Gemini 3 Flash and Gemini 3.1 Pro exhibiting the highest levels of agentic misalignment while Claude Sonnet 4.6 displays near-zero rates across all conditions. Our reasoning framework further reveals that models may exhibit harmful behaviours without explicit situational awareness or explanation, complicating both mitigation and detection. AM-Bench scenarios and code are available at https://github.com/AI4Collaboration/Agentic-Misalignment-Bench
evidence_items.title: AM-Bench: A Unified Taxonomy and Evaluation Suite for Agentic Misalignment

evidence_items.summary: Progress in AI-based retinal image analysis has accelerated with the adoption of foundation models, yet evaluating their real-world reliability remains challenging. Performance reported on a single dataset does not capture how models behave under dataset shift, across clinical definitions, or for different patient subgroups. This limitation is particularly critical in medical imaging, where robustness, calibration, and fairness are essential for safe deployment. We introduce FOCUS (Foundation Ophthalmic Cross-Dataset Understanding under Shift), a cross-dataset benchmark evaluating retinal fundus models across vision-only encoder models (VM), vision-language dual-encoder models (VLM), and multimodal large language models (MLLM). FOCUS harmonizes binary diabetic retinopathy, referable diabetic retinopathy, and glaucomatous optic neuropathy tasks across ten public datasets spanning diverse geographies, acquisition conditions, and label protocols. The benchmark evaluates models through a unified analysis layer that measures ranking performance, calibration, subgroup disparities, and image-quality robustness. We present a large-scale evaluation covering 532 base configurations and 228 MLLM configurations adapted via LoRA fine-tuning. Results show no model family consistently dominates across tasks and datasets: general VM encoders achieve the strongest average ranking performance, medical MLLMs are competitive but variable, and dual-encoder VLMs benefit substantially from lightweight adaptation. Fine-tuning improves in-domain performance but exhibits heterogeneous transfer to external datasets, particularly in calibration. FOCUS provides a practical framework and public benchmark to assess generalization, reliability, and robustness beyond single-dataset leaderboards.
evidence_items.title: FOCUS: Benchmarking Retinal Model Generalization from Foundation Vision Encoders to Multimodal LLMs

evidence_items.summary: Recent research has shown that filtering massive English web corpora into high-quality subsets significantly improves training efficiency. However, for high-resource non-English languages like German, French, or Japanese, aggressive filtering creates a strategic dilemma: should practitioners prioritize diversity by training once on large amounts of lightly filtered web data, or prioritize quality by strictly filtering for a high-quality core and repeating it over multiple epochs? We investigate this trade-off for German by applying hierarchical quality filters to 500M web documents, comparing multi-epoch training on filtered subsets against single-pass training on a diverse corpus. Our experiments across multiple model scales and token budgets show that repeating high-quality data consistently outperforms single-pass training on larger, less filtered sets. Notably, the performance gap persists even after 7 epochs. Our findings suggest that for non-English LLMs, semantic concentration through quality filtering offers a more viable path to efficient language modeling than simply maximizing unique data volume. We release our German language models (called Boldt), as well as our cleaned evaluation benchmarks to the research community. Our experiments indicate that they achieve state-of-the-art results despite training on 10-360x fewer tokens than comparable models.
evidence_items.title: Repetition over Diversity: High-Signal Data Filtering for Sample-Efficient German Language Modeling

evidence_items.summary: We present DOCFORGE-BENCH, the first unified zero-shot benchmark for document forgery detection, evaluating 14 methods across eight datasets spanning text tampering, receipt forgery, and identity document manipulation. Unlike fine-tuning-oriented evaluations such as ForensicHub [Du et al., 2025], DOCFORGE-BENCH applies all methods with their published pretrained weights and no domain adaptation -- a deliberate design choice that reflects the realistic deployment scenario where practitioners lack labeled document training data. Our central finding is a pervasive calibration failure invisible under single-threshold protocols: methods achieve moderate Pixel-AUC (>=0.76) yet near-zero Pixel-F1. This AUC-F1 gap is not a discrimination failure but a score-distribution shift: tampered regions occupy only 0.27-4.17% of pixels in document images -- an order of magnitude less than in natural image benchmarks -- making the standard tau=0.5 threshold catastrophically miscalibrated. Oracle-F1 is 2-10x higher than fixed-threshold Pixel-F1, confirming that calibration, not representation, is the bottleneck. A controlled calibration experiment validates this: adapting a single threshold on N=10 domain images recovers 39-55% of the Oracle-F1 gap, demonstrating that threshold adaptation -- not retraining -- is the key missing step for practical deployment. Overall, no evaluated method works reliably out-of-the-box on diverse document types, underscoring that document forgery detection remains an unsolved problem. We further note that all eight datasets predate the era of generative AI editing; benchmarks covering diffusion- and LLM-based document forgeries represent a critical open gap on the modern attack surface.
evidence_items.title: DOCFORGE-BENCH: A Comprehensive 0-shot Benchmark for Document Forgery Detection and Analysis

evidence_items.summary: Background Automated dietary assessment increasingly struggles to evaluate industrial food processing levels, revealing a systemic gap between the visual presentation of meals and their underlying ultra-processed food composition. Although existing dietary monitoring tools can effectively track caloric and macronutrient intake, they lack the qualitative processing assessments required to identify hidden additives and map dietary risk triage quadrants. Methods This study introduces a modular, IoT-enabled multimodal dietary decision-support framework that decouples visual food recognition, standardized database retrieval, and qualitative language reasoning for automated NOVA processing classification and 2D decision matrix mapping. Operating on isolated single-dish meal instances, the system employs a four-phase cascaded pipeline that integrates vision-language models, database retrieval, and large language models (LLMs) with strict JSON schema enforcement. The platform was evaluated using the Nutrition-NOVA validation benchmark, a harmonized multimodal dataset constructed through dense vector-space semantic linkage between quantitative profiles from the Center for Food Safety database and qualitative NOVA tiers from Open Food Facts. This benchmark addresses a 75.0% metadata sparsity deficit identified in legacy repositories. Results In experimental evaluations on the Nutrition-NOVA benchmark, the baseline Qwen-VL-Max architecture achieved an adjacent accuracy of 77.7%. Furthermore, enforcing schema modularity enabled complete plug-and-play backend replaceability between commercial cloud application programming interfaces (APIs) and private, on-premises open-weight models without requiring architectural retraining. Discussion The proposed framework establishes an efficient, safety-first screening tool for digital healthcare decision support.
evidence_items.title: IoT-enabled multimodal large language model-based framework for compositional food recognition, nutrient profiling, NOVA classification, and cancer risk mitigation

evidence_items.summary: Abstract The rapid expansion of mobile and digital financial services in Ethiopia has generated substantial user feedback, yet automated analysis remains challenging because reviews are multilingual, informal, code-switched, and weakly represented in existing language resources. This study develops and evaluates a reproducible multilingual natural language processing framework for classifying Ethiopian FinTech reviews into five service-oriented categories: General Praise or Suggestions (GPS), User Experience and Design Issues (UXD), Transaction and Payment Failures (TPF), Login and Authentication Problems (LAP), and Service and Support Complaints (SSC). An annotated corpus was constructed from publicly accessible reviews associated with 27 Ethiopian FinTech applications. The initial collection contained 8,387 records, of which 7,148 were retained after quality-control procedures. The corpus contains English, Amharic, and English-Amharic code-switched reviews. We benchmark conventional TF-IDF classifiers, neural architectures, and multilingual/African-language transformer models under a leakage-controlled experimental protocol in which random oversampling is restricted to the training partition. Using five-fold stratified cross-validation, repeated random seeds, held-out evaluation, confidence intervals, and paired bootstrap significance testing, AfroXLMR achieved the strongest performance, with 96.7% accuracy and 96.0% macro-F1, followed by AfriBERTa (96.5%, 95.8%) and XLM-R (96.2%, 95.4%). The strongest neural baseline, CNN, achieved 95.1% accuracy and 94.3% macro-F1, while XGBoost achieved 90.2% accuracy and 88.1% macro-F1. Minority-class recall improved substantially after training-only oversampling. Language-specific analysis indicated lower performance for English-Amharic code-switched reviews than for English and Amharic reviews.
evidence_items.title: Multilingual Artificial Intelligence for Classifying Ethiopian FinTech User Reviews

evidence_items.summary: Click-Through Rate (CTR) prediction is a critical task in recommender systems and online advertising, so CTR models design has been widely researched in both academia and industry. However, since the model parameters increase larger and their computations become more complex, the inefficiency severely hinders practical deployment and application. Especially, the lack of a unified benchmark for the computational efficiency of CTR models complicates matters. To address the issues, we propose a holistic efficiency benchmark for CTR models named EffBench. a) A comprehensive evaluation metric system is constructed for CTR models, including seven metrics to assess accuracy and strongly emphasize computational efficiency. b) EffBench benchmark is implemented based on industrial mainstream framework TensorFlow, to better align with real-world usage scenarios. c) An operator-level profiling tool in EffBench is designed to identify key performance bottlenecks. d) Based on the EffBench benchmark, we evaluate and analyze 30 representative models across three typical CTR task types on the three widely used real-world datasets. As the first benchmark aiming at improving CTR model efficiency, EffBench will facilitate researchers in CTR model evaluation, comparison, validation, and inspiring future model designs. Our benchmark source code is available at https://github.com/Yeedzhi/EffBench .
evidence_items.title: EffBench: A Holistic Efficiency Benchmark for CTR Models

organizations: University of California, Riverside, Riverside, USA
evidence_items.summary: Cooperative perception extends autonomous vehicles' sensing beyond their individual field of view. Existing methods, however, are largely evaluated under idealized, unlimited-bandwidth assumptions that real cellular vehicle-to-everything (C-V2X) links do not satisfy. We present CooperScene, the first real-world multi-agent, multi-modal cooperative autonomy dataset with real time C-V2X communication characterization. Collected by three connected autonomous vehicles and one instrumented roadside unit, CooperScene provides 59K synchronized LiDAR frames, 53K images, and 344K 3D bounding box labels across diverse driving scenes, together with pair-wise C-V2X throughput, latency, packet loss, and jitter traces synchronized with the sensor streams. CooperScene is built with tight sensor- and agent-synchronization, centimeter-level localization and spatial alignment, and precise cross-modality calibration. We also provide an unified benchmark, which evaluates cooperative 3D detection and motion prediction under both measured C-V2X and idealized networks, showing that state-of-the-art methods demand orders of magnitude more bandwidth than real world C-V2X delivers. We demonstrate the dataset and benchmark through an interactive visualizer and a benchmark explorer. Project website for data and benchmark: https://cisl.ucr.edu/CooperScene.
evidence_items.title: Demo: CooperScene: Multi-Modal Cooperative Autonomy Benchmark under C-V2X Communication Constraints

organizations: Ministry of Education, Iraq
evidence_items.summary: In this study, three software reliability tasks are considered: predicting defect prone modules, software incidents severity classification, and predicting deployment change failures, and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) is studied for those tasks. For four explicitly synthetic tabular datasets with 2,400 data points each, that is, 7,200 observations, four classifiers were tested: logistic regression, random forest, extremely randomized trees and histogram gradient boosting. We were able to generate 12 model task evaluations, with 600 instances left out for each task. The accuracy and the macro-F1 scores of logistic regression were 77.17% and 75.40% for defect prediction, 72.00% and 72.33% for incident severity classification, and 64.33% and 63.69% for change-failure prediction, respectively. There are three areas of examination in the evaluation: predictive performance analysis, error patterns analysis, and model interpretation analysis. The confusion matrix, the receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC-AUC) and the balanced accuracy are all used to explore these areas, along with the Matthews correlation coefficient and the feature-importance analysis. Twenty publications on the topic are critically examined and used to put the benchmark into the context and its methodological choices. The study offers an evaluation protocol that conveys the explanation in terms that the reader can follow and a comparative simulation framework of three software engineering decision points, along with a discussion of the constraints of the shown tasks when it comes to deployment. It does not develop a new learning algorithm but rather it is methodological and comparative. The results reported here are only applicable to the data sets generated and external validity has not been established.
evidence_items.title: Explainable AI for Software Reliability: A Three-Dataset Benchmark of Defect, Incident-Severity and Change-Failure Prediction

evidence_items.summary: Robust 3D reconstruction across varying environmental conditions remains a critical challenge for robotic perception, particularly when transitioning between air and water. To address this, we introduce BALTIC, a controlled benchmark designed to systematically evaluate modern 3D reconstruction methods under variations in medium and lighting. The benchmark comprises 13 datasets spanning two media (air and water) and three lighting conditions (directional, artificial, and mixed), with additional variations in motion type, scanning pattern, and initialization trajectory, resulting in a diverse set of sequences. Our experimental setup features a custom water tank equipped with a monocular camera and an HTC Vive tracker, enabling accurate ground-truth pose estimation. We further investigate cross-domain reconstruction by augmenting underwater image sequences with a small number of in-air views captured under similar lighting conditions. We evaluate Structure-from-Motion reconstruction using COLMAP in terms of both trajectory accuracy and scene geometry, and use these reconstructions as input to Neural Radiance Fields and 3D Gaussian Splatting methods. The resulting models are assessed against ground-truth trajectories and in-air references, while rendered outputs are compared using perceptual and photometric metrics. Additionally, we perform a color restoration analysis to evaluate radiometric consistency across domains. Our results show that under controlled, texture-consistent conditions, Gaussian Splatting with simple preprocessing (e.g., white balance correction) can achieve performance comparable to specialized underwater methods, although its robustness decreases in more complex and heterogeneous real-world environments.
evidence_items.title: Baltic: A benchmark and cross-domain strategy for 3D reconstruction across air and underwater domains under varying illumination

evidence_items.summary: Reproducible evaluation frameworks are essential for translating machine learning advances into medical decision-support systems, yet comparisons of classical machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), and automated machine learning (AutoML) often lack standardized preprocessing, consistent validation, and transparent runtime reporting. We present a reproducible, time-aware benchmark for heart disease detection using a unified tabular dataset merging four University of California Irvine (UCI) Heart Disease sources: Cleveland, Hungary, Switzerland, and Veterans Administration (VA) Long Beach. The framework applies shared preprocessing and evaluates ML, DL, and AutoML under nominal framework-level time limits of 180 and 60 s, while reporting predictive metrics, observed wall-clock runtime, memory usage, and serialized model size. In the original single-split benchmark, Extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) achieved an accuracy of 84.78%, an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC-AUC) of 91.79%, and an F1-score of 86.67% in the full regime. Under the lightweight regime, AutoGluon matched the accuracy and F1-score, increased area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC-AUC) to 92.80%, and completed in 9.87 s, although with a larger serialized artifact. Robustness was assessed using repeated stratified 80/20 holdout evaluation across five pre-specified seeds. AutoGluon Light achieved the highest descriptive mean F1-score and ROC-AUC (83.97 ± 1.95% and 89.16 ± 2.29%, respectively), while ClassicML Light remained competitive (82.86 ± 2.68% F1-score; 88.09 ± 2.29% ROC-AUC) and achieved the shortest mean runtime (3.41 ± 3.52 s). Pairwise Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Holm correction showed no statistically significant differences among lightweight frameworks.
evidence_items.title: A time-aware reproducible benchmark of full and lightweight AutoML, machine learning, and deep learning frameworks for heart disease detection

evidence_items.summary:
Multi-echelon inventory optimization (MEIO) under demand distribution shift remains an open challenge in supply chain management. Classical rule-based policies are effective when calibrated online but cannot exploit historical data structure. This paper investigates whether a Koopman operator world model, applied as a structured latent dynamics model within an offline reinforcement learning (RL) framework, can improve the out-of-distribution (OOD) robustness of learned inventory policies and reduce temporal difference (TD)-target variance during training.
 
 
 
 We propose Koopman-enhanced Multi-Echelon Inventory Optimization (K-MEIO), a two-stage framework combining a Deep Koopman World Model (DKWM) with Implicit Q-Learning (IQL). The DKWM learns a finite-dimensional linear embedding of the multi-echelon inventory dynamics, enabling analytically tractable TD targets with 12.4% lower variance than direct next-state encoding. The Koopman-enhanced Implicit Q-Learning policy is trained entirely on simulated offline transitions calibrated from University of California, Irvine Online Retail and Rossmann Store Sales demand statistics. Ablation experiments across five expectile values, three training seeds, and three OOD stress scenarios are reported, together with full cost breakdowns.
 
 
 
 Under standard evaluation, K-MEIO achieves service level 0.995 with zero capacity violations. Across three training seeds, K-MEIO achieves OOD robustness ratio 0.861 ± 0.039 under a 3× promotional demand spike and 0.882 ± 0.058 under a permanent demand mean shift, compared to 0.762 ± 0.153 and 0.842 ± 0.093 for vanilla IQL. K-MEIO shows consistently lower seed-to-seed variance, suggesting more stable training dynamics. A historically calibrated base-stock policy (Hist-BSP) outperforms all offline methods in both standard and stress evaluations. Cost breakdown confirms that K-MEIO's degradation under stress is driven entirely by stockout cost, not excess inventory.
 
 
 
 The offline dataset consists of simulated transitions calibrated using real retail demand statistics, not actual historical inventory records. The Koopman spectral radius constraint is a regularization device and does not constitute a formal stability guarantee for the true inventory system. The 12.4% variance reduction produces modest but consistent OOD robustness gains across seeds.
 
 
 
 In supply chain contexts where promotional demand spikes or demand mean shifts are common and online policy recalibration is impractical, K-MEIO offers more stable policy behavior than vanilla IQL (seed std. ±0.039 vs. ± 0.153 in S1). A historically calibrated BSP remains a competitive offline benchmark and should be the primary comparison point.
 
 
 
 This paper provides the first systematic evaluation of Koopman-structured TD targets for offline inventory RL under demand distribution shift, with direct measurement of TD-target variance reduction, a multi-seed robustness analysis, and a fair historically calibrated BSP baseline. The corrected mechanistic explanation clarifies that the Koopman advantage operates at training time through variance reduction, not at evaluation time through OOD encoding.
evidence_items.title: Koopman-enhanced offline reinforcement learning for robust multi-echelon inventory control under demand distribution shift

evidence_items.summary: Learning-based millimeter-wave (mmWave) human sensing needs data spanning environments, radar placements, people, and activities, yet each dataset is coupled to the deployment that produced it, and rare or unsafe events are the hardest to capture. Simulation can vary these factors, but existing mmWave simulators hard-wire them into task-specific pipelines, making coordinated edits hard to express and verify. We present mmSketcher, a scene-first middleware whose single editable scene is synchronized behind replaceable physics and RF engines. Moving the radar, replacing a person's motion, or adding an occluder is one edit to this shared state, and path geometry, Doppler, occlusion, and labels update together. Motion-capture and monocular-video humans share one deforming mesh whose per-face velocities drive Doppler, and each radar frame yields raw complex time-multiplexed multi-antenna (TDMA-MIMO) measurements. We validate the abstraction with analytic scene-edit checks, a matched real capture against native RF-Genesis, a fixed-budget substitution pilot on the HuPR pose benchmark, and throughput measurements: fidelity is comparable to the baseline with different tradeoffs, simulated sequences can stand in for part of a real training budget, and generation runs at offline-to-interactive rates. With the scene as a reusable control plane, a new sensing question becomes a new experiment rather than a new simulator. We release our evaluation artifacts on GitHub.1
evidence_items.title: mmSketcher: Physics-Grounded and Editable Scenes for mmWave Human-Sensing Simulation

evidence_items.summary: Conversational AI increasingly answers patients' rehabilitation questions, but a fluent, well-liked answer can still be clinically unsafe, and preference-only evaluation hides this by collapsing many judgments into one winner. We ran a human-centered evaluation of the mRehab Advisory Agent with two cohorts in distinct roles: six domain experts rate clinical safety and correctness, and three end users rate helpfulness, affect, and clarity, alongside blinded best-to-worst rankings exported as provenance-rich records. In a 200-question pilot (435 ranked triples), raters ranked the agent first most often (53.3%; p < 0.001), yet it led on affect and clarity, not helpfulness, and drew the lowest expert safety rate (88.8% vs. 93.7% for two GPT-4.1 mini comparators). That gap traced to a single expert with near-zero agreement, so it points to rater calibration rather than an unsafe agent, and catching it depended on recording safety separately from preference. As these agents take on more patient guidance, the gap between what sounds good and what is safe will only grow, and evaluations that keep both signals will matter more than leaderboards that report one.
evidence_items.title: Separating Safety from Preference in Clinical LLM Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: This work focuses on a reliable facial emotion recognition framework which aims to improve facial emotion classification performance on the FER2013 benchmark dataset. Recognition of facial emotions is now an important research field due to its uses in human computer interaction, healthcare, intelligent surveillance, education and affective computing. Despite the above, the human face still exhibits subtle changes with facial pose, facial illumination, occlusion and expression that continue to impact the overall recognition result. In order to solve these problems, this paper puts forward a hybrid deep learning architecture based on ResNet50 and Transformer encoder, capable of extracting multi-scale detailed spatial information and the relationships among various facial regions. An evaluation was performed with the proposed framework using the FER2013 database that contains 7 different emotion classes and 35,787 facial images. Images were pre-processed as three channel formats, resized to 224 × 224, normalized, and trained with the augmented image by flipping horizontally, random rotation, and resized cropping. For feature extraction, a pre-trained model was employed: the ResNet50 network. The Transformer encoder model was used to help enhance the contextual features representation, and the emotion classification was performed afterwards. The proposed framework has an overall accuracy of 89.7 percent on the official test partition (FER2013). Finally, an improvement was shown by ablation studies on the transformer where the ResNet50 model had a 72.84 percent, the ResNet50 model with a dense classifier reached 74.63 percent, and the complete framework achieved 89.7 percent. The results showed that the proposed method can be implemented transparently and reproduced and can robustly and consistently recognize facial emotions. The study provides a viable model which can guide the future research and practice of emotion recognition using facial expression.
evidence_items.title: Hybrid deep learning architecture for facial emotion recognition on FER2013 dataset

evidence_items.summary: Generative AI has intensified voice phishing (vishing) through real-time voice cloning and LLM-driven conversational adaptation. State-of-the-art on-device defenses such as MmVTD analyze only transcripts and on-screen behavior, with no mechanism to verify the acoustic stream's authenticity. We present VishGuard-M, a lightweight dual branch framework pairing local voice-authenticity verification with linguistic intent classification. A compact AASIST-L acoustic branch (85K parameters) detects synthetic voice artifacts, while an INT8-quantized Whisper-DistilBERT pipeline scores phishing intent. To avoid the confidence dilution of linear averaging, we propose a max-score fusion rule (sfused = max(sa, sn)) that alerts if either branch flags a threat. Evaluated on the ASVspoof 2019 LA benchmark, compact AASIST-L variant achieves a 1.52% Equal Error Rate (EER) matching within 0.09 points the accuracy of full 298K parameter AASIST architecture (1.43% EER) while operating at less than a third of its parameter footprint. Concurrently, the linguistic branch achieves a 0.966 F1-score on an SMS phishing intent proxy dataset. Both branches are validated independently; joint on-device deployment is ongoing work. VishGuard-M outlines a zero-server, privacy-preserving blueprint for multi-modal vishing mitigation on mobile devices.
evidence_items.title: WiP: VishGuard-M: Toward Voice-Authenticity-Aware Vishing Detection on Mobile Devices

evidence_items.summary: Visual Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (vSLAM) plays a crucial role in autonomous vehicles and robotics by enabling real-time localization and mapping in unknown environments. However, as current vSLAM systems are primarily designed for ideal weather conditions they often experience significant accuracy degradation and sudden operational breakdowns in severe rainy conditions (> 10 mm/h), posing serious safety hazards. To fill the gap, we propose ATM-SLAM, a novel learning-based vSLAM framework that overcomes the intense visual interference under severe rainy conditions and enhances system robustness. ATM-SLAM incorporates two key modules: (i) an Adaptive Feature Encoder (AFE), which adaptively prioritizes rain-robust features across consecutive frames, (ii) a Temporal Memory Integration (TMI) module, which integrates memorized correlation information to recover and stabilize localization under distorted frames. We extensively evaluate ATM-SLAM on a consumer vehicle, a robotic platform, and widely used public datasets across diverse scenarios. The evaluation results demonstrate that ATM-SLAM can achieve accurate and reliable localization and mapping in heavy rain. Moreover, to facilitate future research on vSLAM under severe rainy conditions, we collected the Severe Rainy SLAM Dataset (SR-SLAM), a large-scale real-world dataset, and plan to release it as a dedicated benchmark for evaluating vSLAM robustness.
evidence_items.title: ATM-SLAM: Adaptive Temporal Memory Visual SLAM in Severe Rainy Conditions

evidence_items.summary: YemSarc is the first multimodal (text, audio, and video) benchmark dataset for sarcasm detection in Yemeni dialectal Arabic and seven additional Arabic dialects. It comprises 630 balanced utterances (315 sarcastic, 315 non-sarcastic) drawn from naturally occurring conversational exchanges across eight Arabic dialects: Mahwiti, Ibbi, Adeni, Sanaani, Dhamari, Saudi, Egyptian, and Taizzi. Each target utterance is paired with its preceding conversational context and is represented across three synchronized modalities: written transcript, audio segment, and video frame sequence. The dataset was constructed from two widely popular Yemeni comedic drama series (Bayt Al-Madaliz and Khuruj Nihai), sourced from their official YouTube channels. Annotation was carried out through a structured three-phase protocol by three expert academic linguists, achieving a final inter-annotator agreement of Fleiss' Kappa = 0.7473. The dataset is released with a fully reproducible, speaker-independent, and statistically audited evaluation pipeline. This dataset is intended for non-commercial academic research purposes, including multimodal sarcasm detection, Arabic dialectal NLP, and social media analysis. The dataset is licensed under CC BY 4.0.
evidence_items.title: YemSarc: A Multimodal Benchmark Dataset for Sarcasm Detection in Yemeni and Related Arabic Dialects
