evidence_items.summary: Precision livestock farming increasingly relies on intelligent monitoring systems to improve animal health, welfare, and farm productivity. However, conventional cloud-centric approaches often face challenges related to data privacy, communication overhead, network dependency, and real-time decision-making. This study proposes a Federated Learning (FL) and Edge-AI framework for distributed livestock health monitoring that integrates Smart Neck Collar sensing, edge computing, MQTT-based communication, and a hybrid Gradient Boosting–Long Short-Term Memory (GBoost-LSTM) prediction architecture. The proposed framework enables local preprocessing, model training, and inference at participating farms while supporting collaborative model learning without transferring raw livestock sensor data to a central server. A simulation-based federated evaluation was designed using livestock health data collected from 150 dairy cows across seven districts of Punjab, India. The proposed framework was compared with previously evaluated centralized machine-learning approaches to assess its predictive performance. The simulated FL-GBoost-LSTM model achieved an accuracy of 95.12%, precision of 93.48%, recall of 88.21%, and F1-score of 90.76% under the evaluation configuration described in this study. The results indicate that federated collaborative learning can provide competitive disease-prediction performance while retaining data locally at participating farms. In addition, the proposed edge-based architecture is designed to reduce dependence on continuous cloud connectivity and support localized health-status assessment. Because the present evaluation is simulation-based and does not constitute a field deployment, the reported communication, latency, privacy, and scalability benefits should be interpreted as framework-level findings rather than validated operational outcomes. Future work will focus on real-world multi-farm deployment, systematic non-IID evaluation, formal privacy-enhancement mechanisms, and comprehensive benchmarking of computational, communication, and energy requirements. Proposed a Federated Learning and Edge-AI framework for distributed livestock health monitoring across geographically separated dairy farms. Integrated Smart Neck Collar sensing, MQTT-based communication, edge computing, and hybrid GBoost-LSTM prediction within a unified architecture. Simulated collaborative model training across distributed farm-level datasets while retaining raw livestock data locally. Achieved 95.12% accuracy, 93.48% precision, 88.21% recall, and 90.76% F1-score under the reported simulation-based evaluation configuration. Compared the proposed federated framework with previously evaluated centralized livestock disease-prediction models to assess predictive performance. Identified communication efficiency, edge inference, non-IID data handling, privacy enhancement, and real-world deployment as key areas requiring further experimental validation.
evidence_items.title: A Federated Edge Artificial intelligence (Edge-AI) Framework For Livestock Health Monitoring

evidence_items.summary: Privacy-preserving healthcare analytics at the edge requires collaborative learning across distributed Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) devices while maintaining strict privacy guarantees, low inference latency, and high predictive accuracy. Existing federated learning frameworks employ static privacy budgets and fixed communication schedules, failing to adapt to heterogeneous clinical contexts, variable network conditions, and diverse device capabilities. Furthermore, conventional edge intelligence methods struggle to efficiently balance multi-objective trade-offs between privacy, utility, and latency under stringent resource constraints. This paper proposes Quantum-Inspired Context-Aware Adaptive Federated Edge Intelligence (QI-CAF-EI), a novel framework that dynamically co-optimizes privacy, utility, and latency through context-aware adaptive control and quantum-inspired optimization techniques while maintaining full compatibility with classical edge hardware. The framework integrates five tightly coupled functional modules: (1) data acquisition and edge preprocessing for privacy-preserving local analytics, (2) quantum-inspired edge intelligence leveraging tensor network decompositions for efficient model compression, (3) context-aware adaptive control that continuously monitors system state and clinical urgency to adjust privacy budgets and communication schedules, (4) secure federated learning employing differential privacy (DP) and homomorphic encryption for gradient aggregation, and (5) explainability and governance mechanisms ensuring regulatory compliance and clinical interpretability. Comprehensive experimental evaluation across five benchmark healthcare datasets MIMIC-III, PhysioNet, NIH ChestX-ray14, UCI Heart Disease, and WISDM IoMT demonstrates significant performance improvements. QI-CAF-EI achieves 3.7–4.5% accuracy improvement over differentially private federated learning, reduces inference latency by 25–36% compared to edge-only baselines, and decreases communication overhead by 40% while maintaining rigorous DP guarantees (ε ∈ [0.3, 2.0], δ = 10⁻5). Theoretical analysis provides formal convergence guarantees, DP proofs, and complexity bounds. The framework enables real-time, privacy-preserving, and resource-efficient collaborative healthcare analytics, addressing critical requirements for safe AI deployment in modern healthcare ecosystems.
evidence_items.title: Quantum-inspired context-aware adaptive federated edge intelligence for privacy-preserving healthcare analytics

evidence_items.summary: We investigate whether conditioning heterogeneous security metadata by semantic type—rather than applying uniform normalization—improves intrusion detection performance by up to 22.9 percentage points. To operationalize this hypothesis, we propose the Modality-Aware Feature Taxonomy (MAFT), a preprocessing framework that classifies IDS features into six semantic groups (temporal, volumetric, behavioral, identity, protocol-specific, and statistical) and applies group-appropriate normalization: robust scaling with outlier clipping for heavy-tailed volumetric features, z-score standardization for temporal measurements, and bounded scaling for categorical and identity fields. MAFT’s contribution is methodological rather than algorithmic: it formalizes IDS preprocessing as a feature-modality conditioning problem, provides a transparent taxonomy-to-scaler mapping for security metadata, and characterizes when such conditioning is likely to matter. We evaluate MAFT through a four-stage progressive ablation across six public IDS benchmark datasets spanning enterprise network traffic (UNSW-NB15, CICIDS2017), IoT environments (ToN-IoT, N-BaIoT, Edge-IIoTset), and industrial control systems (HAI), comprising 24 centralized experiments with multi-seed statistical validation for UNSW-NB15 multiclass and binary classification for all six datasets. In single-seed multiclass experiments, MAFT improves accuracy by + 1.7 to + 22.9 percentage points on four heterogeneous datasets, reduces false alarm rates by up to 12 ×, and improves F1 scores for 8 of 15 classes that achieved 0% F1 under the plain baseline. Multi-seed multiclass validation was performed for UNSW-NB15; the all-dataset multi-seed extension is binary classification and should be interpreted as seed-stability evidence rather than direct multiclass replication. Two datasets with homogeneous, well-conditioned features show negligible change, an observed boundary condition that correlates with feature heterogeneity and helps practitioners assess applicability before full model training. Comparison against eight alternative preprocessing methods shows MAFT’s competitive accuracy alongside consistent cross-dataset applicability without dataset-specific tuning. The results position semantic feature conditioning as an under-examined IDS design choice that can improve gradient-based classifiers without changing downstream model architecture, while also identifying cases where simpler or dataset-adaptive preprocessing is sufficient.
evidence_items.title: Modality aware feature taxonomy for robust AI driven intrusion detection across heterogeneous cyber physical data

evidence_items.summary: The increasing availability of AI-generated synthetic voices poses challenges to the security, privacy, and integrity of digital audio, creating a need for accurate and interpretable detection methods. This study proposes a Frequency-Aware Transformer (FAT) for detecting AI-generated fake voices by incorporating multi-band spectral embeddings, frequency-aware positional encoding, and frequency-guided attention into a transformer-based architecture. The model was evaluated on the ASVspoof 2019 Logical Access benchmark and compared with conventional deep learning, transformer-based, and self-supervised learning baselines. FAT achieved 94.6 ± 0.3% accuracy, 94.3 ± 0.3% precision, 94.7 ± 0.2% recall, 94.5 ± 0.2% F1-score, and 6.3 ± 0.2% Equal Error Rate. Compared with ECAPA-TDNN, the strongest conventional baseline, FAT improved accuracy from 91.3 to 94.6% and reduced EER from 9.7 to 6.3%. The ablation analysis showed that removing self-attention resulted in the largest accuracy reduction of 5.1% points, followed by removal of frequency encoding (3.8 points), frequency bias (2.9 points), and frequency-aware positional encoding (2.5 points), demonstrating the contribution of these components to the observed performance. Cross-dataset evaluation showed that FAT retained discriminative performance under the evaluated dataset shifts, although some degradation occurred on unseen conditions. Under controlled artificial noise corruption, FAT accuracy decreased from 94.6% in the clean condition to 88.0% at 5 dB SNR, while remaining higher than the evaluated baseline models. Attention rollout and SHAP analysis provided interpretable information about the spectral-temporal regions and frequency bands associated with model predictions. Overall, the findings indicate that incorporating frequency-domain information into transformer-based modelling can improve fake voice detection performance and provide complementary interpretability under the evaluated benchmark and acoustic perturbation conditions.
evidence_items.title: Explainable fake voice detection in AI-generated audio using frequency-aware transformers

evidence_items.summary:
PURPOSE
This study was conducted to ascertain how display-dependent timing differences translate into changes in pattern-reversal visual evoked potential (PR-VEP) P100 peak time distributions, using physical measurements, controlled benchmark data, and large-scale routine clinical recordings with cathode ray tube (CRT) and liquid crystal display (LCD) systems.


METHODS
We analyzed PR-VEP recordings acquired before and after a routine transition from CRT to LCD systems. The study integrated three complementary data sources: photodiode measurements of trigger-to-luminance delay, a benchmark dataset of 10 healthy participants, and a retrospective clinical dataset comprising 1772 waveforms from 915 examinations. Cross-sectional peak time distributions and within-eye paired comparisons were evaluated.


RESULTS
Mean trigger-to-luminance delay under the LCD conditions was 13.7 ms. Corresponding prolongation of P100 peak time was observed in the benchmark dataset. In the clinical dataset, the P100 peak time distribution showed a rightward shift (mean difference 12.1 ms, 95% confidence interval 10.45-13.56 ms; Cohen's d = 0.73; p < 0.001). Quantile analysis revealed an approximately constant shift across the distribution. Within-eye longitudinal analyses confirmed that this shift also occurred at the individual level.


CONCLUSIONS
Display-related timing differences produce a systematic shift in PR-VEP peak time distributions. These findings demonstrate that device-dependent peak time offsets present important implications for clinical interpretation, underscoring needs for device-specific reference considerations in electrophysiological practice. Direct measurement of trigger-to-luminance delay might help estimate clinically relevant peak time shifts caused by hardware replacement.
evidence_items.title: From stimulus timing to real-world clinical peak time distributions: CRT versus LCD pattern-reversal VEP.

evidence_items.summary: This paper revisits “Automated Classification of Non-Functional Requirements”, published in the Requirements Engineering Journal in 2007, and reflects on how the underlying problem has evolved over two decades. The original work addressed the central challenge in requirements engineering that quality concerns are difficult to identify because they are distributed across heterogeneous artifacts and only partially documented. It introduced one of the earliest machine-learning approaches for NFR classification and produced the NFR PROMISE dataset, which became a widely used benchmark in this area. To understand the paper’s long-term impact, we conducted a citation review of 55 papers and replicated representative NFR classification approaches spanning two decades. The results show substantial advances in automated classification, culminating in modern LLM and agent-based techniques that outperform earlier approaches on PROMISE. However, improved accuracy has not solved the underlying problem. Contemporary AI-assisted development increasingly blurs the boundaries between Requirements Engineering, architectural design, and implementation. Quality concerns continue to emerge throughout development, but now appear as conversational fragments, implementation discussions, and architectural tradeoffs rather than explicit requirements statements. We argue that the next generation of requirements engineering tools must move beyond classifying documents toward identifying, surfacing, and preserving architecturally significant quality concerns as they emerge throughout development. We then outline a research agenda centered on detecting emerging and missing quality concerns, selective intervention, living documentation of quality decisions, and evaluation beyond classification accuracy. Finally we take a retrospective look at two decades of sharing and reusing the dataset, including the importance of dataset lineage, experimental comparability, and benchmark evolution.
evidence_items.title: Automated classification of non-functional requirements twenty years later: why this isn’t a solved problem

evidence_items.summary: Description This dataset contains expert-elicitation data collected to investigate approaches for aggregating animal-based welfare indicators into an overall welfare assessment for broiler chickens. Two complementary elicitation approaches were used: an indicator-based survey and a situation-based survey. The two approaches were completed by different groups of animal-welfare experts. All published respondent identifiers are anonymized. Indicator-based survey Experts evaluated individual welfare indicators and, where applicable, different severity levels. For each indicator or indicator level, experts provided a welfare impairment score on a 0–100 scale, where 0 represented no welfare impairment and 100 maximal welfare impairment. Experts also assessed the relevance of each indicator for overall welfare assessment and their certainty in the assessment, both on 0–100 scales. In total, 11 welfare indicators were evaluated. Responses are provided in broiler welfare indicator evaluation.csv in long format, with one row per respondent × indicator × level. Twenty experts completed this section. A separate section asked experts to select 10 suitable welfare indicators from a broader list of 26 candidate indicators and assign each selected indicator an importance score between 0 and 100. These responses are provided in broiler welfare preference evaluation.csv . Situation-based survey The situation-based survey used paired comparisons of multidimensional welfare situations. Each comparison consisted of Situation A and Situation B, described by values for multiple welfare indicators. The indicators included in this survey were selected based on the indicator-based survey, resulting in a subset of 10 indicators; flock distribution was excluded. The experimental design consisted of 300 comparison tasks organized into 30 groups of 10 tasks.
evidence_items.title: Welfare expert evaluation of individual broiler welfare indicators and multidimensional welfare situations

evidence_items.summary: Security operations centres investigate a bounded number of alerts per day, yet anomaly detectors for authentication logs are mostly compared by threshold-free metrics. We present AuthBench, an open harness that checks the temporal order of its partitions, ranks events, edge-hours and user-days within each day, gives every red-team campaign the daily budget at which it is first detected, and sets each result against its distribution under a random ranking and against label-free rankings of the same units. On the LANL authentication log, under the protocol of Larroche (2026), whose event set we reproduce exactly, we evaluate ten detectors without reading a label. No detector places an event of any of the 162 red-team campaigns within 10 alerts per day, and the best detects 7 of them within 500. The earliest detections of the operation rest on one fit or on a partial first test day. Ranked by user-day, Euler reaches 51.2% of the campaigns at 500 per day, but ranking users by how many computers they touched that day, with no detector, reaches 56.8%: the coarser unit measures the fan-out of the compromised accounts. In this protocol, neither ROC-AUC nor AUC-PR orders the detectors by their campaign budgets; a campaign-weighted average precision does. The authors' Euler code, rerun on the same data with the defaults of its run script, stays within 0.0027 of its published AUC but below half its published average precision in all five runs; its first author indicates that the published row, a mean of five runs, probably used larger hidden layers and a higher learning rate, which remain to be run. We reconcile both test sets edge by edge. The labelled activity is one intrusion, mostly from one host: these results are a case study of one operation.
evidence_items.title: AuthBench: Temporally Leak-Free, Alert-Budget Evaluation of Authentication Anomaly Detectors, with a LANL Case Study

evidence_items.summary: This dataset accompanies the article "Weaving Rather Than Understanding: A Philosophical Analysis of Large Language Models Translating Traditional Chinese Medicine". It contains: (1) the eight Chinese source passages of the Guizhi decoction-related formulae of the Shanghan Lun, with bibliographic pointers to the two standard published English translations, neither of which is reproduced; (2) the prompt templates used to elicit the renderings; (3) the cleaned English renderings of six large language models (GPT-4.1, Qwen2.5, Mistral Large 2, GLM-4.5, Doubao-Seed-1.6, DeepSeek-V3) at three levels of context; (4) the coded entries of ten domain experts, comprising 420 relation-identification judgements and 35 six-dimension ratings, together with the two rating instruments and a codebook; (5) the analysis code, which reproduces every statistic reported in the article from the deposited entries using only the Python standard library; and (6) the complete statistical results. Headline findings: relations carried by a lexical marker were identified in 90.0% of judgements, those requiring inference in 68.3%, and the single relation whose content has no lexical trace in 56.7%. The intraclass correlation across the renderings rated by two or more experts is 0.323, and identification rates range from 47.6% to 100% across the ten experts — the disagreement being the article's central empirical finding. No third-party translation is reproduced. The signed consent forms and the code-to-model mapping are withheld, as explained in the README.
evidence_items.title: LLM Translation of Guizhi Decoction Formulae: Model Outputs and a Ten-Expert Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: This poster presents the Research Data Director, a persona-based architecture for applying agentic AI to the preparation, description, and publication of research data.  This was presented at the Research Data Alliance p-27 Plenary as both poster and presentaion within the session  'From AI Governanece to AI Deployment Session: Trust-Centered Strategies for Agentic AI.  Agentic AI infrastructures are systems in which language-model agents reason together from a situation, utilize call tools, and coordinate with one another rather than following a fixed script. They offer new capacities for the labor-intensive work of making research data Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable (FAIR). The central design choice of this blueprint is to organize that capacity not by abstract technical function but by professional persona: each agent is modeled on a credentialed human role in a research library or institution and specified as an expert with defined competence, experience, higher education and bounded authority, and an obligation to escalate decisions beyond its scope. A coordinating Research Data Director dispatches a team of specialist persona based agents for intake, metadata generation, verification, FAIR evaluation, and provenance. The system uses two established multi-agent patterns: orchestrator-workers dispatch and an evaluator-optimizer critique loop. The environmental open ended persona approach takes advantage of LLM model intelligence to yield more coherent, auditable, and trustworthy behavior than capability-based decomposition, while going through a rigorous verification, fact checking and FAIR ethical process while keeping every irreversible act under human authority. The document specifies both the conceptual architecture and a concrete, buildable implementation — agent specification files, shared-memory design, human-checkpoint logic, and open agent protocols (MCP and A2A) — beginning with a minimal working prototype.
evidence_items.title: The Research Data Director A Persona-Based Agentic AI Blueprint and Application for FAIR Research Data, Metadata, and Schema and Crosswalk Workflows

evidence_items.summary: Most agent-memory benchmarks frame long-term memory as retrieval: can an agent recover the relevant record from a long and evolving history? Scientific agents face a stricter problem: a correctly remembered fact may still be invalid to use. The same reported test result can support confirmation when the outcome and stopping rule were fixed in advance, yet only exploration when the outcome was selected from twenty inspected results. We call this scientific use validity: whether remembered evidence is eligible to influence a decision under the state governing its interpretation. We introduce SciValidityBench, an executable benchmark factory with 64 TaskSpecs spanning five validity modules and six scientific domains. TaskSpecs couple generated experimental histories with scientific-state definitions, programmatic decision oracles, controlled interventions, and automatic scoring. The SciStateForge compiler-reader framework turns distributed histories into explicit decision-governing state. Counterfactual pairs and targeted corruption-repair controls then test whether models use those dependencies and localize failures. Across four model families, compiled scientific state improves valid decision-making by 9.2-18.8 percentage points over a generic Event Graph. Retrieval alone does not reproduce this cross-family gain, while content-identical flat and typed views show that the improvement comes from exposing governing state rather than a particular graph serialization. SciValidityBench thus shifts memory evaluation from finding the right fact to deciding whether that fact should control the decision.
evidence_items.title: The Right Fact, the Wrong Decision: SciValidityBench for Scientific Agent Memory

evidence_items.summary: Electric vehicles (EV) play a crucial role in transforming the transportation sector to become more sustainable, cleaner, and energy efficient. Given that EVs are generally parked and ready for charging for a great majority of time, advanced charging management techniques can take advantage of this opportunity to lower charging costs and more effectively harness the potential of renewable energy sources (RES). To address this objective, the paper proposes an optimal charging management strategy based on model predictive control (MPC), which relies on a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) algorithm for online optimization of charging power of individual EVs within a fleet. The proposed strategy is formulated in two forms: (i) direct optimization of individual EV charging power and (ii) optimization of aggregate charging power distributed to individual EVs through a heuristic algorithm (hierarchical approach). The two strategies are evaluated against an offline optimization benchmark in terms of charging cost, RES energy utilization, and related optimization time execution for the case of one-week period, virtually electrified delivery vehicle fleet of a local retail company, and a two-tariff electricity price model. A dumb charging strategy, which simply performs charging under maximal power immediately upon EVs connection, is also used as an evaluation baseline.
evidence_items.title: MILP-based Model Predictive Control of Electric Vehicle Fleet Charging in  the presence of Electricity Production from Renewable Energy Sources

evidence_items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) and autonomous tool-using agents (such as OpenClaw and Claude Code ) suffer from threefundamental systems bottlenecks during extended operation: (1) Context Rot, the progressive degradation of factual recall,temporal rule tracking, and safety policy compliance as historical scrollback and noisy tool logs accumulate in the prompt; (2)Linear-to-Quadratic Token Inflation, where standard chat APIs re-transmit the entire conversation history on every turn (O(n)prompt token accumulation and O(n²) attention compute) while frontier reasoning models consume hundreds of output tokens perturn; and (3) Open-Loop Unverified Execution, where conventional Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) acts solely as apassive pre-generation filter with no post-generation causal verification or destructive tool-call veto. This paper presents the blackbox systems architecture, mathematical formulation, live Teacher–Student gateway telemetry, N = 10,000-document ablationbenchmarks, and independent multi-model peer assessments of QDAS Brain™ (Quantum-Dynamic Associative SynapticEngine).
evidence_items.title: QDAS Brain™: A Closed-Loop Sparse Associative Memory, Token Compression, and Autonomous Agent Arbitration Gateway — Empirical Benchmark at N = 10,000 Memories and Independent Multi-Model Systems

evidence_items.summary: Background The accurate detection of clinical symptoms in electronic health records (EHRs) is pivotal for advancing large-scale genetic and longitudinal studies in psychiatry. Free-text clinical notes are an essential source of symptom-level information, particularly in psychiatry; however, the automated extraction of symptoms from clinical text remains challenging. Objective We aimed to evaluate the ability of open-source generative large language models (LLMs) to detect psychiatric symptom-level concepts from clinical text in Spanish and to develop a new fine-tuned, open-source LLM that can be shared without risk of exposing patient information. Methods We tested 11 open-source generative LLMs for their ability to detect 109 psychiatric concepts from clinical text, using annotated EHR notes from a psychiatric hospital in Colombia. The LLMs were evaluated both “out-of-the-box” and after fine-tuning and compared against a traditional natural language processing (tNLP) method developed from the same data. To develop a fine-tuned LLM that can be shared without risk of exposing patient information, we created a novel synthetic dataset, leveraging real concept annotations while generating fully synthetic clinical text, and fine-tuned a top-performing LLM on these data. Fine-tuned model generalizability was assessed through cross-site evaluation using data from a second independent hospital in Colombia. Results We show that while base LLM performance was poor to moderate (zero-shot: 0.2-0.6 macro-F1; few-shot: 0.2-0.74 macro-F1), it improved significantly after fine-tuning (0.75-0.86 macro-F1), with several fine-tuned LLMs outperforming the tNLP method. In total, 100 psychiatric concepts could be reliably detected (F1>0.8) using either a fine-tuned LLM or tNLP.
evidence_items.title: Generative Large Language Models for Psychiatric Concept Detection in Spanish-Language Electronic Health Records: Development and Evaluation Study

evidence_items.summary: AI agents must decide when another search is worth its cost. Answer-success probabilities capture question difficulty, while this decision requires estimating the additional benefit of search. We introduce SearchHorizonBench, a benchmark for learning and evaluating search value from execution experience. Paired continuations and repeated executions separate expected search gain from generation noise and connect prediction quality to decision utility. The resource contains 45,632 executions across 3,168 questions. On 1,632 held-out questions, historical calibration reduces Brier error by 16.2%, with the improvement concentrated in success-level information. Search gains have a standard deviation of 21.4 percentage points, and tested historical estimators explain less than 2% of this variance in point estimates. Matched-configuration learning curves probe this distinction across training scales. At the reference token price, free selection observations yield a 2.49-point utility opportunity over the best constant action, driven primarily by gain information. Reusable histories, frozen splits, strong baselines and scoring tools provide a common foundation for developing and evaluating value-aware search agents.
evidence_items.title: SearchHorizonBench: A Benchmark for Search Value in AI Agents

evidence_items.summary: Objective: To evaluate the triage accuracy, response quality, safety, and repeatability of widely used large language models (LLMs) in urologic emergencies and to examine their potential clinical utility and risks. Methods: We developed 50 standardized clinical vignettes covering 10 categories of urologic emergencies, including testicular torsion, acute urinary retention, and Fournier gangrene. The set comprised high-risk vignettes requiring immediate emergency care, borderline vignettes, and atypical vignettes containing misleading cues. Six commercially available LLMs—Kimi 3.0, DeepSeek V4, Qwen 3.8-MAX, GPT-5.6 Sol (ChatGPT), Claude Opus 4.8, and Ant Afu (AQ)—were evaluated in Chinese-language interactions. Each vignette was submitted three times in independent conversations. Two urologists with more than 10 years of clinical experience assessed triage accuracy using a three-level reference standard (immediate emergency department [ED] evaluation, routine outpatient evaluation, or home observation). They also rated response quality across eight dimensions using a 5-point Likert scale and evaluated medical-error severity (0–3), response stability, and Chinese readability. Overall differences were assessed using the Friedman test, followed by pairwise Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Holm adjustment. Results: A total of 900 responses were generated. Overall three-class accuracy was 89.11%, and the macro-averaged F1 score was 85.73%. Qwen achieved the highest accuracy (94.00%), whereas Claude achieved the lowest (80.67%). However, none of the pairwise comparisons between models reached statistical significance after Holm adjustment. All models generally recognized scenarios requiring immediate ED evaluation, but their ability to distinguish routine outpatient evaluation from home observation varied substantially.
evidence_items.title: Evaluation of Large Language Models for Emergency Triage in Urology: A Multi-Model Study

evidence_items.summary: Background: Large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, and Mistral are increasingly used to obtain medical information, but their accuracy in carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS) management is uncertain. This study evaluated whether LLM-generated recommendations align with American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS) clinical practice guidelines (CPGs). Methods: Four LLMs (ChatGPT-4, Gemini, Claude-3, Mistral-7B) were queried with standardized prompts derived from AAOS CTS CPGs. Each prompt was asked 3 times per model, and responses were synthesized. Two blinded reviewers graded outputs as concordant, discordant, or indeterminate, with disagreements resolved by consensus. Concordance distributions were compared using χ 2 testing with Bonferroni correction. Inter-rater reliability was measured with Cohen’s κ. Results: Across 252 recommendations, 72.6% were concordant, 11.5% discordant, and 15.9% indeterminate. ChatGPT achieved the highest concordance (92.1%) and lowest discordance (1.6%), while Mistral performed poorest (52.4% concordance, 17.5% discordance). Reviewer agreement was excellent (κ = 0.91). Conclusions: Over 1 in 4 LLM-generated CTS recommendations were not concordant with AAOS CPGs. ChatGPT outperformed other models, though variable performance underscores the need for clinician oversight and careful validation before clinical use.
evidence_items.title: Evaluation of Large Language Model Concordance With AAOS Clinical Practice Guidelines for Carpal Tunnel Syndrome

evidence_items.summary: Masked diffusion language models repeatedly compute representations for unresolved tokens, but conventional denoisers do not explicitly retain these representations for reuse across steps. We introduce Temporal Self-Conditioning Diffusion Language Model (TDLM), which lets each unresolved position attend to its own history of hidden representations within a frozen denoiser. This gives later predictions access to computation already performed. Training uses self-generated trajectories and a simple cross-entropy objective for tokens revealed between consecutively sampled decoding steps, while causal temporal attention permits parallel evaluation during training. On LLaDA, the temporal modules add only approximately 0.84% trainable parameters. Across LLaDA and Dream, the main comparison shows up to 7.15× faster generation than the corresponding original diffusion language model, with competitive answer quality on the evaluated tasks. These results motivate temporal memory as a practical way to make more effective use of repeated denoising computation.
evidence_items.title: TDLM: Temporal Self-Conditioning Diffusion Language Model

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Objective To evaluate the extent to which large language models (LLMs) reproduce human assessments of the quality of stroke-related information on social media. Background Social media is a major source of health information, yet content quality varies. The reliability of LLMs in evaluating stroke-related social media content against human assessments remains uncertain. Methods This cross-sectional study evaluated 50 TikTok and Instagram videos using human reference scores and three AI models: ChatGPT, Microsoft 365 Copilot, and Claude. Publicly unavailable videos and those featuring songs or lacking transcribable speech were excluded. Spoken audio was transcribed using a free tool, and transcripts were submitted to all three models with an identical standardized prompt. Scores were compared using Mann–Whitney U tests; Spearman’s correlation assessed associations with human ratings, and linear regression quantified explained variance. Results The median human reference score was 37.00 (IQR, 35.00–45.00). All AI models scored significantly lower: ChatGPT, 34.50 (p = 0.001); Microsoft Copilot, 33.50 (p < 0.001); and Claude, 26.00 (p < 0.001). All models correlated significantly with human ratings, with the strongest association for Claude (ρ = 0.593; p < 0.001), followed by ChatGPT (ρ = 0.550; p < 0.001) and Copilot (ρ = 0.396; p = 0.004). Claude explained 32.1% of the variance in human scores (R² = 0.321), compared with 31.4% for ChatGPT and 14.8% for Copilot. Inter-model correlation was strongest between ChatGPT and Copilot (ρ = 0.862; p < 0.001). Conclusions All three LLMs showed significant positive correlations with human ratings but systematically assigned lower scores. Claude showed the strongest correlation, whereas Microsoft Copilot showed the weakest. These findings highlight the limitations of LLMs in reproducing human judgments and the need for further validation before their use as standalone evaluators of social media content.
evidence_items.title: Can Large Language Models Judge Stroke Information on Social Media? A Cross-Sectional Comparison of Large Language Models Against Human Ratings of Health-Related Videos

organizations: Cogdel School Chengdu
evidence_items.summary: Formal mathematics has a data problem, and large language models have become one of the tools applied to it. LeanConjecturer mined 40 seed files from Mathlib and produced 12,289 candidate statements, of which 3,776 resisted the automated tactic used as a filter. AlphaGeometry solved 25 of 30 olympiad geometry problems by letting a language model propose auxiliary constructions whenever symbolic deduction stalled. FunSearch improved on earlier results for the cap set problem by having an evaluator score programs written by a model. Evidence of this kind still supports a narrower claim than mathematical discovery. Five studies are compared in this review: LeanConjecturer, the Conjecturing-Proving Loop, AlphaGeometry, FunSearch, and Unlearning as Ablation. Using literature analysis and comparative case analysis, task objectives, generation mechanisms, verification procedures, and evidential limits are examined side by side. Two findings stand out. External verification is what makes candidate selection and iterative repair function in each system, and each system demonstrates a different slice of the work: conjecture supply, proof repair, geometric construction, program optimization, and, in the case of Unlearning as Ablation, a proposal for auditing knowledge provenance. Correctness, novelty, and independence from previously acquired target knowledge remain three separate questions that require three separate kinds of evidence. A more reliable evaluation framework would combine auditable knowledge boundaries, dependency checking, and expert assessment of mathematical significance.
evidence_items.title: Large Language Models for Mathematical Discovery: Generation, Verification, and Knowledge Provenance

organizations: Guangdong University of Science and Technology

evidence_items.summary: Background Increasing use of large language models in nursing education has raised questions about the association between reliance on these tools and academic distress. This study examined direct and specific indirect associations between large language model dependence (LMD) and academic anxiety (AA) through artificial intelligence addiction (AIA) and academic burnout (AB). Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted from March to April 2026 among 473 nursing students in Guangdong Province, China, including students undertaking clinical placements. The four constructs were assessed using items selected from published self-report instruments. Partial least squares structural equation modeling was performed with age and sex included as covariates. Direct and specific indirect associations were evaluated using bootstrapping with 5,000 resamples. Results Cronbach’s α ranged from 0.914 to 0.944, composite reliability from 0.935 to 0.954, and average variance extracted from 0.560 to 0.721. Heterotrait–monotrait ratios ranged from 0.485 to 0.733, supporting discriminant validity. Model fit evidence was mixed: SRMR was 0.068, whereas NFI was 0.812, below the 0.90 reference value. The model explained 49.2% of the variance in academic anxiety. Large language model dependence showed a small positive direct association with academic anxiety ( β = 0.138, 95% CI [0.006, 0.278], p = 0.048). Significant specific indirect associations were identified through academic burnout ( β = 0.205, 95% CI [0.123, 0.303]) and through artificial intelligence addiction followed by academic burnout ( β = 0.098, 95% CI [0.049, 0.147]); both p &lt; 0.001. Conclusion Large language model dependence was positively associated with academic anxiety among nursing students, with specific indirect associations through academic burnout and through artificial intelligence addiction followed by academic burnout.
evidence_items.title: The association between large language model dependence and academic anxiety among nursing students: statistical indirect associations through artificial intelligence addiction and academic burnout

organizations: Department of Organization and Management, Faculty of Economics and Business, University of Zagreb, Trg J. F. Kennedyja 6, 10000 Zagreb, Croatia
evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence in corporate boards refers to the use of data-driven computational systems, including machine learning, predictive analytics, natural language processing and generative models, to support the work of boards of directors in one-tier systems and supervisory boards in two-tier systems. Executive management, including management boards in two-tier systems, is considered insofar as it supplies information to or is overseen by these bodies. Such systems are applied to the established functions of the board: monitoring and control, strategic direction, advice and counsel to executive management, and the provision of information, expertise and external linkages. Applications range from anomaly and compliance monitoring to environmental scanning, scenario modeling and the synthesis of board materials. A distinction is essential between decision support, in which systems supply information and analysis; decision augmentation, in which board members and systems jointly shape an evaluation; and autonomous decision-making, in which a system determines an outcome without human deliberation; board-level use is discussed in the literature almost entirely in the first two modes. The central governance tension is that capabilities which expand the information-processing capacity of a body constrained by limited meeting time and by dependence on management-supplied reporting also introduce opacity, vendor dependence and new difficulty in attributing responsibility. Under prevailing corporate governance arrangements, formal responsibility for board decisions remains with the human members of the relevant governing body. Responsible use therefore rests on explicit governance arrangements: defined human oversight, documentation, verification, data governance and board-level competence.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Corporate Boards

evidence_items.summary: Introduction Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being explored in dental education as a tool to support teaching, learning, assessment, and clinical decision-making. This systematic review synthesized current evidence on the implementation and educational impact of AI technologies in undergraduate, postgraduate, and continuing dental education. Methodology A PRISMA-guided systematic review was conducted using Scopus, PubMed, and IEEE Xplore. Studies published between 2020 and 2025 evaluating AI applications in dental education were identified using predefined PICO criteria. Educational outcomes included knowledge acquisition, diagnostic accuracy, clinical reasoning, procedural skills, learner engagement, and perceptions of AI-assisted learning. Results The included literature reflects an expansion from machine learning, deep learning, and computer vision systems primarily evaluated for diagnostic support toward generative AI platforms, including large language models and retrieval-augmented generation systems. Across the included studies, AI applications were frequently associated with favorable diagnostic and examination performance and, in selected educational contexts, with supportive findings related to clinical reasoning, technical competency, feedback, and self-directed learning. However, the evidence was predominantly based on technical performance assessments and observational or cross-sectional designs. Discussion AI is increasingly being explored as a potential complementary educational resource, with applications including interactive tutoring, adaptive learning, and support for clinical reasoning. Nevertheless, heterogeneous methodologies and limited longitudinal evidence indicate the need for standardized educational evaluation and responsible curricular integration. Conclusion AI shows potential as a complementary resource in dental education.
evidence_items.title: Artificial intelligence in odontology education

organizations: University of Birmingham, School of Computer Science, University of Birmingham, Birmingham, United Kingdom
evidence_items.summary: Learning paths personalized by behavior have become common among personalized learning systems. However, the traditional methods are usually inefficient at building coherent paths as the learner's knowledge state changes dynamically, and the prerequisite structure exists. In light of this problem, we present a generative learning-path optimization framework based on EdNet-KT1 interaction dataset, Transformer knowledge tracing model, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct candidate generator, and constraint-aware reranking. Mastery profiles of learners are extracted, and then five ten-resource candidate paths are generated and sorted according to learning gain, prerequisites, difficulty deviation, and repetition. We compare our method to collaborative filtering, GRU4Rec, and knowledge-tracing greedy recommendation on offline experiments. The generative optimizer gets NDCG@10 of 0.589, future-concept coverage of 0.721, and prerequisite violation rate of 0.031, and thus outperforms the best baseline on all three metrics. Ablation analysis shows that the prerequisite violation rate rises to 0.091 without constraints, and the learning gain drops to 0.104 without the learning gain term, respectively. Moreover, the full model still achieves better NDCG@10 performance on all learner history categories than other baselines, costing 0.84 s per learner with the memory peak of 13.6 GB. This research demonstrates the effectiveness of combining the generation of learning paths with pedagogical constraints.
evidence_items.title: Personalized Learning Path Optimization Based on Generative Artificial Intelligence

evidence_items.summary: Objective Clarify the effects of large-language-model types and health-education content categories on generated-text quality (patient-education suitability, overall quality) and readability, so as to provide empirical evidence for standardized AI-assisted health-communication applications. Methods This cross-sectional study was conducted between July 10 and July 15, 2026. Twenty herpes zoster-related questions were developed by a dermatologist and a pharmacist and categorized into five themes. The questions were then entered into five mainstream large language models (GPT-5, Doubao, DeepSeek, Qianwen, and Gemini), generating 100 textual responses. Response quality was assessed using the Chinese version of the Patient Education Materials Assessment Tool for Printable Materials (C-PEMAT-P) and Global Quality Score (GQS). Readability was evaluated via seven indices including the Automated Readability Index (ARI) and Flesch Reading Ease Score (FRES). Readability outcomes were compared using one-way repeated-measures analysis of variance with Greenhouse–Geisser correction. C-PEMAT-P raw totals and ordinal GQS scores were compared using Friedman tests. Post-hoc comparisons were adjusted using the Holm method. Category-level comparisons were performed using linear mixed-effects models with likelihood-ratio χ 2 tests for continuous outcomes and an ordinal generalized estimating equation with a Wald χ 2 test for GQS. Results Significant overall differences among models were observed for all seven readability indices and both assessment scores (all p &lt; 0.001). Median C-PEMAT-P raw total scores were 12.50, 11.00, 10.00, 9.00 and 9.00 for GPT-5, Doubao, DeepSeek, Qianwen and Gemini, respectively; corresponding median GQS scores were 5.00, 4.00, 4.00, 3.00, and 3.00. After Holm correction, GPT-5 achieved higher scores than each of the other models on both assessment measures.
evidence_items.title: Artificial intelligence chatbots as information sources for herpes zoster: an evaluation of patient-education suitability, overall quality, and readability

organizations: Drs. Kiran & Pallavi Patel Global University (KPGU), Vadodara, Gujarat, India
evidence_items.summary: The transition from academic education to professional employment requires students to communicate technical skills, projects, certifications, education, and experience in a form that is relevant to a specific job. This paper presents an AI-based resume analysis and job-matching approach designed to provide understandable, job-specific feedback to engineering students. The system accepts a PDF resume and a target job description, extracts resume text using pdfplumber with pypdf as a fallback, and submits the normalized information to an AI analysis component. The revised methodology makes the compatibility score more transparent by interpreting it through three dimensions: required-skill coverage, semantic relevance between resume evidence and job requirements, and evidence strength from projects, education, and experience. The system returns four structured outputs: an ATS-style compatibility score, matched skills, missing or insufficiently represented skills, and actionable recommendations. Unlike a commercial Applicant Tracking System, the score is explicitly positioned as a decision-support estimate rather than an employer-generated recruitment score. Implementation-level testing on three sample technical cases produced compatibility scores of 78%, 64%, and 71%, with a mean of 71.0%. These values demonstrate functional variation across job-specific inputs but are not treated as predictive accuracy because the current study does not use a sufficiently large labeled benchmark. A literature-grounded comparison further shows that existing approaches emphasize resume information extraction, skill taxonomy alignment, deep-learning recommendation, or job recommendation, whereas the proposed system integrates these ideas into a student-facing feedback workflow.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence (AI)-Based Resume Analysis and Job Matching

organizations: Dazhou Vocational College of Chinese Medicine
evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background As AI becomes integrated into nursing education and clinical practice, students must develop the competence to use, evaluate, and ethically govern AI-generated information. However, the psychological mechanisms linking students’ emotional responses to AI and their AI literacy remain underexplored in vocational nursing contexts. This study aimed to examine the mediating role of artificial intelligence (AI) self-efficacy in the relationship between AI anxiety and AI literacy among higher vocational nursing students. Methods A cross-sectional study was conducted using a convenience sample of 921 nursing students from five higher vocational colleges in Sichuan, China. Participants completed the Chinese Artificial Intelligence Anxiety Scale, the revised Chinese Artificial Intelligence Self-Efficacy Scale, and the Artificial Intelligence Literacy Scale. Structural equation modeling was used to test the mediating hypothesis. Results AI anxiety was negatively correlated with AI self-efficacy (r = − 0.470) and AI literacy (r = − 0.370), while AI self-efficacy was positively correlated with AI literacy (r = 0.392). AI self-efficacy partially mediated the association between AI anxiety and AI literacy, accounting for 42.22% of the total effect (indirect effect β = −0.171, 95% BC CI [− 0.255, − 0.100]). After adjustment for covariates, attitude toward nursing and residence remained independently associated with AI literacy. Conclusions AI literacy among higher vocational nursing students is shaped by psychological (AI anxiety, AI self-efficacy), professional (attitude toward nursing), and educational (residence) factors. AI education should be embedded in competency-based nursing preparation with emphasis on critical evaluation, safe application, professional accountability, and equitable access to structured learning opportunities.
evidence_items.title: Artificial intelligence anxiety and literacy among higher vocational nursing students: the mediating role of artificial intelligence self-efficacy in a cross-sectional study

evidence_items.summary: The incorporation of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the design and analysis of renewable energy systems has become a revolutionary method for enhancing efficiency, reliability and sustainability. AI-driven models provide intelligent forecasting, optimization, and regulation of renewable energy sources, including solar, wind, hydro and biofuels. Utilizing techniques such as machine learning, deep learning, and evolutionary algorithms, AI enables precise forecasting of energy production, dynamic load regulation and fault identification. This chapter examines the approaches and frameworks for integrating AI into the design and performance evaluation of renewable energy systems. Focus is directed towards data-driven enhancement of system components, energy storage administration, and smart grid incorporation. The results indicate that AI integration improves energy conversion efficiency and operational stability while facilitating the shift to cleaner, more adaptable energy systems.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence-Integrated Design and Analysis of Renewable Energy Sources

organizations: Christ The King Cathedral High School
evidence_items.summary: Diagnosis of an ACL injury is followed by a personalized rehabilitation program and subsequent decisions regarding sport resumption. AI algorithms may be used in assessing such patients and readiness for sports participation using imaging and biomechanical parameters. This review summarizes the current status of AI-supported ACL diagnosis via clinical examination and MRI, rehabilitation and return-to-sport assessment. Using wearable sensors with machine learning, clinicians can quantify movement during the clinical examination of knee joint. Furthermore, deep-learning models showed promise in detection of ACL tears via MRI imaging. During the rehabilitation process, AI can help quantify movement-related load, detect strength asymmetries and predict functional recovery afterwards. Return-to-sport models can integrate physical and psychologic patient's data to predict readiness to resume training and the risk of re-injury. Nevertheless, all these applications answer different clinical questions and good performance in research datasets does not ensure the effectiveness of these tools in clinical practice. The limitations in the patient populations, measurement approaches and definitions of outcome, as well as a lack of external validation, decrease the generalizability of results. Thus, AI models should give clear and verifiable information which clinicians can apply in clinical practice.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence in ACL Injury Diagnosis and Physical Therapy Rehabilitation

evidence_items.summary: Plain Language Summary How Artificial Intelligence Could Improve Psychiatric Drug Development Developing new medicines for mental health conditions is difficult, expensive, and often unsuccessful. One reason is that people with the same diagnosis can differ greatly in their underlying biology and in how they respond to treatment. Clinical trials also rely heavily on symptom ratings and can be affected by placebo responses. This editorial explains how artificial intelligence (AI) could help at several stages of psychiatric drug development. AI can help researchers identify promising drug targets, design new treatment molecules, and use biological, brain-imaging, and clinical data to predict treatment response and improve clinical trials. Emerging approaches include digital twins, synthetic control groups, and digital measures of symptoms and behaviour. However, these technologies are still developing and should not be viewed as a solution to all the challenges of psychiatric drug development. Wider use will require representative datasets, strong data governance, transparent and interpretable models, rigorous clinical validation, and appropriate regulation.
evidence_items.title: From Target to Trial: Artificial Intelligence in Psychiatric Drug Development

evidence_items.summary: Abstract. We study revenue maximization in the unit-demand single-buyer setting. Our main result is that Uniform-Ironed-Virtual-Value Item Pricing guarantees a tight 3-approximation to Duality Relaxation Benchmark (Chawla, Malec, and Sivan, EC’10 and GEB’15; Cai, Devanur, and Weinberg, STOC’16 and [ SIAM J. Comput., 50 (2021), pp. STOC16-160–STOC16-200]), breaking the barrier of 4 since Chawla et al. [ Proceedings of STOC’10, 2010, pp. 311–320] and Chawla, Malec, and Sivan (EC’10 and GEB’15). To our knowledge, this is the first benchmark-tight revenue guarantee of any simple multi-item mechanism. Technically, all previous work employs Myerson Auction as an intermediary. The barrier of 4 follows as Uniform-Ironed-Virtual-Value Item Pricing achieves a tight 2-approximation to Myerson Auction , which then achieves a tight 2-approximation to Duality Relaxation Benchmark . Instead, our new approach avoids Myerson Auction , thus enabling the improvement. Central to our work are a benchmark-based 3-competitive prophet inequality and its fully constructive proof. Such prophet inequality variants will likely find applications in, e.g., multi-item mechanism design, when the optimal revenue objective is relaxed to various more accessible benchmarks. We complement our benchmark-tight ratio with an impossibility result. All previous works, including ours, follow the single-dimensional representative approach introduced by Chawla, Hartline, and Kleinberg [ Proceedings of EC’07, 2007, pp. 243–251]. Against Duality Relaxation Benchmark , it turns out that this approach cannot beat our bound of 3 for a large class of Item Pricing .
evidence_items.title: Benchmark-Tight Approximation Ratio of Simple Mechanism for a Unit-Demand Buyer

evidence_items.summary: Introduction Assessing residual contamination in coastal wetland soils after oil-well retirement requires comparisons with both active oil-well sites and natural reference wetlands. Methods We analyzed a September 2022 soil survey from the Liao River estuary wetlands in northeastern China, comprising five active oil-well plots, five retired oil-well plots, and three reference wetland plots. Three separately collected surface soil samples were averaged per plot, giving 13 independent analytical units. Soil properties, total petroleum hydrocarbons (TPHs), and five trace metals were compared among well-status groups. Results Mean TPH concentrations were 35.71 g/kg in active plots, 12.95 g/kg in retired plots, and 1.20 g/kg in reference plots (exact Kruskal–Wallis P &lt; 0.001; false-discovery-rate-adjusted q = 0.0015). Total organic carbon (TOC) followed the same ordering (43.15, 29.76, and 18.99 g/kg, respectively; P &lt; 0.001; q &lt; 0.001) and was positively associated with TPHs (Spearman rho = 0.76, P = 0.003). No overall group differences were detected for As, Cd, Cr, Cu, or Pb after multiple-testing correction, although one active plot showed locally elevated As, Cd, and Cr benchmark ratios. Discussion Retired plots had lower mean TPH concentrations than active plots, but all retired-plot values exceeded the reference range. These findings support monitoring residual petroleum contamination after oil-well retirement and targeted assessment of local metal enrichment.
evidence_items.title: Contrasting petroleum hydrocarbon contamination across active, retired and reference wetlands in the Liao River estuary

evidence_items.summary: Which computational features can predict the functional consequences of kinase mutations, and where do they stop working? We benchmark five feature families spanning physics-based, docking and learned paradigms — FoldX folding stability, AutoDock Vina docking perturbation, FoldX interaction energy, AlphaMissense and ThermoMPNN-D — against deep mutational scanning of FGFR1–4 kinase domains under pemigatinib and futibatinib selection (7,522 unique variants; Tangermann et al. 2026), adding an erdafitinib-specific docking dimension the screen did not cover. The capability map is non-uniform in three ways. Classical features stay below 0.74 across the panorama but transmit strong signal inside annotated hotspots (0.65–0.88, region-level q ≤ 4.5 × 10⁻⁶). ThermoMPNN-D crosses the conventional 0.7 line where classical FoldX does too: FGFR3 activation reaches 0.877 (95% CI 0.798–0.938, q = 5.1 × 10⁻⁶) and resistance 0.702 — distributed across the domain, not hotspot-driven. Resistance to erdafitinib specifically never exceeds 0.63 on the experimental structure (0.663 on one modelled pose). We trace this staircase to the mechanistic homogeneity of each phenotype and document three distinct failure modes: drug-resistant variants are enriched among those AlphaMissense calls benign; docking features degrade whenever the ligand pose is modelled rather than experimental; classical FoldX has an isoform-specific blind spot on FGFR1. The map converts into 30 falsifiable predictions absent from the screen and from clinical databases. Mechanistic homogeneity, not model sophistication, sets the ceiling for mutation-effect prediction.
evidence_items.title: Mechanistic homogeneity, not model sophistication, sets the ceiling for mutation-effect prediction: a five-family FGFR benchmark against deep mutational scanning

evidence_items.summary: Embodied foundation models now allow robots to act on open-ended instructions, yet success on long-horizon physical tasks also depends on the runtime around the model, which organizes the task, invokes skills, guards execution, and retains experience. Digital agent research treats this runtime, known as the harness, as a first-class design object that can be engineered and even improved from experience, since the same model can perform very differently under different harnesses. Such harness designs do not carry over directly, because physical execution is embodiment-specific, partially observed, time-constrained, and often irreversible, which also makes experience costly to learn from. Embodied AI systems increasingly build similar runtimes, yet the field still lacks a unified view of them. This survey treats the physical agentic harness as a research object in its own right. We define it as the runtime system that maintains task and execution state for an embodied foundation model and mediates the model’s interaction with the physical world through one or more physical bodies. We then review over 200 works and organize them by six functional responsibilities: task orchestration, digital resources, embodied capabilities, execution governance, digital-physical interaction, and persistent evolution. This organization offers a common lens for comparing methods across communities, making explicit how model decisions reach physical execution and how grounded evidence flows back. The reviewed benchmarks and applications provide limited evidence of individual runtime contributions, particularly the effects of execution governance and sustained gains from persistent evolution. We close with open problems in model-harness co-design, capability composition, real-time decision making, distributed execution, and continual improvement from physical experience.
evidence_items.title: Where the Harness Meets the Physical World: A Survey of the Physical Agentic Harness

evidence_items.summary: Cortical resources are allocated into systems specialized for processing ecologically relevant features of the world. These features are typically studied in isolation using controlled experimental stimuli, making it difficult to assess the relative importance of different kinds of features that tend to overlap during natural vision. In the current study, we evaluated the relative contributions of action, agent, and scene features in predicting cortical activity while participants viewed a 1-h nature documentary. We tested four sets of model features: semantic vectors capturing the observed action, agent, and scene features derived from an annotation of the stimulus, as well as low-level visual motion-energy features. We used banded ridge regression to fit vertex-wise encoding models from the combination of all four sets of features. While each set of features predicted neural activity in the expected areas, the action features predicted more widespread activity. A variance partitioning analysis revealed that the action features captured the most unique variance in neural activity across a much larger extent of cortex than the agent or scene features. Our findings suggest that cortical activity during dynamic, natural vision is dominated by features for understanding the actions of others.
evidence_items.title: Action features dominate cortical representation during natural vision.

evidence_items.summary: Machine-learning research on water cyber-physical systems (CPS) is constrained by datasets that are either real but chemically poor, or simulated but free of sensing noise and attacks. We present AquaSense-ICS, an open dataset and benchmark that co-registers (i) a 25.4 h recording window (8.0 h of recorded data, 26% coverage) from a Raspberry Pi 5 edge node (TDS probe and BME680 ambient sensor, 1-2 s sampling, 23,688 records), with (ii) a looped network of 13 nodes (10 junctions, 2 reservoirs, 1 tank) simulated in EPANET-MSX for six water-quality species, (iii) a parameterised library of cyber-attacks (false data injection, replay, denial of service, drift) and unintentional sensor faults with sample-level ground truth, and (iv) augmented and TimeGAN-generated sequences, flagged by an origin column. The attack, fault and water-quality labels are traceable to a seeded generator, a documented rule or a simulation input. We show that the most common way of benchmarking such hybrid data, random row splits and labels computed from the input features, yields near-perfect but uninformative scores (macro-F1 = 0.9998 for Random Forest), and we replace it with a leakage-aware protocol using chronological splits and held-out attack types rather than label reconstruction. Under this protocol, no model exceeds the constant "normal" predictor for attack classification (macro-F1 = 0.465), and the best detectors reach a mean AUROC of 0.64 on attack types unseen during training (0.35-0.93 depending on the type), leaving substantial headroom. Data and simulation files are released under CC BY 4.0 at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23390541, and attack generators and benchmark code under MIT.
evidence_items.title: AquaSense-ICS: A Hybrid Real-Simulated Cyber-Physical Dataset and Leakage-Aware Benchmark for Smart Water Quality Monitoring and Attack Detection

evidence_items.summary: AI agents are increasingly proposed as autonomous experimenters, yet the benchmarks that test them mostly offer cheap experiments that answer at once. Experiments in physical facilities are different: they take months, occupy scarce equipment and cannot be undone. We present SlowLab, a benchmark in which an agent runs a one-year campaign in four simulated greenhouse compartments on a site whose crop, facility and prices are hidden. The agent decides when to plant which climate policy, whether to stop a crop and which measurements to read while crops grow, and at the end recommends one policy, which a private evaluator scores in weather the agent never saw. In a preregistered study on 48 unseen sites, three low-cost language-model agents ended near a standard grower setting and clearly below a Bayesian-optimisation baseline that starts from that setting. They ran the facility as two synchronous batches, so measurements taken during the season never changed what they planted, and these measurements improved no method's result. Letting other methods re-read the evidence a campaign had collected did not yield significantly better recommendations, which points to where the models start and which experiments they try. Code is released under the MIT license.
evidence_items.title: SlowLab: Benchmarking Autonomous AI Agents on a Year of Experiments They Cannot Undo

evidence_items.summary: Language model agents often abandon correct work when a user challenges it, yet simply telling them to stand firm makes them ignore real mistakes. Once an agent reads a complaint, it tends to discount its own earlier checks in order to agree with the user. We introduce Thinking-in-Bets, a training-free method in which an agent writes a short private record of its main claims, the checks supporting them, and its confidence before reading user feedback. When challenged, the agent consults this Claim Checklist to keep verified work intact while investigating uncertain or newly challenged parts. We evaluate five Gemini models (3.5 Flash-Lite, 3.5 Flash, 3.6 Flash, 3.8 Flash, and 4.0 Argon) across eight benchmarks: SWE-Together, SWE-Interact, and DeepSWE for software engineering, Agents' Last Exam for professional reports, Humanity's Last Exam and SycEval for academic reasoning, Vals Finance for financial analysis, and Terminal-Bench for command-line tasks. Recording claims before criticism nearly eliminates false reversals in patch review and protects passing report drafts under mistaken pushback, whereas writing the same record after reading the complaint recovers very little of the gain. In multi-turn coding, pre-reply claim records substantially reduce unnecessary file edits after mistaken complaints, and gating the record so it is written only when the agent is uncertain lowers token overhead while fixing more real bugs than the baseline. Even in non-interactive tasks without user feedback, listing the key claims in a draft and re-checking the weakest one before submission improves both answer accuracy and confidence estimates across all tested models.
evidence_items.title: Thinking-in-Bets at Test Time Reduces Sycophantic Revisions in LLM Agents

evidence_items.summary: We introduce StreamEval with four key features: (1) First interactive streaming video generation benchmark. (2) Fully open source. Benchmark data, evaluation code, protocols, and scoring rules are publicly available. (3) Comprehensive coverage. Five tasks cover avatar dialogue, avatar performance, world generation, instruction editing, and reference editing, with 300 scripted cases lasting 15 to 300 seconds. Ten metrics assess task execution, state consistency, visual fidelity, and audiovisual coordination. (4) Monthly updates. We will evaluate new and updated models and publish leaderboard results monthly. Results from 37 models show that high visual quality and identity retention do not necessarily coincide with reliable request execution or sustained state consistency. The leaderboard is available at https://streameval.ai.
evidence_items.title: StreamEval: Evaluating Interactive Streaming Video Generation Models

evidence_items.summary: Deep Research agents rely on long-horizon reasoning and iterative tool use to solve complex information-seeking tasks. However, adaptive decision-making over these trajectories remains challenging, as agents may stop prematurely when further evidence is needed, continue unnecessarily after sufficient evidence has been gathered, or fail to redirect unproductive trajectories. Existing solutions either require costly model retraining and dense turn-level supervision, or rely on heuristic control rules that are not directly optimized for downstream research utility. This motivates a lightweight, utility-aware alternative for Deep Research control. We formulate adaptive rerouting in long-horizon Deep Research as a state-conditioned trajectory correction problem. Based on this view, we introduce RIVO, a lightweight plug-in framework for adaptive trajectory correction. The agent estimates its research state from lightweight signals and determines whether trajectory redirection is needed. Once triggered, the plug-in modifies the Host token logits to steer generation toward a more promising research direction. Theoretical analysis shows that, under a value-alignment condition and bounded local curvature, a sufficiently small logit intervention can locally improve expected downstream research utility. We further construct BrowseCore, a curated dataset with a paired local corpus, for efficient and controlled Deep Research experimentation. Building on this resource, the plug-in is trained from downstream outcomes, enabling it to learn corrections that improve subsequent research and final task performance. Extensive experiments across multiple Deep Research benchmarks and control settings demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, showing that lightweight logit intervention can improve long-horizon research without retraining the underlying Host model.
evidence_items.title: RIVO: Lightweight Adaptive Rerouting for Deep Research Agents

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background Large language model (LLM) benchmarking in clinical medicine is increasingly reliant on LLM-based assessment frameworks; in these systems, one AI scores the outputs of another. This practice relies on the assumptions of evaluator neutrality and rubric consistency. These assumptions have not been empirically tested in clinical fields. Objective In this study, we aim to directly examine these assumptions by using the PARM (Planning-Action-Reflection-Memory) framework as a theoretical lens to characterize endovascular device selection and clinical reflective reasoning as a clinical field. Methods We developed a scoring rubric (C1-C6) with 40 clinical vignettes and 6 criteria across 5 endovascular fields (peripheral artery disease, abdominal aortic aneurysm, chronic venous insufficiency, coronary in-stent restenosis [ISR], and cerebrovascular/neuroendovascular; 8 vignettes per field). Four LLMs were evaluated as clinical decision support systems: GPT-4o (M1), Claude Sonnet 4.6 (M2), Gemini 1.5 Pro (M3), and Llama 3.3 70B (M4). Two LLMs served as independent raters with the same evaluation criteria: Claude Sonnet 4.6 (rater 1) and GPT-4o (rater 2). The rater identity was intentionally disclosed; the primary research question concerned rater scoring behavior rather than the absolute performance of the model. Human assessment was intentionally excluded because its inclusion would have shifted the study question from rater disagreement to rater accuracy, a distinct and secondary question. Interrater reliability was measured using intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC 2,1) two-way random effects modeling. Results The combined ICC(2,1) was 0.153 (95% CI 0.007‐0.295). In this exploratory study, the low ICC was not distributed randomly: the magnitude of score differences varied across models (M2 Δ=+5, M4 Δ=+31, M1 Δ=−46, and M3 Δ=−158 points).
evidence_items.title: Systematic Scoring Differences in Large Language Model–Based Clinical Benchmarking Reveal Evaluator-Dependent Divergence: Controlled Evaluation Study

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have recently emerged as a promising tool for automatic generation and optimization of high-performance compute kernels. This rapidly growing area spans across hardware platforms and targets programming models such as AscendC, CUDA, and Triton. However, the literature remains fragmented, with substantial variation in generation workflows, training strategies, evaluation protocols, benchmark assumptions, hardware platforms, and reported metrics. This survey provides a structured review of LLM-based automatic kernel generation. We introduce a taxonomy based on the generation-time workflow, separating direct generation, refinement via structured feedback, search-based generation, and adaptive tool-orchestrating agentic systems. We further analyze orthogonal design axes including learning strategy, input representation, output representation, and hardware platform. Beyond method classification, we examine evaluation practices, including benchmark data, harnesses, integrity policies, as well as performance metrics, and discuss why reported results are often difficult to compare. Finally, we use Ascend NPU kernel generation as a cross-platform case study, highlighting challenges introduced by AscendC, host-device co-design, toolchain constraints, and limited public data. We conclude by identifying open problems in robust evaluation, higher-level task optimization, cross-platform transfer, production deployment, and benchmark design.
evidence_items.title: Automatic Kernel Generation with Large Language Models: Taxonomies, Evaluations, and Cross-Platform Challenges

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) may revise decisions after observing peer answers or conversational history. We study wrong-peer conformity - the conditional switch from a private answer to a preselected incorrect option supported by controlled peer-style signals - under a fixed-signal design. On 500-item CommonsenseQA (CSQA) and Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU) samples, Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, Phi-3.5-mini-instruct, and Gemma2-2B-it receive identical wrong targets and answer-only signals while presentation schedule, response schedule, retained history, or source-label wording varies. Sequential-Stepwise sharply reduces wrong-target adoption relative to Sequential-Final for Qwen and Phi but increases it for Gemma on both datasets. A seven-condition ablation shows that extra calls without retained outputs do not explain the Qwen difference; for Qwen2.5-3B, the same broad retained-history pattern appears on both CommonsenseQA and MMLU, where token-matched neutral assistant history reproduces much of the reduction and a short acknowledgment does not. Gemma does not show the same large reduction. In a separate token-matched control, replacing “Source” with “Model” suppresses wrong-target adoption for Qwen and Gemma on both benchmarks. Exploratory Qwen2.5 extensions further reveal sensitivity to checkpoint choice, peer count, and generic-justification message format. Paired inference, 30 aligned subset draws, and pre-exposure target-plausibility stratification support the directional protocol result. Thus, interaction protocol and contextual wording alter the effective conversational input, with effects that remain model- and setting-dependent.
evidence_items.title: Protocol-dependent conformity in open-weight large language models under fixed wrong-peer signals
