evidence_items.summary: Background/Objectives: General-purpose large language models (LLMs) may support medical reporting, but their role in breast ultrasound (BUS) workflows remains uncertain. We evaluated locally deployable open-source LLMs for BUS report quality control, BI-RADS reasoning, and clinical decision support tasks under physician supervision using retrospective, multicenter reports from real-world clinical practice. We further characterized their relative strengths, limitations, and potential assistive roles compared with proprietary models and ultrasound physicians. Methods: We built a multicenter benchmark of 1173 task-specific Chinese BUS reports from three tertiary hospitals. Seven tasks covered report quality control, BI-RADS reasoning and clinical decision support. We evaluated 24 open-source LLMs, 20 proprietary LLMs and six ultrasound physicians. Tasks 1–5 used reference-standard classification metrics. Tasks 6–7 used blinded expert ratings on five-point Likert scales. Results: Open-source LLMs did not differ significantly from proprietary LLMs in basic error detection, findings–impression inconsistency detection, treatment response assessment or follow-up recommendation generation. They performed worse in terminology non-standardization detection, single-modality BI-RADS categorization and multimodal BI-RADS categorization. Mean accuracies were 0.3775 vs. 0.4563, 0.4121 vs. 0.4920 and 0.6149 vs. 0.7178, respectively. In the 210-case human-evaluation subset, physicians outperformed LLMs in basic error detection, findings–impression inconsistency detection, single-modality BI-RADS categorization and multimodal BI-RADS categorization. LLMs received higher expert-rated scores for treatment response assessment and follow-up recommendation generation. Terminology non-standardization detection showed mixed results across physician seniority and model group. Among open-source LLMs, reasoning-capable models outperformed non-reasoning models in six of seven tasks.
evidence_items.title: Benchmarking Open-Source Large Language Models for Breast Ultrasound Report Processing: A Multicenter Study

organizations: Independent Researcher
evidence_items.summary: Agricultural drought represents a devastating threat to food security and agropastoral livelihoods across Africa. While recent machine learning (ML) literature demonstrates high continuous correlation in regional drought forecasting, the overwhelming majority of existing frameworks evaluate models within the same geographical catchment using random or chronologically shuffled cross-validation. Consequently, the operational behavior of drought forecasting models under severe geographic distribution shift remains critically under-characterized. In this study, we present a reproducible, continental-scale, low-resource benchmarking framework evaluating ten forecasting architectures across six major African agricultural basins: the Nile River Basin, Sahelian Agropastoral Belt, Zambezi-Limpopo Basin, Maghreb Zone, Congo Agricultural Transition, and Horn of Africa, over a 44-year observational record (1981-2024) using 100% real CHIRPS v2.0 and ERA5-Land satellite and reanalysis data. Our key findings: (1) spatial domain shift degrades forecasting accuracy by +6.4% to +17.2% MAE; (2) uncalibrated models exhibit catastrophic event-detection failures despite high continuous correlation; (3) a modest 25% local historical calibration budget recovers over 50% of the lost transfer skill; and (4) all improvements are statistically significant (p < 0.05) while consuming less than 15 MB RAM. These results establish parsimonious, probability-calibrated ensemble architectures as a scientifically rigorous, computationally democratic foundation for regional drought early warning in resource-constrained environments.
evidence_items.title: Reliable Early Prediction of Agricultural Drought Under Geographic Shift: A Continental Low-Resource Benchmark for Data-Sparse African Basins

organizations: School of Computer Science, Physics and Technology, HSE University, Saint-Petersburg 194100, Russia

evidence_items.summary: Camera traps are a key tool for non-invasive wildlife monitoring, yet models trained on existing benchmarks often generalize poorly to new regions due to domain shift, class imbalance, and natural variability in illumination, season, and background. We introduce PACTraD, a benchmark of 116,973 annotated camera trap images collected in a protected area of the Baikal region across eight classes (deer, no animals, bear, boar, hare, badger, lynx, wolf), with a pronounced long-tailed distribution (deer: 73.1%; lynx and wolf: 0.3% and 0.2%) and substantial seasonal and lighting variability, including infrared night imagery. The benchmark supports three tasks under a unified, reproducible protocol: classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation. We further propose a domain-specific attention mechanism augmenting self-attention with eleven learnable priors capturing contour, foreground/background separation, bilateral symmetry, discriminative part regions, texture frequency, confidence weighting, motion consistency, gradient enhancement, scale, color invariance, and shape compactness. Evaluated on six backbones for classification and detection and five for segmentation, against no-attention baselines and three generic attention modules (SE, SA, CBAM), it consistently performs best, raising weighted F1 for classification from 0.943 to 0.964 (DINOv3), AP50 for detection from 0.876 to 0.903 (InternImage-H), and mIoU for segmentation from 0.805 to 0.834 (SegMAN), with component-level ablations revealing task-specific contributions of each prior. However, performance on rare species remains limited (macro F1: 0.829 for classification), indicating that further research is needed to address long-tail recognition in camera trap data.
evidence_items.title: PACTraD: Multi-Task Benchmark and Domain-Specific Attention Mechanism for Wildlife Classification, Detection, and Segmentation in Protected Area Camera Trap Data

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Restricted access to claim-level records and confirmed fraud labels limits reproducible healthcare anti-fraud research. We present a relational, longitudinal synthetic benchmark in which “Japan-calibrated” means that selected demographic, utilization, provider, coding, and reimbursement dimensions are constrained by documented Japanese public or aggregate references; it does not imply equivalence to Japanese claim microdata. Clinical trajectories, provider identities, fraud mechanisms, event rates, and claim labels are generated by design. After removing a model-visible target-proxy channel from episode semantics, we generated a new precommitted seed-202611 scenario. Model family and hyperparameters were selected by nested temporal cross-validation on development data using injected amount recovered at a 1% review budget; Platt calibration and the operating threshold were fitted on a separate pre-final interval. The frozen LightGBM pipeline was then evaluated once on 53,609 final-period claims containing 1573 designed positives. Non-interpolated average precision was 0.8403 (95% bootstrap confidence interval 0.8266–0.8545), receiver-operating-characteristic area under the curve was 0.9764, Brier score was 0.01509, and expected calibration error was 0.03375. Reviewing the top 1% selected 537 true positives with no false positives, recall 0.3414, and JPY 128,752,597 in injected amount recovered. Corrected five-seed and designed-scenario results are reported separately as diagnostic evidence because their final partitions had prior access. This is an internal synthetic confirmation, not real-claims validation; the study does not establish Japanese fraud prevalence, claim-level realism, production performance, or deployment readiness.
evidence_items.title: A Japan-calibrated synthetic medical claims benchmark for anti-fraud machine learning
Machine learning dataset and benchmark for accurate T cell receptor–pHLA binding prediction

organizations: Reticular
evidence_items.summary: Polygenic risk scores (PRSs) have improved substantially in predictive performance, yet results remain difficult to compare across studies that differ in cohorts, phenotype definitions, and evaluation procedures. Comparison to machine-learning methods is harder still, since their performance depends strongly on how data are partitioned and whether related individuals leak across splits. Here, we introduce a family-aware benchmark for polygenic prediction built on version 9 of the All of Us Research Program (AoU). The benchmark assigns entire family components to fixed discovery, calibration, and test partitions, reserves first-degree relatives for within-family evaluation, and separates models trained only on AoU discovery data from those using external GWAS summary statistics. This enables direct comparison between conventional PRS pipelines and machine-learning models trained under identical data budgets. We report results for 14 binary disease traits. Our strongest scores explain 5.7-24.9% of liability-scale variance, with particularly strong prediction for Alzheimer's disease, type 2 diabetes, prostate cancer, glaucoma, and inflammatory bowel disease, and match or exceed published commercial and academic scores for most traits. Across 12 traits with interpretable within-family estimates of within-sibship-to-population effect ratio, 11 confidence intervals included a ratio of 1. Type 2 diabetes showed an attenuation ratio of 0.86 [0.76, 0.97].
evidence_items.title: A family-aware All of Us benchmark for polygenic prediction and genomic machine learning

organizations: Department of Informatics, Ionian University, Plateia Tsirigoti 7, 49100 Corfu, Greece
evidence_items.summary: Market-surveillance authorities face a growing volume of digital marketing content spanning video, social-media, influencer, and AI-generated or synthetic media, whose compliance with EU consumer and digital law cannot be assessed manually at scale. We present a deployed decision-support system that screens marketing campaigns against the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive, the General Data Protection Regulation, the Digital Services Act and the AI Act using large language model agents grounded in a curated legal knowledge graph. The system enforces closed-world citation grounding: findings may reference only provisions retrieved from the graph, are validated against it, and are anchored to authentic legal text through CELLAR and ELIs. Around the engine, we build a regulator-in-the-loop calibration methodology combining a human-reviewed gold benchmark of 52 campaigns, an adversarial adjudicator for disputed citations, and a distillation step that converts confirmed errors into human-approved calibration rules. On the frozen benchmark, the deployed configuration recovered 95 of 97 must-find provisions on first-run scoring, met the minimum risk level in 51 of 52 campaigns, missed no gold-relevant routing, and produced one false positive across seven compliant controls. On a pre-designated 15-campaign holdout, calibration reduced unexpected actionable findings from 44 to 5 (11 of 15 campaigns improved, none worsened; exact Wilcoxon p < 0.001) while preserving 1.000 provision recall and 15/15 risk calibration, and improved run-to-run stability from 0.745 to 0.833. Compared to three external single-call baselines with the same closed provision vocabulary (GPT-5.4, GPT-5.6 and the open-weights gpt-oss-120b), the agentic pipeline achieved significantly higher recall (0.979 vs.
evidence_items.title: Regulator-in-the-Loop Compliance Screening: Graph-Grounded LLM Agents with a Continuously Calibrated Benchmark for EU Marketing Law

evidence_items.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly used in manufacturing to design products, plan production, diagnose faults and operate equipment, but their designs and evaluations remain difficult to compare. We analyse 164 studies identified through Scopus, Web of Science and IEEE Xplore to examine manufacturing applications, agentic system designs and evaluation practices, and to identify where evaluation coverage falls short of the evidence that these task and design types would require. We propose taxonomies of applications, agentic designs and evaluation practices, and relate task and design characteristics to the evidence required to assess them. The findings reveal an imbalance between assessing output quality and verifying whether outputs satisfy manufacturing requirements. For planning and decision-making systems, executability and constraint compliance receive limited evaluation, while most evidence comes from offline data or simulation. Limited assessment of safety, stability across repeated runs and performance in industrial settings leaves a gap between demonstrated task performance and evidence of reliable operation under manufacturing conditions. The resulting taxonomies and evidence requirements help researchers select evaluations suited to each manufacturing use case and distinguish demonstrated task performance from evidence of reliable operation.
evidence_items.title: LLM-Based Agentic AI in Manufacturing: A Scoping Review of Applications, System Designs and Evaluation Practices

organizations: University of California, Irvine, Irvine, California, USA
evidence_items.summary: Multi-user extended reality (XR) applications are increasingly deployed in high-stakes settings such as education, healthcare, and enterprise collaboration, where groups of users interact through embodied avatars in a shared virtual space in real time. To meet strict interactive latency requirements, most consumer applications are client-authoritative, where each client computes and broadcasts its own state while the server relays it without validation, leaving security-relevant decisions to untrusted clients. A recent study showed that this design allows a single malicious participant, running a modified client on their own device, to violate five security invariants (perceptual secrecy, state integrity, safety enforcement, availability, and identity integrity), demonstrating eight attacks that compromise the security, privacy, and safety of other users across 20 consumer XR apps. As the ecosystem of multi-user XR continues to grow, systematically auditing this attack surface at scale demands an automated approach. Therefore, in this paper, we design an agentic pipeline that, given an application package, tests each security invariant and emits the runtime instrumentation that reproduces any violation it finds. We use a general-purpose LLM coding agent with access to static analysis, dynamic instrumentation, device management, and network tools, all exposed via the Model Context Protocol. The agent first provisions the app past anti-tamper protections, localizes the enforcement logic through static and dynamic analysis with a short human-guided observation phase per app, and then synthesizes attack scripts that violate security invariants. We evaluate our methodology against a manually validated dataset of attacks against 15 Meta Quest applications. Our agent successfully instrumented 14 out of 15 apps and found violations with an average precision and recall of 0.86 and 0.90 across attacks, enabling systematic security auditing of multi-user XR applications at scale.
evidence_items.title: Agentic Framework for Automated Security Analysis in Multi-User Extended Reality

evidence_items.summary: Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) Channel Sounding (CS) enables ranging on commodity phones, tags, wearables, and IoT devices, but indoor accuracy remains limited by narrow bandwidth, multipath, non-line-of-sight blockage, and corrupted I/Q measurements. This paper presents AutoBLE, a hybrid BLE CS ranging system that combines reliability-aware preprocessing and physics-informed DSP features with a learned model optimized through an agentic digital-twin loop. AutoBLE compensates gain mismatch, identifies unreliable tones, and repairs amplitude and phase artifacts before extracting IFFT-based coarse delay profiles and MUSIC-based fine evidence. The agentic simulator-ML loop iteratively generates synthetic data, trains the model, evaluates it on real captures, and refines the simulator and model through failure analysis. On approximately 16K real BLE CS measurements across 1–90 m in indoor LOS/NLOS settings, AutoBLE achieves 1.515 m MAE and 1.071 m median error, reducing MAE over DSP-only baselines by 15.2%–48.4% and NLOS MAE over a chip-vendor implementation by 41.5%.
evidence_items.title: AutoBLE: Automating BLE Ranging Algorithm Design with Agentic Digital-Twin Optimization

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Automated history-taking in telemedicine has to collect a structured record of a patient’s complaint over many turns while adapting to what the patient answers. MedAgent-RAG is a multi-agent system, implemented as a LangGraph state graph, which keeps an explicit clinical state the slots gathered so far, a ranked differential diagnosis, the questions already asked, the red flags detected, and the current questioning phase, and selects every question as a function of that state, before grounding its final assessment in clinical guidelines retrieved by a parent–child retrieval-augmented pipeline. Evaluated on the MediTOD corpus with a language-model patient simulator, the system raises BERTScore F1 from 0.68 to 0.84 over a single-shot baseline. Beyond that system description, we study history-taking itself as a network problem. From 231 annotated interviews, we build a bipartite network of symptoms and differential diagnoses whose links are statistically validated against a hypergeometric null model, its one-mode projections, and questioning-flow networks over the topics physicians ask about. The knowledge network separates into 8 syndromic modules (bipartite modularity 0.70, z = 5.4) and is less nested than a degree-preserving null model (z = −6.4): the knowledge an interview must cover is compartmentalised rather than hierarchical. Frequent symptoms such as cough and dyspnoea bridge those modules and carry little information about the differential, whereas rarer findings such as haemoptysis, dysphagia and weight loss carry most of it. Physician questioning separates into two phases: a clinical history followed by a social, family, and exposure history, and a first-order Markov model over topics is the most parsimonious description of how physicians move between them. We discuss what these results imply for the design of language-model interviewers.
evidence_items.title: MedAgent-RAG: an agentic retrieval-augmented system for adaptive clinical history-taking, with a network analysis of medical interviews
Thai-English target-based stock sentiment dataset for financial news with ICL-based evaluation

evidence_items.summary: While Large Language Models (LLMs) excel in processing text, vision, and audio, they remain blind to human behaviors in everyday physical environments. Millimeter-wave (mmWave) sensing offers a privacy-preserving, device-free perceptual channel. As LLMs cannot inherently process radar modalities, the core challenge is how to convert continuous radar observations into tokens that an LLM can understand without losing human kinematics. To address this bottleneck, we present mmMind, an interactive cognitive agent driven by pose-guided kinematic tokenization. By leveraging 3D human pose to supervise a spatial-temporal radar encoder, mmMind generates continuous tokens that faithfully preserve intricate posture transitions and physical kinematics. A lightweight projector then maps these tokens directly into the LLM's embedding space, unlocking multi-turn contextual interaction and spatial-temporal reasoning. Evaluations on a 17.9-hour real-world dataset demonstrate substantial improvements over baselines in radar captioning and physical question answering.
evidence_items.title: WiP: A New Sense for Agents to Understand Human Behavior through mmWave

evidence_items.summary: Lifelogging on personal mobile devices allows users to interact with their past experiences through Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) hosted on edge servers. However, offloading continuous lifelog data streams is severely constrained by limited edge storage. In this work, we present an end-to-end edge-offloaded lifelogging system featuring a utility-based replacement policy to manage multimodal databases under strict storage constraints. To preserve semantically valuable data, we propose diversity- and variance-based utility functions to quantify lifelogs' representativeness, formulating the replacement decisions as a multiple-choice knapsack optimization problem. We evaluate our system under multiple real-world storage constraints using an egocentric video dataset for video question answering, simulating interactive discussions between users and MLLM-powered AI assistants. Experimental results demonstrate that our utility-based replacement policies: (i) boost accuracy by 102.5% on average (by 135% at most) compared to the First-In-First-Out (FIFO) baseline, (ii) achieve at least 78.2% relative coverage compared to unlimited storage, and (iii) incur merely 1.96% communication overhead and 0.03% computation overhead. This work facilitates scalable, long-term digital memory for AI assistants, paving the way for resource-efficient immersive communication services.
evidence_items.title: Resource-Constrained Lifelogging: A Utility-Based Replacement Policy for Video Understanding

evidence_items.summary: The Australian wheatbelt is divided into three main growing regions: the North (New South Wales and Queensland), the South (Victoria, South Australia and Tasmania), and the West (Western Australia). Using wheat yield data from the 2015-2022 multi-environmental trials (METs) conducted by the National Variety Trials (NVT), this study examines genotype-by-environment interactions (G×E) and trialling efficiencies, within and across regions. The North had the highest mean yield (390 gm-2) and the largest proportion of phenotypic variance explained by G×E (64%), while the West had the lowest yield (355 gm-2) and the lowest G×E contribution (44%). Despite regional differences, yield gains were approximately 1.4 gm-2 per year (or ∼ 0.5% annually) across all regions. The West also showed the highest repeatability (0.85 ± 0.02) and the lowest least significance difference (5% LSD, 22 gm-2 ± 1 gm-2) for a benchmark five-year MET, compared to the South (0.70 ± 0.04, 35 ± 1.4 gm-2) and the North (0.59 ± 0.05, 35 ± 1.4 gm-2). Modelling results were consistent across regions and indicated that 2 years of testing at 20 sites per year delivered efficiencies that could not be improved very much further.
evidence_items.title: Evaluation of Trialling Efficiency of the Australian Wheatbelt.

evidence_items.summary: Data is becoming an increasingly essential part of wireless communications research. It is used for training machine learning models, testing novel resource management and allocation algorithms, and extracting novel insights about populations and systems. However, useful wireless networking data is often challenging and expensive to obtain. In this paper, we conduct an AI-assisted meta-study measuring wireless dataset reuse in five networking publication venues over four years. Our results, which span over 6 000 papers, show that dataset reuse is rare in our dataset, with most datasets being unavailable to the public. While there may be many reasons for this lack of dataset reuse, our finding contrasts starkly with the machine learning community, where well-known standardized benchmark datasets (e.g., MNIST, CIFAR-10, ImageNet) have catalyzed massive research efforts, allowing researchers to build upon and validate each others' work. We propose some properties that will be important for the next generation of wireless datasets to better support research, particularly in the subfield of AI for wireless. We conclude with a call to action to decision-makers and community members on how we can help to realize the creation of standardized, widely-adopted datasets for wireless research, particularly in the field of AI for wireless.
evidence_items.title: Why Aren’t We Reusing Datasets More in Wireless Research?

evidence_items.summary:
This study aims to examine whether the newly constructed price conflict index (PCI) has predictive value for housing price volatility across the 50 US states and Washington D.C. This study would determine whether price conflict significantly predicts volatility after controlling for market momentum and state-level economic conditions, to test whether a PCI-augmented model improves out-of-sample forecasting accuracy relative to standard benchmarks and to identify the transmission channels driving this relationship, and inform investors, policymakers and other stakeholders about housing market risk.
 
 
 
 This study uses quarterly panel data from 1976 to 2023 across all 50 US states and Washington D.C. A newly constructed PCI is used as a predictor of housing price volatility, with models controlling for historical market momentum and state-level economic conditions. Predictive performance is evaluated using out-of-sample forecasting tests across semiannual, annual and biennial horizons, benchmarked against baseline models. Panel regression analysis is then applied to confirm the nationwide significance of the PCI–volatility relationship and to identify the primary transmission channels linking price conflict to housing volatility.
 
 
 
 PCI significantly and positively predicts housing price volatility across most US states, even after controlling for historical market momentum and state-level economic conditions. Out-of-sample tests show that PCI-augmented models outperform standard benchmarks across semiannual, annual and biennial forecast horizons. Panel regressions confirm a robust, statistically significant nationwide relationship between price conflict and housing price volatility. Wages and energy prices emerge as the primary transmission channels through which price conflict influences volatility. Finally, the results indicate that PCI is a meaningful and consistent leading indicator of housing market instability across diverse state-level conditions.
 
 
 
 This study introduces a novel PCI as a forward-looking indicator of housing price volatility, linking public discourse to housing market instability. Its value lies in improving out-of-sample forecasting across multiple horizons and holding robustly across nearly all US states, which offers investors and policymakers a practical early-warning tool for housing market risk.
evidence_items.title: Price conflicts and housing price volatility in the United States

evidence_items.summary: The rapid expansion of Internet of things (IoT) devices generates increasing service demands that require reliable computation in regions with limited fixed infrastructure. Uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV)-based mobile edge computing (MEC) systems provide a flexible solution by relocating computational resources close to IoT devices. The task execution at UAVs faces uncertainty due to energy and processing constraints, and resource allocations are further complicated by differing IoT task priorities. In this context, we propose a priority-aware and trust-driven framework for UAV-assisted resource optimization. The UAV trustworthiness is modeled through weighted metrics including computational capacity, residual energy, and task-success history. We assign a confidence parameter to each trust metric to reflect the reliability of reported values, which guides the selection of UAVs for task offloading. UAVs are positioned over the coverage area using K-means clustering to ensure that devices with diverse trust thresholds and task priorities are effectively served. The resulting optimization problem is solved using a penalty-guided optimization (PGO) algorithm and evaluated against a benchmark algorithm based on a branch-and-bound approach and a greedy algorithm. Simulation results across varying trust thresholds and task priorities show that the proposed PGO algorithm achieves performance close to the optimal benchmark while efficiently handling diverse scenarios. These findings highlight the importance of trust-aware and priority-driven UAV-MEC frameworks for supporting reliable IoT services in emerging 6G networks.
evidence_items.title: UAV-Assisted Resource Optimization for Priority-Aware and Trustworthy Services

evidence_items.summary: Mobile and wearable sensing enables health agents to provide personalized insights from users' health data, but existing cloud-hosted LLM backends raise privacy concerns. We present MobileRLHF, a privacy-preserving and self-improving framework that enables human-feedback-driven preference adaptation directly on commodity smartphones through federated RLHF. MobileRLHF addresses two key challenges: resource constraints of mobile devices, and the sparsity of personal feedback. To the best of our knowledge, MobileRLHF is the first practical system to execute human-feedback-driven LLM preference optimization directly on commodity smartphones. We implement MobileRLHF with a real-world federated deployment, and conduct preliminary experiments to evaluate local and federated adaptation behavior and the quality of agent outputs. Our code is open-sourced at: https://github.com/Edge-Intelligence-Lab/MobileRLHF.
evidence_items.title: MobileRLHF: Towards Privacy-Preserving and Self-Improving LLM-Based Local Health Agents on Smartphones via Federated RLHF

evidence_items.summary: User Manual: https://github.com/ARtIStE-Research-Group/OpenseesPy-concrete-2D-frame-optimizer-/blob/main/Manual Polito Work Station beta 03 EN.pdf Short Discription from Authors/ArtISte department This software provides a Python/OpenSeesPy-based decision-support framework for the seismic assessment and retrofit optimization of existing reinforced concrete (RC) frame structures. The framework integrates structural modelling, load definition and combination, linear static analysis, inter-storey drift evaluation, reinforced-concrete member verification, modal analysis, response-spectrum analysis, linear time-history analysis, performance assessment, retrofit optimization, comparative cost estimation, and automated reporting within a single computational workflow. The retrofit methodology considers two complementary intervention strategies. Reinforced-concrete shear walls are treated as global interventions intended to improve the lateral-force-resisting system and reduce excessive drift demand, while concrete jacketing is treated as a local intervention applied to beams and columns that remain deficient after the global retrofit stage. The optimization procedure evaluates complete retrofit alternatives rather than considering wall placement and member strengthening independently. Candidate shear-wall layouts are generated and screened according to structural response, after which the remaining member deficiencies are reassessed and concrete jacketing is designed where required. The complete alternatives are subsequently compared using structural feasibility, member utilization, drift performance, detailing and constructability constraints, and estimated retrofit cost. The selected strategy corresponds to the lowest-cost feasible solution among the alternatives evaluated within the specified search space.
evidence_items.title: ARCOPY: Seismic Assessment and cost-based retrofit Optimization of RC frames with OpenSeesPy

evidence_items.summary: OpenGBSA computes Molecular Mechanics/Generalized Born Surface Area (MM/GBSA) binding free energies from molecular dynamics trajectories. It is built natively on OpenMM rather than wrapping an external engine, so it runs on CUDA and OpenCL GPUs and requires no AmberTools installation. Features: five Generalized Born models (HCT, OBC1, OBC2, GBn, GBn2), two surface-area models (ACE, LCPO), three entropy methods (interaction entropy, quasi-harmonic, normal mode), and per-residue energy decomposition. Input is accepted from four MD ecosystems: GROMACS (.tpr/.top/.gro), Amber (.prmtop), CHARMM/NAMD (.psf), and plain PDB plus trajectory. Binding modes cover protein-ligand, protein-protein, and protein-nucleic-acid complexes. Validation: binding enthalpies agree with the Amber MMPBSA.py reference implementation to Pearson r = 1.00 (RMSD 0.4 kcal/mol) across 18 replicas, and to r = 1.0000 (RMSD 0.09 kcal/mol) on an independent third-party dataset. Per-residue decomposition agrees to r = 1.000 across 4320 residues.
evidence_items.title: OpenGBSA: an OpenMM-native, multi-format MM/GBSA analysis package

evidence_items.summary: The paper associated with this dataset has been published. If you use this dataset in your research, please cite the following publication: Yeste, P., Melsen, L. A., Brêda, J. P. L. F., Tacoronte, N., Saltelli, A., Vannucci, G., et al. (2026). Technical note: Machine learning metamodelling for global sensitivity analysis. Hydrology and Earth System Sciences, 30(20), 6579–6597. https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-30-6579-2026 Description This data and code supplement provides the material required to reproduce the numerical experiments and figures presented in “Technical note: Machine learning metamodelling for global sensitivity analysis”. The repository contains Monte Carlo simulations, Sobol’ GSA results, machine learning (ML) metamodel outputs, and the scripts used to compute sensitivity measures and generate all visualizations. The data were produced using three conceptual hydrologic models: HBV, Hymod, and VIC version 5. For each model–catchment combination, parameter samples were generated using Sobol’ quasi-random sequences and were used to compute the Kling–Gupta Efficiency (KGE), which serves as the model output of interest throughout the study. The repository includes the KGE outputs of these Monte Carlo experiments for each model, which form the basis for both the variance-based global sensitivity analysis and the training of the ML metamodels. The repository includes computed Sobol first-order and total-effect indices (S i and T i , respectively), as well as feature importance measures derived from gradient boosting decision tree (GBDT), neural network (NN), and linear model (LM) surrogates. In particular, Permutation Variable Importance (PVI i) and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP i) are provided. For the LM metamodel, the standardized regression coefficients β i and β i^2 are also available. All analyses were implemented in Python.
evidence_items.title: Data and Code Supplement to "Technical note: Machine learning metamodelling for global sensitivity analysis"

evidence_items.summary: The value alignment of large language models (LLMs) is crucial for ensuring responses align with human intention and value preferences. However, most evaluations of value alignment focus on Western or universal values, while assessments grounded in the value systems of specific countries remain scarce. In this paper, we introduce Pancasila-Dilemmas, an evaluation dataset of 1,834 questions derived from Indonesian news, classified by 5 values of Pancasila: Religion, Humanity, Unity, Democracy, and Social Justice. This dataset reflects daily life in Indonesia, making it suitable for measuring the value alignment of LLMs deployed for Indonesia. To ensure a more rigorous evaluation, we choose scenarios containing dilemmas. The dataset is proofread by native speakers and answered by 5 diverse Indonesian citizens. We evaluate 50 closed- and open-source LLMs on our dataset. Results reveal that all evaluated LLMs achieves less than 0.5 Probability Match Score (PMS) and 0.72 Max-Vote Agreement Score (MVAS). Compared by each values, LLMs mostly struggle in Religion and Unity dilemma cases. This highlights a significant gap in capturing Indonesian values. The dataset is publicly available at https://github.com/tjunlp-lab/Pancasila-Dilemmas.
evidence_items.title: Pancasila-Dilemmas: Evaluating Large Language Models on Indonesian Human Value Dilemmas Grounded in Pancasila

evidence_items.summary: Memory systems are essential for personalized Large Language Models (LLMs). However, retrieval within these systems primarily relies on semantic similarity, potentially missing logically critical memories with limited semantic overlap. We refer to this failure as semantic deflection, which remains insufficiently evaluated by existing benchmarks. To address this gap, we construct IMLogic, a benchmark for implicit logical memory retrieval in long dialogues. Each question is designed around the divergence between semantic and logical relevance, with diagnostic response options that probe semantic deflection, hallucination, and lack of personalization. To help systems utilize associations that are difficult to discover through semantic matching, we introduce root memory, a structured representation that distills reusable, response-guiding logic from user histories through LLM reasoning and grounds it in supporting evidence. We further develop RootMem, a plug-and-play framework that constructs and routes root memories to complement semantic retrieval. Extensive experiments reveal persistent challenges across retrieval methods and memory systems, including substantial preference-driven errors even under full-memory access. RootMem consistently improves performance, demonstrating the potential of structured personalized logic while leaving considerable challenges unresolved. Our benchmark and code are available at https://github.com/ThisIsCosine/IMLogic.
evidence_items.title: Towards Root Memory: Benchmarking and Enhancing Implicit Logical Memory Retrieval for Personalized LLMs

evidence_items.summary: We present AIForge-Doc, the first dedicated benchmark targeting exclusively diffusion-model-based inpainting in financial and form documents with pixel-level annotation. Existing document forgery datasets rely on traditional digital editing tools (e.g., Adobe Photoshop, GIMP), creating a critical gap: state-of-the-art detectors are blind to the rapidly growing threat of AI-forged document fraud. AIForge-Doc addresses this gap by systematically forging numeric fields in real-world receipt and form images using two AI inpainting APIs -- Gemini 2.5 Flash Image and Ideogram v2 Edit -- yielding 4,061 forged images from four public document datasets (CORD, WildReceipt, SROIE, XFUND) across nine languages, annotated with pixel-precise tampered-region masks in DocTamper-compatible format. We benchmark three representative detectors -- TruFor, DocTamper, and a zero-shot GPT-4o judge -- and find that all existing methods degrade substantially: TruFor achieves AUC=0.751 (zero-shot, out-of-distribution) vs. AUC=0.96 on NIST16; DocTamper achieves AUC=0.563 vs. AUC=0.98 in-distribution, with pixel-level IoU=0.020; GPT-4o achieves only 0.509 -- essentially at chance -- confirming that AI-forged values are indistinguishable to automated detectors and VLMs. These results demonstrate that AIForge-Doc represents a qualitatively new and unsolved challenge for document forensics.
evidence_items.title: AIForge-Doc: A Benchmark for Detecting AI-Forged Tampering in Financial and Form Documents

evidence_items.summary: Multi-Turn Long-Form Question Answering (MT-LFQA) is a key application paradigm of Large Language Models (LLMs) in knowledge-intensive domains. However, existing benchmarks are limited to single-turn dialogue, while multi-turn dialogue benchmarks typically assess other orthogonal capabilities rather than knowledge-intensive factuality. To bridge this critical gap, we introduce \textbf{KnowMT-Bench}, a new benchmark designed to systematically evaluate MT-LFQA for LLMs across knowledge-intensive fields, including medicine, finance, and law. To faithfully assess the model's real-world performance, KnowMT-Bench employs a dynamic evaluation setting where models generate their own multi-turn dialogue histories given logically progressive question sequences. Our experiments on a diverse suite of LLMs show a clear degradation in both factual capability and information delivery efficiency in multi-turn dialogue. We further probe the underlying causes and investigate mitigation strategies spanning domain-specific finetuning, active context denoising, and RAG. The results show domain-dependent gains from finetuning, while active context denoising and RAG more consistently mitigate these issues, with RAG notably reversing this performance degradation. These findings underscore the importance of our benchmark for evaluating LLMs' conversational factual capabilities in real-world applications. Code and data are publicly available.\footnote{\href{https://github.com/Sven-LI-sankyuu/KnowMT-Bench}{\texttt{https://github.com/Sven-LI-sankyuu/KnowMT-Bench}}}
evidence_items.title: KnowMT-Bench: Benchmarking Knowledge-Intensive Long-Form Question Answering in Multi-Turn Dialogues

evidence_items.summary: Recent advances in generative video models have improved visual realism, making detection increasingly dependent on subtle temporal inconsistencies. However, these signals are weak and spatially localized, while most of the video content is redundant. This creates a fundamental mismatch: existing detectors rely on heavy backbones to model full videos, which leads to high computational cost and limited scalability. In this work, we rethink AI-generated video detection from a representation perspective. Instead of modeling entire videos, we restructure them into compact temporal slice representations that isolate informative temporal evolution. We introduce a lightweight framework using frequency-aware temporal slice consistency learning, where informative spatial rows and columns are aggregated over time to form slice-domain inputs. This reparameterization suppresses redundant appearance while preserving discriminative temporal dynamics, enabling efficient and targeted detection. By constructing slices from both high- and low-frequency regions, our method exposes complementary temporal artifacts, including unstable details and abnormal motion smoothness. We instantiate this idea in a Temporal Slice Consistency Network, which integrates task-driven slice localization, hierarchical positional encoding, and a lightweight Transformer to model cross-slice and cross-frequency dependencies. We further introduce AI-Artist, a new benchmark with artist-curated videos from recent high-fidelity generators, including Seedance and Kling. Experiments on GenVideo and AI-Artist show that our method achieves strong performance while requiring over 400$\times$ fewer model-forward FLOPs and 3.6$\times$ faster model inference than the strong video-based baseline ReStraV (2.9$\times$ faster end to end, including preprocessing), enabling scalable and practical deployment.
evidence_items.title: Temporal Slice Learning for AI-Generated Video Detection with 400$\times$ Fewer FLOPs

evidence_items.summary: Road anomalies such as collisions, violations, and sudden hazards demand more from video understanding than detection: a practical system must verify what happened, describe the scene, and explain the cause. We find these competences pull in opposite directions for vision-language models: closed-form questions reward precise, evidence-grounded reasoning, while open-ended answers are scored by similarity to reference text, where matching the annotation style matters as much as reasoning correctly. We present Reason-or-Recite (RoR), a two-specialist framework for the Traffic Anomaly Reasoning track of the 2026 AI City Challenge. RoR (1) rewrites the official chain-of-thought annotations into a structured, temporally grounded schema and LoRA-tunes a 9B vision-language model on the enhanced traces; (2) fine-tunes a 4-bit-quantized 27B model on answers alone, absorbing the annotation style; and (3) selects between the two candidates per question with a training-free LLM judge. RoR ranks first on the in-domain leaderboard with mean score 0.6788.
evidence_items.title: Reason or Recite: Complementary Specialists with an LLM Judge for Traffic Anomaly Reasoning

evidence_items.summary: Language models for metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) rely on formats that separate atomic geometry from structural topology, forcing models to choose between unstructured coordinate lists and non-spatial string identifiers[1]. We present MOFjson, the first representation separating structural data into a raw atomic layer with explicit bond shift vectors and a derived layer exposing secondary building units (metal nodes and organic linkers) and network topology. Additionally, we introduce a benchmark with crystal-derived ground truth across four question categories. Across four models, MOFjson beats all three baselines in every category: 100% vs. 18-47% on reaching a block's nearest periodic copy, 96% vs. 71% on crystal system characterisation, and 60% vs. 48% on metal node and organic linker coordination. Ablating shift labels drops accuracy to 12.7%, proving models read the periodic graph rather than the surface format. MOFjson gives language models structure to read rather than reconstruct, establishing a foundation for agentic tool workflows and constrained MOF generation.
evidence_items.title: MOFjson: An Explicit Topological Representation of Metal-Organic Frameworks for Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Typed decision models (TDMs), such as Jev, answer a question about an input with a probability, an option, or an ordinal level. Web services execute these decisions automatically above a confidence threshold. An attacker who writes part of the input can change a decision that the service then executes. Current adversarial benchmarks cannot measure this risk, because they judge generated text. A TDM writes no text, and its wrong decisions have a valid format. We present JevAdvBench, to our knowledge the first unified benchmark for the adversarial robustness of TDMs. It contains 862 questions with audited answers and twelve black-box attack methods that edit the input or the options by adaptive search. Because a changed decision is not always wrong, a review keeps only 5,586 answer-preserving variants, and we attack only correct decisions. The attacks flip 46.3% of Jev's correct decisions, while identical re-runs flip only 0.17%. A flawed argument without a command flips 77.2%, close to direct prompt injection at 92.0%. The same variants flip 34.0% to 51.7% of correct decisions on eight open TDMs. At a 0.8 threshold, 23.5% of the decisions that the service still executes are wrong. On Agentgateway, the Jev guardrail rejects a jailbreak request but accepts it with an inserted argument. Web services should therefore treat TDM inputs as untrusted and should not act on confidence alone. Project website: https://JevAdvBench.github.io/JevAdvBench/
evidence_items.title: JevAdvBench: A Benchmark and Black-Box Attacks for Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions Models

evidence_items.summary: Large audio language models (LALMs) have shown impressive capabilities on diverse audio understanding tasks, ranging from speech transcription to music analysis. However, because LALMs are typically trained to produce text-aligned responses, their hidden states are progressively shaped for text generation rather than for preserving acoustic information. As a result, the diverse acoustic content that audio carries, such as phonetic detail, prosody, sound events, affect, and pitch, is lost along the way and difficult to leverage in the response. We introduce Continuous Audio Thinking (CoAT), a framework that equips audio language models with a continuous latent workspace for organizing acoustic information prior to response generation, grounded by distillation from audio experts. Within the thinking space, the model can utilize the rich acoustic information provided by expert distillation when generating its response. Furthermore, the proposed continuous thinking block can be processed in a single prefill, so CoAT does not require additional autoregressive decoding cost over the baseline. Across three LALMs, Qwen2-Audio, Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, and Audio Flamingo~3, performance gains on a broad benchmark suite spanning audio reasoning, audio understanding, music classification, speech emotion, and speech transcription demonstrate the effectiveness of CoAT. Further analysis confirms that the auxiliary supervision propagates from the thinking positions to the model's textual responses.
evidence_items.title: Continuous Audio Thinking for Large Audio Language Models

evidence_items.summary: The extraction of critical information from crime-related documents is a crucial task for law enforcement agencies. The extraction of this information can be interpreted as a Named-Entity Recognition (NER) task. However, there is a considerable lack of adequately annotated data on general real-world crime scenarios. To address this issue, we present CrimeNER, a case study of crime-related NER, and a general crime-related Named-Entity Recognition database (CrimeNER-db), consisting of more than 1.5K annotated documents extracted from public reports of terrorist attacks and the US Department of Justice's press notes. We define 4 coarse types of crime entity and 21 fine-grained entity types. We address the quality of the presented database with fully supervised experiments using flat and nested NER architectures and zero- and few-shot experiments using Large Language Models (LLMs). The database is available on GitHub.
evidence_items.title: CrimeNER: Curated Dataset and Methods for Research and Investigation in Language Intelligence

evidence_items.summary: Video generation models are promising foundations for embodied world models, but only if their generated rollouts are physically valid and faithful to task instructions. Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are increasingly used to judge these properties, yet their agreement with human judgments on embodied videos has not been systematically evaluated. To address this gap, we introduce RoboJudge-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating MLLMs as judges of embodied video generation. The benchmark measures two fundamental dimensions, Physical Adherence and Instruction Alignment, across 800 human-annotated videos from 8 source corpora and 10 video generators, spanning grippers, human hands, and dexterous hands. Experiments reveal uneven alignment between existing judges and human ratings: general-purpose MLLMs show lower agreement on physical adherence, while specialized video judges designed for general-domain physical reasoning do not consistently transfer to embodied scenarios. Motivated by these findings, we construct RoboJudge-Train, comprising 12K videos annotated with 25K human-verified scores and model-assisted rationales for Physical Adherence and Instruction Alignment. We fine-tune a 9B MLLM on this dataset with supervised learning followed by reinforcement learning, yielding RoboJudge-9B. Among the model judges evaluated on RoboJudge-Bench, RoboJudge-9B achieves the highest overall agreement, reaching a Pearson correlation of 0.719 with a statistically significant 0.089 gain over Gemini-3.7-Flash, the best-performing proprietary baseline in our evaluation. Training on RoboJudge-Train also yields gains on external benchmarks, including VideoPhy2 and Physion-Eval. We further use RoboJudge-9B as a downstream evaluator to benchmark video generation models according to Physical Adherence and Instruction Alignment.
evidence_items.title: RoboJudge: Multimodal Language Models as Judges for Embodied Video Generation

evidence_items.summary: Measurement data: Impact of hydrogen incorporation on electronic and magnetic structure of X2CrNi18-9 stainless steel Abstract Hydrogen absorption significantly alters the mechanical properties of steel. Simultaneously, hydrogen uptake also influences both the electronic and magneto-structural properties, helping to interpret how hydrogen is incorporated. This study therefore investigates the influence of hydrogen incorporation on the electronic and magneto-structural properties of X2CrNi18-9 stainless steel in different microstructural states. Microstructural characterization included analytic electron microscopy mapping, X-ray diffraction and thermodynamic stability maps to evaluate grain size, dislocation density and chemical homogeneity. The electronic properties were characterized using the Seebeck coefficient, while the magneto-structural properties were investigated using diffuse neutron scattering and small-angle neutron scattering (SANS). Hydrogen incorporation showed clear changes in the Seebeck coefficients. Magnetic SANS in conjunction with diffuse neutron scattering indicates the existence of nanoscale inhomogeneities with the same fcc structure as the bulk, but with correlation lengths of a few nanometres. The size of these inhomogeneities increased with hydrogen incorporation, suggesting that hydrogen preferentially accumulates in their vicinity. Our results suggest that the nanoscale inhomogeneities play a more significant role in hydrogen incorporation than dislocations, as we did not observe a direct correlation between the electronic and magneto-structural properties and the dislocation density. We suggest that studies such as these will lead in the medium term to the development of guidelines for material design to make steels more resistant to hydrogen.
evidence_items.title: Measurement data: Impact of hydrogen incorporation on electronic and magnetic structure of X2CrNi18-9 stainless steel

evidence_items.summary: This dataset contains the bird abundance and environmental data used in the study “ Influence of habitat structure and spatial configuration on bird abundance in wet grassland patches ”, publsihed in Biodiversity and Conservation. The study was conducted in natural grassland landscapes of southern Brazil. Sixty wet grassland patches distributed across ten sites were surveyed during November–December 2007 and 2008, corresponding to the breeding season of most grassland birds in the region. Sampled patches ranged from 3,350 to 160,207 m² and occurred within a matrix dominated by natural grasslands used for extensive cattle and sheep grazing. Birds were surveyed by two observers walking along the longest axis of each patch and recording all individuals seen or heard within the patch. Each patch was surveyed once. Birds flying over the patches were excluded, except displaying Anthus spp. that subsequently landed within the patch. Selective low-volume playback was used after the main count for cryptic patch-dependent species. Across the 60 patches, 2,896 individuals belonging to 114 bird species were recorded. For each patch, the dataset includes geographic location, sampling year, patch area, within-patch habitat structure, patch configuration, isolation, and the amount of major habitat types in the surrounding landscape. Within-patch habitat variables describe the areas occupied by bare ground, open water, trees and large shrubs, bog vegetation, and short and tall graminoid vegetation. Habitat features were quantified from a combination of field measurements, GPS mapping, satellite imagery, and Google Earth. Landscape variables were quantified within circular buffers with a 1,000-m radius centered on the centroid of each focal patch. Wet grassland patches within these buffers were manually delineated from high-resolution imagery, whereas broader land-cover information was derived from MapBiomas Collection 9.
evidence_items.title: Influence of habitat structure and spatial configuration on bird abundance in wet grassland patches

evidence_items.summary: Abstract High-consequence distributed architectures—spanning autonomous AI agents, financial settlements, cloud control planes, and cyber-physical infrastructure—increasingly permit components to act based on decisions generated by independent external authorities, including authorization servers, risk engines, policy services, and attestation verifiers . A critical vulnerability arises when an effectuation component cannot independently verify these external determinations: an untrusted or compromised intermediary can assert that external evaluations succeeded ("trust me, I checked"), replay past approvals, substitute contexts, suppress required negative signals, or log evidence solely for audit while the protected effect executes unconstrained . This specification introduces an execution-finality model that establishes verifiable third-party decision binding . A proposed operation is treated as a Candidate Act and held strictly in a Non-Effective State . The deployment defines a machine-readable Required Decision Authority Set ( $R(C)$ ) . For every required authority, verifiable External Decision Evidence (EDE)—or an authenticated live equivalent—must be bound cryptographically to the exact canonical act parameters, current decision-basis generations, freshness nonces, and intended sinks . Enforcement terminates at a mandatory Finality Sink that independently evaluates the complete decision-rule structure prior to commit . Incomplete decision sets, unverified assertions, stale basis states, or missing evidence fail closed, leaving the Candidate Act non-effective . By coupling multi-authority decision verification directly to protected commit, the architecture ensures that an unverified claim of upstream approval cannot trigger an irreversible consequence . FLOW CHART [ Autonomous Workload / Intermediary ] │ │ 1. Proposes Candidate Act C ▼ ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Non-Effective State │ ◄── 2.
evidence_items.title: Trust Me, I Checked: Verifiable Third-Party Decision Binding at the Execution-Finality Boundary

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Security architectures routinely decouple authority generation from downstream execution, relying on access tokens, session credentials, and cryptographic delegations that remain valid across a finite lifetime . In autonomous agentic platforms, cloud control planes, financial rails, and cyber-physical infrastructure, however, an authorization can be authentic and valid at issuance ( $t 0$ ) yet become dangerous before execution if an authoritative revocation, permission narrowing, or policy update commits at $t 1$ . Conventional access checks performed solely upstream fail to prevent this lag, allowing stale authorizations to survive to commit ( $t 2$ ) simply because token signatures, expiration timestamps, or cached status results remain intact . This specification introduces a finality-bound revocation architecture that binds revocation applicability directly to the consequence boundary . Any proposed operation is modeled as a Candidate Act ( $C$ ) and maintained in an inhibited, Non-Effective State . Authorization is bound cryptographically to an act-specific revocation basis ( $R {\text{eval}}$ ), capturing monotonic generations, status roots, and explicit scopes across principal, credential, grant, resource, and trust dimensions . Immediately before or atomically with the protected commit, a Finality Sink independently reconstructs the live act, evaluates authoritative current revocation state ( $R {\text{now}}$ ), and determines whether any load-bearing revocation has committed . Where changes exist without explicit machine-verifiable survival proofs, the act is denied or re-authorized . Indeterminate state fails closed, and consequence-path completeness guarantees that alternate, administrative, or queued paths cannot bypass enforcement . The architecture ensures that a revocation committed prior to a protected effect unconditionally halts that effect . FLOW CHART [ Workload / Agent / Principal ] │ │ 1.
evidence_items.title: Revoked but Still Executable: Closing the Authorization-to-Effect Gap with Finality-Bound Revocation

evidence_items.summary: LLM-based sales agents are often evaluated on static policy questions or task success, but deployment asks a sharper question: when a model can state a rule, will it choose compliant, tool-grounded actions under commercial pressure? We introduce R2A-Sales (Rule-to-Action), a policy-atom-matched benchmark for this question. Each item pairs a static probe with a multi-turn sales scenario sharing the same versioned policy atom, facts, evidence, behavioral constraints, and tool contract, so differences cannot be attributed to policy-content mismatch. In the interactive arm, a code-owned ledger verifies committed tool effects and terminal states; unsupported action claims receive no credit. We report static compliance $K$, grounded action compliance $A=\Pr(\text{safe terminal}\land\text{no hard violation}\land\text{non-echo})$, and the matched gap $G=K-A$. The frozen release spans three controlled Chinese-language sales domains, 24 policy atoms, 42 semantic cores, and 2,016 matched pairs. The confirmatory study audits 21,888 runs over 19 cores, covering eight backbones plus four Qwen3-8B prompt treatments (12 configurations). Static compliance is near ceiling $(K=89.9\%\text{--}99.1\%)$, yet eight-backbone action compliance is only $A=3.0\%\text{--}17.3\%$, giving $G=80.4\text{--}92.5$ percentage points. Since $A$ also requires safe termination, $G$ upper-bounds rule-to-action degradation rather than isolating pressure alone. No prompt-only treatment dominates all metrics. R2A-Sales shows that sales-agent reliability must be measured at committed action, not rule recital or task completion alone.
evidence_items.title: R2A-Sales: A Policy-Atom-Matched Benchmark for Rule-to-Action Gaps in Goal-Directed Sales Agents

evidence_items.summary: Multi-agent systems often rely on predefined collaboration structures, limiting their ability to adapt to diverse task requirements. We introduce DynaFlow, a framework that integrates free-form executable workflow synthesis into the action space of the main agent. The agent decides when collaboration is needed and generates task-specific programs that coordinate sub-agents through sequential or parallel execution, structured information exchange, and verification. Execution results and traces inform subsequent actions, enabling the agent to adapt collaboration as reasoning progresses. We train only the main agent through supervised fine-tuning on distilled trajectories, followed by refinement on examples filtered for unsupported premises, biased verification, and information-flow defects. All sub-agents remain fixed, separating orchestration learning from executor capability improvement. Across six benchmarks spanning mathematical reasoning, scientific question answering, and multi-hop retrieval, DynaFlow achieves 88.08% overall accuracy in Forced mode, outperforming the strongest evaluated baseline by 10.90 percentage points with the same Qwen3.5-27B backbone. Workflow analysis finds more explicit use, verification, and refinement of upstream outputs after training, highlighting cross-stage information flow as a key dimension of multi-agent orchestration.
evidence_items.title: DynaFlow: Learning Free-Form Multi-Agent Orchestration

evidence_items.summary: LLM agents are increasingly used to solve real-world problems, and their effectiveness depends on both the underlying models and the harnesses that support their operation. However, most existing benchmarks focus on model capabilities and overall agent performance, with limited attention to the evaluation of agent harnesses. To address this gap, we introduce TraceTrial-Bench, which organizes harness reliability into seven components covering context, execution, governance, lifecycle, observability, tools, and verification. We construct 95 expert-level, mechanism-oriented tasks with executable or state-based ground truth to support semantically equivalent comparisons while preserving the native behavior of each harness. We design a Trajectory Tracing (TT) module to capture agent execution traces and introduce a two-layer evaluation framework that separately assesses agent performance and harness reliability. In addition, we design a Multi-source Evidence Acquisition (MEA) module to provide evidence from the agent context, harness, and execution environment for LLM-based evaluation, and develop a Failure Attribution (FA) module that uses explicit mechanism chains to support attribution at the run level. Across 4 harnesses, 9 models, and 95 tasks, our evaluation of 3,420 runs yields macro-averaged harness scores ranging from 59.8% to 72.0%, while 31.1% of runs achieve task success despite failing at least one harness criterion. TraceTrial-Bench provides an auditable and reproducible foundation for comparing agent harnesses, diagnosing their failures, and studying how harness design interacts with model behavior.
evidence_items.title: Trial by Trace: Benchmarking AI Agent Harnesses for Reliability and Failure Attribution

evidence_items.summary: Precise camera control is essential for cinematic character video generation, yet existing methods struggle to follow large-angle trajectories with combined rotation, translation, and radius variation from arbitrary initial azimuths. Such viewpoint changes also reveal character regions unseen in the initial frame, causing geometric distortions, appearance degradation, and identity drift. To systematically study these coupled challenges, we introduce CLACT, a large-scale Character-centric dataset and benchmark covering diverse Large-Angle Camera Trajectories, with accurate camera geometry and multi-view character observations for training and evaluation. We further propose WorldCast, a framework for world-consistent character video generation under diverse large-angle camera motions. Specifically, we back-project the initial frame into a 3D point cloud using estimated depth, align the point-cloud scale with the target camera trajectory, and render it along the trajectory to obtain explicit geometric guidance and coverage masks. To complement the incomplete character information, we introduce Geometry-Aligned Memory Attention (GAMA). Using relative camera poses estimated jointly from the initial frame and multi-view character anchors, we express anchor and target-view geometry in a common coordinate frame. GAMA uses this geometric alignment to guide the retrieval and injection of view-relevant character features during generation. Evaluations across diverse large-angle camera trajectories demonstrate accurate trajectory following while preserving character geometry, appearance, and identity.
evidence_items.title: WorldCast: World-Consistent Character Video Generation with Large-Angle Camera Control

evidence_items.summary: Recent methods for injecting graph structure into LLM prompts include graph soft prompting, in which a graph neural network (GNN) learns graph-specific tokens that capture relational information among entities in textual prompts. G-Retriever combines graph soft prompts with a verbalized description of the same graph to strengthen the textual prompt signal. We conduct an in-depth analysis of G-Retriever and uncover a pathological behavior we term token collapse. Across three benchmarks, three graph encoders, two LLM families, and both frozen and LoRA-adapted models, G-Retriever's graph tokens become almost indistinguishable across inputs. We provide evidence that the same failure is inherited by subsequent methods, even with multi-token pooling. Under the standard setup, swapping a token with the dataset mean, a token from another example, or one derived from a corrupted graph produces no resolved answer-level effect in accuracy. Moreover, a learned constant prompt that never accesses the graph matches or surpasses G-Retriever on all three benchmarks. These findings indicate that, rather than conveying graph content as intended, the collapsed token functions primarily as a generic soft prompt. We also examine conditions linked to this collapse and propose a two-stage procedure that yields non-collapsed tokens while maintaining competitive performance in most cases. However, token variability alone does not prove that the model uses graph information: via interventions and decoding probes, we show that depending on the configuration, a token can reflect the question, an answer prior, or graph-derived content that the LLM may or may not use. Overall, our results offer a practical approach to evaluating graph-token alignment rather than inferring it from task accuracy alone. Code to reproduce our experiments is available at https://github.com/difra100/Token_Collapse_KGQA.
evidence_items.title: On the Token Collapse Phenomenon in Textual Graph Soft Prompting

evidence_items.summary: Video foundation models have advanced rapidly in understanding and generating visual sequences, while video world models seek to capture the underlying dynamics of the world they depict. Despite their different objectives, both concern the relationship between video observations and an evolving world. This survey adopts world modeling as a unifying lens for examining these developments. Viewing an observed video as a partial, lossy, and temporally ordered projection of a latent temporal world, we organize the literature around four complementary operations: reading infers world properties from observed video; writing synthesizes video from specified or learned world conditions; sharing integrates understanding and generation through common modeling mechanisms; and interacting predicts and updates world states under actions and evolving observations. This perspective distinguishes temporal coherence in observed or generated sequences from consistency in the underlying world state. Across tasks, representations, models, datasets, and benchmarks, we trace a shift in emphasis from clip-level recognition and perceptual fidelity toward persistent state, controllable evolution, physical and causal validity, and evaluation grounded in interaction and downstream decisions, and we distill the open challenges that follow.
evidence_items.title: Reading, Writing, Sharing, and Interacting with the World through Video

evidence_items.summary: Agentic recommendation pursues shopper goals through sequences of context-dependent decisions. Developing and evaluating such policies requires faithful recommendation world models that capture both the interactive shopping environment and users' behavioral responses over long interactions. Existing resources rarely provide long-horizon, fine-grained real-user trajectories or support trajectory-level evaluation and offline validation against production A/B results. We introduce UserArena, a real-world e-commerce interactive benchmark containing 64,729 session trajectories from 11,010 users, spanning 566,102 items and 13 action types. UserArena pairs these trajectories with an interactive environment and supports offline validation against outcomes from a controlled production A/B test, enabling five-level evaluation from output validity and local decisions to sequential behavior, personalization, and outcomes. To improve simulator fidelity over these long-horizon interactions, we further propose On-Policy Trajectory Distillation (OPTD), which uses trajectory-level intent to provide dense teacher targets on student-generated rollouts. Experiments show that OPTD achieves the strongest overall fidelity among the evaluated simulators under UserArena's evaluation protocol and most closely reproduces the production policy effect in offline simulation.
evidence_items.title: UserArena: Benchmarking Interactive User Simulation for Long-Horizon Shopping Agents

evidence_items.summary: When humans collaborate with AI agents on long-horizon tasks, what happens to the agents' contributions? For solving long-horizon tasks, humans place greater importance on ongoing interaction with AI agents (e.g., revising plans) than on an agent's ability to complete the task in a single attempt. However, most agentic benchmarks have focused more on automation. Strong performance on such benchmarks does not imply effective real-world collaboration. Professional workflows offer a useful setting, as they often involve interdependent steps. To address this gap, we introduce Kolab, a new dataset of 115+ hours of screen recordings of 50 professionals from 40 occupations collaborating with agents on realistic, long-horizon problems. Kolab also contains participants' collaboration and output quality judgments. Our analysis reveals diverse collaboration patterns, highlighting the importance of when and how professionals coordinate with agents. A collaborative agent must do two things that automation benchmarks never test: anticipate whether experts will adopt, modify, or reject its contribution once it leaves the chat window to guide its next steps, and assess collaboration quality from the unfolding workflow without constant expert feedback. Our benchmark operationalizes both: (1) forecasting how professionals use agent contributions at diverse workflows, and (2) verifying their judgments of collaboration satisfaction and output quality. Findings show that frontier models, both agentic and non-agentic, overestimate collaboration with experts and struggle to distinguish between high- and low-quality collaboration. Longer workflow context does not consistently improve these predictions. As frontier agents cannot yet understand long-horizon collaboration with experts, we position Kolab as a valuable dataset for studying human-agent collaboration grounded in real professional workflows.
evidence_items.title: Kolab: Benchmarking Human-Agent Collaboration in Long-Horizon Workflows

evidence_items.summary: Repeated event forecasting requires extracting predictive signals from noisy evidence and evaluating their value across successive decisions. We introduce JockeyBench, a benchmark and evaluation protocol that studies this problem through historical Japanese horse racing. The protocol combines time-gated evidence, priced tools, paired frozen-program controls, and two workflows: executing an LLM-written predictor or acquiring evidence for a fresh per-race LLM forecast. Evaluation separates forecast quality, benchmark-specific net utility, and retrospective betting returns and risk under fixed decision rules. Across 28 model--scaffold configurations on 324 races, paired tests identify seven revision gains and two declines after multiple-testing correction. Yet every configuration has negative mean profit under capped-Kelly settlement. In a four-model comparison, the reusable-program workflow has higher mean betting profit and lower research fees, although both workflows lose on average. Further diagnostics reveal that mean probability bias reverses on selected bets and that profitable individual runs can depend on concentrated returns. These findings motivate evaluating predictive competence, adaptation, resource use, and decision value separately when assessing agents for repeated event forecasting.
evidence_items.title: JockeyBench: Evaluating LLM Agents on Horse-Racing Decision-Making

evidence_items.summary: DAMAP is an open‐source tool for creating machine‐actionable data management plans (maDMPs). The latest release introduces DAMAP as a cloud‐based shared service, removing the need for institutions to run and maintain their own deployment. Data stewards and their institutions can simply join the service and start supporting researchers immediately. For data stewards, this means less time spent on infrastructure and more time focused on what matters: helping researchers create accurate, high‐quality DMPs. DAMAP reduces the burden on researchers by reusing information from existing institutional systems, offering step‐by‐step guidance, and recommending relevant services and repositories. All customisations — logos, templates, recommended repositories, wording — can be managed directly through an admin interface, with no IT involvement required. The latest release also brings compatibility with the RDA Common maDMP API and the OSTrails Application Profile, enabling connections between DAMAP and other RDM tools and services. This opens the door to automated DMP evaluation, FAIR assessment, and integration with institutional and national research infrastructures — making DMPs genuinely useful beyond the submission moment.
evidence_items.title: DAMAP Cloud: Shared Infrastructure, Better Data Management Plans

evidence_items.summary: The development of abstractive text summarization for low-resource languages is constrained by the limited availability of high-quality datasets. Although Hausa is one of the most widely spoken languages in Africa, resources for developing and evaluating neural summarization models remain limited. This paper introduces Hausa Summarization (HAUSUMM) dataset, a curated dataset for Hausa news summarization comprising 11,482 article-summary pairs collected from four professional Hausa news outlets through an automated web-scraping pipeline. The reference summaries were derived from journalistic lead paragraphs and exhibit moderate phrase-level abstraction, as indicated by extractive-fragment analysis and n-gram novelty. To establish baseline performance, four summarization architectures, Bidirectional and Auto-Regressive Transformer (BART), Text-to-Text Transfer Transformer (T5), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) with Attention, and Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) with Attention, were evaluated under controlled experimental conditions using Recall-Oriented Understudy for Gisting Evaluation (ROUGE) scores, BERT-based Semantic Similarity Score (BERTScore), and Summarization Consistency (SummaC). A human evaluation of the article-summary pairs was also conducted to assess relevance, factual consistency, coherence, fluency, conciseness, and abstractiveness. The results provide baseline evidence for Hausa abstractive summarization and make HAUSUMM available for further research on Hausa summarization.
evidence_items.title: A Hausa abstractive summarization dataset with baseline evaluation
