evidence_items.summary: Cancer patients with clinically similar tumors can exhibit substantial differences in disease progression and treatment response. Patient-specific gene regulatory networks (GRNs) may capture regulatory heterogeneity that is not represented by gene expression alone. However, strategies for clustering patients using these high-dimensional networks have not been systematically evaluated and it remains unclear whether clustering based directly on millions of patient-specific regulatory edge weights is computationally feasible at scale. We benchmarked feature-selection and clustering approaches for patient-specific GRNs inferred with PANDA and LIONESS across 9,778 primary tumor samples from 33 cancer types. We compared three data representations: gene expression, gene indegrees summarizing regulatory input to each gene, and complete networks of transcription factor-gene edge weights. Twenty combinations of four feature-selection methods and five clustering algorithms were evaluated using consensus clustering. Performance was assessed based on mean silhouette score, PAC score, concordance, computational time, and memory usage. Standard deviation-based feature selection combined with k-means clustering achieved the strongest overall performance for both GRN-derived representations, with overall scores of 0.997 for edge weights and 0.985 for indegrees, while remaining computationally efficient. Edge-weight- and indegree-derived clusters showed clinical, biological, and prognostic associations that were complementary to those obtained from gene expression. Together, these findings provide a practical framework for network-based cancer patient stratification and highlight the potential of GRN-derived features to reveal clinically relevant tumor heterogeneity beyond gene expression alone.
evidence_items.title: A Pan-Cancer Benchmark of Clustering Strategies for Patient-Specific Gene Regulatory Networks

organizations: AGI Institute, School of Computer Science, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai 200240, China;
Shanghai Innovation Institute, Shanghai, China
evidence_items.summary: Predicting transcriptional responses across cellular contexts requires transferring both expression direction and differential-expression priority. We developed a compact numerical method that combines public perturbation summaries with a differential-expression kernel fitted to H1 CRISPRi training targets. The method centers an independent KOLF2.1J source on known training targets, transfers its response signs and magnitude ranks, and uses isotonic regression to render predicted expression means. We evaluated the frozen model retrospectively on the released public TEST100 of the 2025 Virtual Cell Challenge, using an external KOLF source released in 2026. The model achieved DES 0.371834, PDS 0.8614, and MAE 0.302206. With reconstructed historical anchors, its composite score was 0.341344, compared with the archived champion score of 0.340052, a difference of +0.001292. The comparison showed higher DES and lower PDS, with zero normalized MAE contributions for both methods. Source centering also improved development PDS across all three TRAIN folds and official VALIDATION. These results demonstrate a practical numerical approach to cross-context perturbation transfer and differential-expression ranking.
evidence_items.title: Centered cross-context perturbation transfer on the public 2025 Virtual Cell Challenge benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence is now used to evaluate other systems. Large language models (LLMs) generate assurance profiles, control questions and test cases, judge benchmark outputs, and support automated red teams. At the same time, the evaluated systems are often LLM-based agents themselves. In this position paper, we argue that this situation creates a new type of assurance problem. Three basic assumptions of classical evaluation are broken: (1) the evaluator and the target can fail in the same way (correlated blind spots); (2) the evaluation criteria are written by the same type of model that is evaluated (circular criteria); and (3) the target can influence the inputs of the evaluator (injectable evaluation). We connect this problem to known results in computer science and propose seven principles for what we call metaassurance. Finally, we present four testable propositions for future research.
evidence_items.title: WHO ASSURES THE ASSURER? A POSITION ON META-ASSURANCE FOR AI-MEDIATED EVALUATION

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are used to generate user interface (UI) code, yet the accessibility of this code is difficult to evaluate in a controlled way. Existing evaluations typically examine full-generated webpages or loosely specified tasks, which makes it difficult to determine where accessibility outcomes come from. We introduce PACE for “Prompt Accessibility Controlled Evaluation,” a benchmarking testbed for controlled evaluation of accessibility in LLM-generated HTML form components. Using PACE, we evaluated the accessibility of 58 form components generated by five developer-centric LLMs with variations across three system prompts with increasing accessibility guidance, and three request variants containing increasing detail about each form components. We collected 10 trials per configuration for a total of n = 26, 100 outputs. Our findings show that accessibility in LLM-generated code moved with prompt construction and with the circumstance around it (e.g., model, form component, and measure used to assess the output). This pattern calls for evaluation designs that can better separate sources of variation in the accessibility of LLM-generated code.
evidence_items.title: Prompt and Circumstance: Evaluating Accessibility in LLM-Generated HTML Form Components

organizations: University of Milan
University of Milano-Bicocca
evidence_items.summary: Where a human looks is not random, nor is it merely a reflex to visual salience. It is a decision shaped by goals, constrained by language, and driven by the need to resolve uncertainty. We propose Eyegent , an active vision agent built on this premise: that visual search is best understood as sequential Bayesian inference over semantically grounded hypotheses, with fixations serving as epistemic actions. Given an image and a natural-language query, Eyegent constructs a discrete hypothesis space of candidate segmentation masks, maintains an explicit posterior belief distribution, and selects each fixation to maximise expected information gain—updating beliefs via vision–language model verification and terminating when uncertainty falls below a principled risk threshold. We formalise this process as Bayesian Active Semantic Grounding (BASG), a computational-level account that provides formal guarantees on belief concentration, entropy reduction, and bounded decision risk. The framework is neurobiologically grounded in the large-scale network organisation of the human brain, with the Salience Network identified as the dynamic orchestrator of semantic, inferential, and oculomotor processes. Critically, Eyegent requires no gaze supervision and no task-specific training: it is zero-shot, modular, and built entirely from off-the-shelf components. Evaluated on RefCOCO-Gaze and AiR-D, two benchmarks coupling language-driven visual tasks with human eye-tracking ground truth, Eyegent achieves competitive or state-of-the-art performance among zero-shot methods across semantic, spatial, and structural scanpath metrics, and approaches supervised baselines on several dimensions. The result is a system that does not merely predict where humans look, but generates scanpaths for the same reason humans generate them: to find out.
evidence_items.title: Eyegent: Visual Attention Orchestration on Concepts

evidence_items.summary: As AI becomes embedded in accessibility research, critical questions arise about representation, participation, and power. This focused critical review examines 26 papers presenting empirical, user-facing AI-based interactive systems involving people with disabilities, drawn from the ACM Digital Library (2019–2026). The corpus is dominated by work with people who are blind or have low vision and by generative AI approaches such as large language models and diffusion models; several disability communities remain sparsely represented. People with disabilities participated most consistently in evaluation, while earlier involvement in problem framing was rare. Most papers acknowledged ethical concerns only in passing; few treated them as structuring design constraints.
evidence_items.title: Representation, Participation, and Power in AI-Based Interactive Systems for Accessibility: A Critical Review

evidence_items.summary: Thymomas can disrupt normal thymopoiesis through reduced expression of the autoimmune regulator (AIRE) gene, leading to immune dysregulation and paraneoplastic syndromes such as Good’s syndrome. This rare condition is characterized by hypogammaglobulinemia, profound B-cell lymphopenia, T-cell dysfunction, neutralizing autoantibodies against cytokines such as interferon-α and interleukin-12, and increased susceptibility to opportunistic infections, particularly those caused by intracellular and encapsulated pathogens. We present the case of a 54-year-old Colombian woman with a previously unidentified anterior mediastonic mass who presented with chronic diarrhea, severe neutropenia, and mucocutaneous herpes simplex infection. Immunological evaluation demonstrated hypogammaglobulinemia (IgG 473 mg/dL), undetectable IgM (< 21 mg/dL), and an absence of circulating B cells on flow cytometry (CD19⁺ < 1%). Bone marrow flow cytometry revealed a markedly expanded CD8⁺ T cell population with an inverted CD4/CD8 ratio and a complete absence of B lymphocytes, without evidence of dysplasia or hematologic malignancy. The preserved trilineage hematopoiesis in the bone marrow biopsy suggests an immune-mediated mechanism of neutrophil destruction rather than primary bone marrow failure. Due to severe neutropenia and a high risk of infection, and following a multidisciplinary risk-benefit assessment, temporary immunomodulatory therapy was initiated with rabbit antithymocyte globulin (rATG, 3.5 mg/kg for 5 days), cyclosporine, and filgrastim, along with intravenous immunoglobulin replacement and antiviral therapy with acyclovir, to stabilize hematological parameters and allow for invasive procedures. After clinical stabilization, the patient underwent video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery with complete resection of the mediastonic mass. Histopathological analysis confirmed a type A thymoma, establishing the diagnosis of Good syndrome. Following thymectomy and the initiation of regular intravenous immunoglobulin replacement therapy, the patient has not experienced any new opportunistic infections. Good’s syndrome should be suspected in patients with thymoma presenting with hypogammaglobulinemia, inverted CD4/CD8 ratio, and opportunistic infections. This case highlights the importance of early immunological evaluation and the need for careful multidisciplinary risk-benefit assessment when considering potent immunosuppressive agents such as rATG in patients with pre-existing combined immunodeficiency. When administered with close monitoring for viral reactivation and appropriate antimicrobial prophylaxis, targeted immunomodulatory therapy may offer a viable rescue strategy for the management of severe immune-mediated cytopenias prior to definitive surgical treatment.
evidence_items.title: Thymoma associated good syndrome presenting with combined immunodeficiency severe neutropenia and opportunistic infection

evidence_items.summary: Avian pathogenic Escherichia coli (APEC) is the cause of avian colibacillosis, which leads to huge economic losses in poultry production worldwide, and presents significant zoonotic antimicrobial resistance (AMR) risk. Cell‐permeable itaconate derivatives exhibit dual antibacterial and immunomodulatory properties; however, they have not been systematically evaluated against APEC, and their underlying molecular mechanisms remain poorly defined for this pathogen. In the present study, we systematically explored the anti‐APEC therapeutic potential and mechanism of action of 4‐octyl itaconate (4‐OI) using an integrated approach of in vitro phenotypic, ex vivo macrophage, biochemical genetic, and dual in vivo infection models. In vitro phenotypic assays revealed that 400 μM 4‐OI significantly inhibited the growth of the clinical isolate O78‐type APEC94 and increased its susceptibility to physiological osmotic and acid–base stress (pH 5–7) and decreased the biofilm formation by 64%, swarming motility by 57%, macrophage adhesion by 42%, and cellular invasion by 35%. Ex vivo, 4‐OI showed a dose‐dependent inhibitory effect on the intracellular survival of APEC in RAW264.7 macrophages, with equivalent efficacy to tetracycline, and without any host cell cytotoxicity. Mechanistic qPCR confirmed that 4‐OI inhibits the transcription of five key virulence genes (fimC, luxS, wza, iroN, and menB) by 2.4–5.3‐fold. Further biochemical pull‐down, LC‐MS/MS, site‐directed cysteine mutation, and gene knockout/overexpression assays demonstrated that 4‐OI directly alkylates the conserved cysteine residues of LuxS, isocitrate lyase (Icl), and OmpA, thereby simultaneously disrupting bacterial quorum sensing, glyoxylate shunt metabolism, and outer membrane integrity. The virulence‐attenuating effect of 4‐OI was confirmed by metabolite complementation assays, which showed that glyoxylate and menaquinone biosynthesis are defective. In vivo therapeutic evaluation showed that 50 mg/kg 4‐OI could significantly suppress APEC‐induced mouse mortality from 87.5% to 12.5%, reduce bacterial loads in serum and all visceral tissues, and downregulated proinflammatory cytokines (IL‐1β and TNF‐α) to relieve over‐immune pathological damage. 50 mg/kg 4‐OI increased the survival of chicken embryos to 86.7% and reduced the bacterial loads in the allantoic fluids by 83% in poultry‐relevant specific pathogen‐free (SPF) chicken embryo models. Moreover, 4‐OI exhibited antibiofilm and antiadhesion activity against various epidemic APEC serotypes and clinical multidrug‐resistant isolates with no effect on the diversity or composition of chicken cecal microbiota. Collectively, our findings support 4‐OI as a safe alternative to conventional antibiotics for treating avian colibacillosis, acting via cysteine alkylation to repress multiple virulence‐ and metabolic‐related targets. This work establishes a multifaceted preclinical proof‐of‐concept dataset supporting further development of 4‐OI as an anti‐multi‐drug resistance (MDR) candidate agent; additional farm‐relevant in vivo trials will be required prior to real‐world application for safeguarding poultry health and global food safety.
evidence_items.title: 4‐Octyl Itaconate Suppresses Virulence of Multidrug‐Resistant Avian Pathogenic Escherichia coli via Cysteine Alkylation of LuxS, Icl, and OmpA

evidence_items.summary: The Jackfruit bronzing disease represents a significant phytosanitary constraint affecting Artocarpus heterophyllus production. In this context, the exploration of plant‐associated microorganisms as a source of potential biological control agents aligns with sustainable agricultural strategies. This study is aimed at isolating, characterizing, and evaluating the in vitro antagonistic interactions, and antimicrobial potential of indigenous rhizospheric and endophytic bacteria with the potential to be developed as biocontrol agents for the control jackfruit bronzing causal agent Pantoea stewartii subsp. stewartii. A total of 138 bacterial isolates were obtained from rhizospheric soils and internal plant tissues, with a predominance of rhizospheric bacteria (78.3%). In vitro antagonism assays revealed that only rhizospheric isolates exhibited inhibitory activity against the phytopathogen, identifying 12 strains with consistent antagonistic capacity. These isolates were further characterized to elucidate the potential mechanisms involved in microbial antagonism. Functional analyses demonstrated that the antagonistic isolates possessed multiple extracellular enzymatic activities, predominantly lipase, followed by amylase and cellulase activities, whereas protease activity was absent. Additionally, selected isolates exhibited biosurfactant production, suggesting their role in pathogen inhibition. Antibiosis was confirmed through the production of diffusible antimicrobial compounds. Furthermore, molecular screening revealed the presence of nonribosomal peptide synthetase (NRPS) gene fragments in several strains, supporting their genetic potential to synthesize bioactive secondary metabolites. Phylogenetic identification based on 16S rDNA gene sequencing assigned the isolates to bacterial taxa known for their ecological versatility and functional attributes. Overall, this study provides evidence that rhizospheric bacteria associated with jackfruit harbor significant antagonistic and antimicrobial capabilities against jackfruit bronzing causal agent. These findings contribute to the understanding of microbial interactions and functional traits associated with plant microbiota. This study provides the first assessment of microorganisms associated with jackfruit.
evidence_items.title: Rhizospheric Bacteria From Artocarpus heterophyllus Exhibit Antimicrobial Traits and Antagonistic Activity Against Pantoea stewartii subsp. stewartii, Causal Agent of Jackfruit Bronzing Disease

evidence_items.summary: Trauma-associated surgical acute abdomen is a time-sensitive emergency in which delayed recognition of intra-abdominal hemorrhage, hollow-viscus perforation, or mesenteric ischemia can lead to shock, peritonitis, organ failure, and death. Blunt and penetrating mechanisms produce different but overlapping patterns of solid-organ, intestinal, mesenteric, and abdominal wall injury. Initial management depends principally on hemodynamic status, resuscitation response, and signs of peritoneal irritation. Focused assessment with sonography for trauma and contrast-enhanced computed tomography support rapid evaluation, although subtle bowel and mesenteric injuries may remain occult. Patients with persistent instability or clear operative findings require prompt exploration, whereas selected stable patients can undergo targeted imaging, observation, or diagnostic laparoscopy. Damage-control surgery prioritizes immediate hemorrhage and contamination control, temporary closure when necessary, and physiologic recovery before definitive reconstruction. Solid-organ bleeding may require packing, resection, or endovascular embolization; intestinal disruption may require repair or resection; and mesenteric avulsion demands assessment of perfusion and bowel viability. Outcomes depend on injury burden, speed of intervention, physiologic derangement, associated trauma, and institutional resources. This narrative review summarizes injury patterns, diagnostic limitations, operative strategies, and reported outcomes in trauma-related surgical acute abdomen, emphasizing timely decision-making and individualized surgical escalation.
evidence_items.title: Surgical Acute Abdomen Following Abdominal Trauma: Diagnostic Priorities, Damage-Control Surgery, And Clinical Outcomes

evidence_items.summary: This study examines the evolution of cooperation between the Republic of Uzbekistan and the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) from the establishment of UNICEF’s country presence in 1994 to October 2026. Its purpose is to identify the partnership’s principal historical stages, distinguish institutional outputs from changes in child well-being, and assess the opportunities and limitations of the 2026–2030 cooperation framework. A qualitative historical-documentary design is applied to United Nations agreements, UNICEF country programme documents, official progress reports, and publicly available national and international child-related indicators. Comparative reading and descriptive analysis reveal four overlapping phases: establishment of a rights-based legal and operational framework (1994–2007), consolidation of sectoral cooperation (2008–2016), integration with extensive national reforms (2017–2024), and transition to a more explicitly systems-oriented programme (2025–2026). Uzbekistan’s estimated under-five mortality rate fell from 69.1 per 1,000 live births in 1994 to 13.4 in 2024; preschool coverage and social protection also expanded, although disparities in service quality and child protection remain. The analysis concludes that UNICEF’s contribution is best understood in terms of technical cooperation, convening, evidence production, and institutional capacity rather than sole responsibility for national outcomes. Continued progress will require better disaggregated monitoring, adequate financing, stronger local service delivery, and rigorous evaluation of implementation.
evidence_items.title: THREE DECADES OF UZBEKISTAN–UNICEF COOPERATION: HISTORICAL EXPERIENCE, MAJOR STAGES, RESULTS AND PROSPECTS (1994–2026)

evidence_items.summary: The last five years of research on sustainability labelling, reported in 175 journal articles, documents its effectiveness in increasing consumer choices of more sustainable food products. Some sustainability labels come out as stronger than others and their impact varies across products, countries, and individual consumers, depending on label characteristics, knowledge, familiarity, and perceived issue importance. When combining multiple labels, each of them usually has a positive effect on choices, but their marginal effects are lower than if the label is used alone. Many consumers lack sufficient knowledge about certification requirements and benefits of labelled products, which leads to confusion and vulnerability to ‘greenwashing’ attempts. Also, high societal focus on one sustainability topic can divert limited attention away from other important topics. Hence, it is important for businesses to exercise restraint regarding uncertified claims and for policy to connect and balance sustainability issues and facilitate consumers' mental connections between certified sustainability labels.
evidence_items.title: The Impact of Sustainability Labelling on Consumers' Evaluation and Choice of Food Products: A Systematic Literature Review

evidence_items.summary: Research activities in environmental monitoring, Earth observation , and sensing technologies generate large volumes of heterogeneous datasets, ranging from sensor measurements and satellite imagery to geospatial analyses and model outputs. While these data represent valuable scientific assets, their publication and reuse remain challenging due to the effort required for metadata creation , standardization , interoperability , and long- term accessibility .   To address these challenges, Eurac Research has renewed its Environmental Data Platform (EDP), a research data infrastructure supporting the entire data lifecycle, from processing to publication and dissemination . The EDP combines established open-source technologies for metadata cataloguing , data management, and interoperable services with custom components developed and released as open source by Eurac Research . This integrated architecture provides a centralized environment for publishing and accessing environmental datasets through standardized web services and APIs , in line with FAIR principles and international standards.   The recent evolution of the EDP focused on improving the FAIRness of research outputs through enhanced metadata management, DOI assignment , linked data technologies , and integration with external discovery services such as Data.europa.eu and local data infrastructures . These improvements increase dataset visibility , support persistent citation , and facilitate data discovery and reuse by researchers and stakeholders.   To further promote high- quality metadata creation , the EDP now integrates the F - UJI assessment tool within the metadata catalogue . Researchers receive immediate feedback on the FAIRness of their metadata records , making FAIR compliance transparent and measurable .
evidence_items.title: Enhancing FAIRness for Research Data through the  Environmental Data Platform at Eurac Research

evidence_items.summary: Presentation at the online workshop "Open Transfer: How Does Open Science Lead to Successful Technology Transfer?" (Open Transfer in Practice), organized by TransferAllianz e.V., 21 October 2026, as part of the OpenTransfer project. Data using it does not reduce it, yet most research data is never reused. Based on the guide "OpenTransfer: Data" (2026), the talk covers: FAIR is not open, and findable is not accessible: publishing metadata makes closed data findable without giving the data away; not every dataset: invest transfer effort in a few high-value datasets (relevance, leverage, replacement cost, credibility); data cannot always be open: ethics and consent, export control, contracts, economic value and rights, and the matching agreements (NDA, MTA, DTA/DSA, consortium agreement, license); access and payment are two separate choices: open can be paid and exclusive can be free; decide per asset, not per project; where the transfer office should come in along the data value chain: at data generation, not only at licensing; two HZDR cases with different routes: THEREDA and OPTIMA; a new role for transfer: from protecting IP to legal and organizational hygiene plus product thinking. The talk ends with discussion questions on obstacles, visibility of closed data, and the support researchers and transfer offices still need.
evidence_items.title: The role of transfer in data transfer

evidence_items.summary: Due to relatively long parking and related connection times charging of electric vehicles (EV) is characterized by flexibility, which could be exploited for different benefits such as charging cost minimization or better utilization of intermittent renewable energy sources (RES). To this end, a predictive and optimal hierarchical charging management method of EV fleet characterized by computational efficiency and good scalability is proposed herein. The method relies on an aggregate EV fleet model, a model predictive control (MPC) which employs a dynamic programming (DP)-based algorithm for on-line optimization of an aggregate charging power, and a heuristic algorithm that distributes the aggregate charging power to individual EVs. The heuristic algorithm is set to prioritize EVs with lower state-of-energy levels and sooner time-of-departure. The proposed charging management strategy is demonstrated for the case of virtually electrified delivery vehicle fleet of a local retail company and virtual electricity production from RES, and verified against the globally optimal benchmark obtained offline by the DP algorithm.
evidence_items.title: Hierarchical Model Predictive Control-based Electric Vehicle Fleet  Charging Management

The fraction ρ obeys a first-order law, ρ = 1 + m/B′, set by the volume scaling of the non-self-consistent XC energy difference, confirmed on 16 new solids. evidence_items.summary: ABSTRACT : Driven by the Fourth and Fifth Industrial Revolutions, global financial institutions are aggressively deploying artificial intelligence (AI) technologies to optimize operations, risk management, and customer engagement. However, empirical investigation into AI adoption dynamics within emerging economies remains critically sparse, as established technology acceptance frameworks predominantly reflect advanced or industrialized environments. This study investigates the primary determinants—encompassing both technological, organizational, and environmental drivers and barriers—influencing AI adoption across the banking sector in Cambodia, evaluating 25 hypotheses to establish an integrated conceptual model tailored to emerging financial settings. A mixed-methods design with concurrent triangulation was executed. Quantitative data were gathered via a survey of 83 banking institutions and analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). Qualitative insights were extracted via content analysis on 17 semi-structured interviews. As a result, PLS-SEM path modeling confirmed 17 of 25 hypotheses as statistically significant drivers. Primary drivers include top management’s innovativeness, business scope, top management’s support, familiarity with innovation, and relative advantage. Surprisingly, traditional economic and structural inhibitors—technical complexity, cost, centralization, formalization, organization size, slack, government policies, and geographical settings—were statistically unsupported as firm-level barriers in the quantitative model. Nonetheless, qualitative content analysis supported 24 of 25 factors, exposing a profound perception-reality gap where operational friction is overridden by top-down executive mandates and competitive survival pressures.
evidence_items.title: Drivers and Barriers to Artificial Intelligence Adoption in the Banking Sector: Evidence from Cambodia

evidence_items.summary: This report is prepared in alignment with EU STOPP deliverable D3.5, Monomaterial packaging development to facilitate recyclability of flexible plastic food packaging. Flexible films have a major share in food packaging industry for safety and shelf life. The EU Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation (PPWR) mandates all packaging to be recyclable by 2030. The state-of-the-art multifunctional films such as Polyethylene Terephthalate – Polyethylene – Polypropylene (PET-PE, PET-PP) impose various sorting and recycling challenges. PP offers good physical and aesthetic properties, outstanding barrier for water vapour but limited Oxygen barrier which is critical for food shelf life. The PPWR and supporting design for recycling (DfR) standard EN 18120-7 (CEN-2026) enforce all flexible PP-PE as monomaterial without Oxygen barrier PET layer in the material composition. The RecyClass protocol on Recyclability Evaluation defines PP monomaterial films to be 90% composed of PP with maximum thickness of 250 µm. The EN 18120-7 guidelines prohibit use of barrier coating such as aluminium foil. Additives which do not impede recycling and reuse can be compounded with PP at weight percentage less than 7.5. These include for instance aluminium and silicon oxides AlOx , SiOx, and Ethylene Vinyl Alcohol (EVOH). The research objective is to improve the Oxygen barrier level of monomaterial PP films based on film thickness enhancement, modulating cast film and biaxial stretching parameter, and additives. The methodology is based on full factorial design and Pearson correlation to systematically investigate distinct and synergetic sensitivity of BOPP processing parameters to barrier properties. The optimum BOPP barrier performance is realised in 40-50 µm thickness range with further 50% increase 50% at 100-120 µm range beyond which there is no major improvement.
evidence_items.title: D3.5: Monomaterial Packaging Design

evidence_items.summary: Paper P6 of a ten part series P1-P10 on Interaction, Cohesive Emergence, and Fundamental Constants in Generalised Trace Dynamics P6 — Mirror configurations and parity tests The Stage~1 paper of this series [1] found that, in the trap-plus-sea scheme of the constants paper [2], the state of trace dynamics selects a parity-conjugate pair --- two spin-$\tfrac12$ fuzzy spheres that are mirror images of each other, $Q^{(2)}=-Q^{(1)}$ --- as the ground state of the seven-matrix model for $\omega/m\gtrsim0.1$--$0.2$, and left as the first open question whether that pair survives the cubic term $(\ii\mu/3)\varphi {ABC}\Tr Q AQ BQ C$ of the companion paper \CP, which is odd under $Q\to-Q$ and which the companion paper's own geometric phase needs. This note answers it, from both ends. In the companion paper's model, where the spheres are cubic-driven, \tagP\ a sphere of the opposite handedness has no stationary radius at any angular velocity inside the bound, any $f=1$ two-sphere configuration must consist of blocks of opposite handedness and so forgoes the cubic energy of a same-handed pair, and at the benchmark that cost ($19.9$) exceeds the state's largest possible gain ($1.5$) by an order of magnitude; \tagD\ the mirror-pair start relaxes to the configuration the Stage~1 paper found for two atoms --- two vacuum-handed spheres with their frames as anti-parallel as handedness allows (overlap $-0.51$, planes $59^\circ$ apart, against the handedness-limited optimum $-\tfrac12$, $60^\circ$; on the spheres the anticommuting fraction is $(1-\text{overlap})/2=0.76$, the missing quarter being what handedness costs).
evidence_items.title: The cubic against the mirror: does the parity-conjugate pair of the Adler--Millard ensemble survive the cubic term of the octonionic matrix model? :Paper P6 of a ten-part series P1-P10

evidence_items.summary: Paper P9 of a ten part series P1-P10 on Interaction, Cohesive Emergence, and Fundamental Constants in Generalised Trace Dynamics P9 — Jordan response and conserved collective charges Exceptional Jordan spectra can acquire physical significance only after a dynamics, a state and a normalization prescription have been specified. We investigate this issue in a finite canonical matrix extension motivated by generalized trace dynamics. Seven Hermitian $3\times3$ matrices interact through commutator, octonionic cubic and radial quartic terms. At prescribed matrix charge we construct a relative equilibrium, certify consistency of its three-amplitude ansatz and find a locally positive normal Hessian. A principal spin projection defines an explicit Albert-algebra readout. After removal of the charge phase, its 20 independent linear readings miss three collective directions; retaining them permits regular elimination of 39 gapped coordinates and gives a positive induced kinetic matrix. Hidden $SU(2)$ rotations preserve the Jordan element and invariant spectra, although fixed-component responses change. A different effect survives for Jordan-invariant probes: static relaxation and slow closed-system evolution have distinct susceptibilities. We derive the positive collective-charge correction and the bound $0\preceq\chi {\rm dyn}\preceq\chi {\rm stat}$. At the benchmark the quadratic Jordan invariant has an $8.0702\%$ response deficit, and the generalized susceptibility ratios are $(0.916283932,1)$, equally for two independent Jordan roots. Nineteen prescribed nearby cases retain the tested stability and response properties. This supplies a reproducible dynamics-to-Jordan-response calculation in a specified finite parent. It does not derive that parent from microscopic generalized trace dynamics, identify its roots with fermion masses, or determine observed fundamental constants.
evidence_items.title: Jordan Spectral Response and Conserved Collective Charges in a Matrix Extension of Generalized Trace Dynamics: Paper P9 in a ten-part series P1-P10

evidence_items.summary: Paper P7 of a ten part series P1-P10 on Interaction, Cohesive Emergence, and Fundamental Constants in Generalised Trace Dynamics P7 — Nonlinear instability and exact descent A useful benchmark for cohesive emergence must select its matrix background dynamically and retain the modes that remain light. We study these questions in a seven-matrix $G 2$-invariant mechanics with a cubic interaction and a positive radial quartic. At radial-to-commutator ratio $\lambda/g^2=1/2$, we prove that every positive-radius associative Pauli stationary configuration of multiplicity at least three, with nonnegative mass squared, fails to be a zero-charge classical local minimum. An exact rational deformation has lower energy on a uniform finite amplitude interval throughout this parameter family, despite a nonnegative benchmark Hessian. We then construct a competing irreducible $N=6$ stationary configuration from rank-three tensor operators on spin five-halves. Its benchmark normal Hessian is numerically positive. In an explicitly traceless canonical quantum model, we calculate the hard-mode radial response, the induced interaction on seven retained fermion modes, and a coupled rotor--fermion ordering operator in one specified charge representation. The distinction between exact identities, numerical stability and conditional quantum results is maintained throughout. These results sharpen a finite dynamical test for the GTD programme; they do not reconstruct physical spacetime, Standard Model colour or measured fundamental constants.
evidence_items.title: Vacuum selection and collective quantum response in an octonionic matrix model: Paper P7 in a ten-part series P1-P10

evidence_items.summary: As foundation models evolve from information generation to digital work execution, agents are increasingly capable of completing complex tasks across tools, applications, and workflows. However, existing research lacks a unified perspective on how agents reliably accomplish delegated work. To address this gap, we present a work-centric, system-level perspective that views work agents as systems combining foundation models and runtime harnesses to execute tasks in stateful workspaces and deliver verifiable outcomes. We introduce two complementary dimensions, work persistence and work openness, to characterize working conditions, and classify digital work into five forms according to task scope and organization. Building on this framework, we identify five core capability families required for reliable work execution and examine approaches to model optimization, harness optimization, and their joint optimization. We further analyze existing evaluation methods and metrics from the perspective of work outcomes. Finally, we discuss future research directions, including sustained work delegation, adaptation to open environments, and the interaction between work execution and capability improvement. This paper provides a unified framework for understanding, optimizing, and evaluating work agents, supporting the development of systems capable of delivering reliable, verifiable, and practically valuable work outcomes.
evidence_items.title: Work Agents: Systems, Capabilities, and Optimization

evidence_items.summary: Reusable Web-agent verification requires a rule to follow changing requirements and support subsequent execution. We introduce AgentProofBench, which connects paired tests of a frozen acceptance rule to execution from identical saved openings. The resource spans 97 tasks, 79 families, and four Web services. Experiments with DeepSeek Flash/Pro establish two linked measurements. Across 48 families, complete-panel and decision-replay tests retain 82/96 Flash and 79/96 Pro source programs; paired reuse-rebuild BA intervals are [-5.47, 1.57] and [-10.16, 0.00] percentage points. Across 22 execution families, deployment-state panel correctness separates program assignments whose two saved openings are both delivered correctly: 32/33 assignments with error-free panels, versus 1/11 with panel errors. All reference-defined program-gate regressions and withheld deliveries occur in the latter group. Neutral continuation attains the highest correct delivery under the tested generic feedback, providing a concrete baseline for measuring the value added by a gate. Released instructions, states, programs, reference rules, and trajectories connect each test failure to its execution consequences. AgentProofBench makes reusable verification assessable at both the requirement and policy levels.
evidence_items.title: AgentProofBench: Benchmarking Reusable Verifiers for Web Agents

evidence_items.summary: Background. Clinicians score the NIH Stroke Scale (NIHSS) at the bedside, often under time pressure, and ambient AI tools that listen to clinical encounters are now entering practice. It is not known whether software can score the NIHSS from the exam conversation itself, rather than extract a score that has already been written in a note. Methods. We created 112 synthetic code-stroke cases. One hundred were allocated in proportion to real code-stroke presentations, and 12 stress cases tested special scoring rules. For each case, a large language model (Claude Opus 5.5) wrote a reference score form (the answer key) and a speech-to-text-style exam transcript, with main-set transcripts split evenly between a narrated and a telegraphic examiner style. A second model (Claude Fable 5.1), blind to the key, scored every transcript and agreed with the key on 99.2% of items. Each transcript was then scored by Jev, a decision model, and by gpt-6-luna, a general large language model (LLM). The primary outcome was item-level accuracy against the key. Results. The LLM scored 99.0% of items correctly (95% CI 98.4-99.4) and Jev 94.4% (93.2-95.4; McNemar p < 0.001), with exact totals in 101 and 63 of 112 cases. Jev was faster (median 0.15 vs 5.78 s per exam) and cheaper (USD 0.23 vs 0.67 per 1,000 exams). With telegraphic examiners, accuracy fell from 98.0% to 90.9% for Jev and from 100% to 97.7% for the LLM. In a post-hoc analysis that kept only the examiner's words, accuracy stayed high when the examiner narrated (Jev 96.9%, LLM 98.8%) but dropped to about 80% when the examiner used shorthand. Most of Jev's errors fell on four items (language, extinction and neglect, LOC questions and visual fields), and on each it tended to repeat the same mistake, for example scoring slurred speech as aphasia. Its confidence flagged most of these errors. Re-checking the 14.8% of items with confidence below 0.70 would have caught 86% of them, and a simulated hybrid reached 98.8% accuracy.
evidence_items.title: Scoring the NIH Stroke Scale from bedside exam transcripts: a synthetic benchmark of a decision model and a large language model

evidence_items.summary: Training Large Language Models (LLMs) via Reinforcement Learning (RL) at the network edge faces a fundamental obstacle: existing distributed RL frameworks assume static, homogeneous clusters, incompatible with the heterogeneous hardware of Multi-access Edge Computing (MEC) infrastructure. We present ElasticScale, an elastic orchestration system that organizes heterogeneous accelerators into disaggregated rollout and trainer instances, via a HeterogeneousRayWorkerGroup abstraction that manages non-uniform hardware topologies and a multi-instance Federated Weight Averaging protocol that aggregates updates across trainers of differing speeds. On an emulated heterogeneous cluster, ElasticScale achieves up to 2.09× the throughput of a synchronous colocated baseline at equivalent convergence on mathematical reasoning benchmarks, and we further characterize how rollout-trainer imbalance triggers training collapse, yielding practical guidance for allocating compute across heterogeneous edge nodes.
evidence_items.title: ElasticScale: Elastic Large Language Model Reinforcement Learning Training on Heterogeneous Mobile Edge Clusters

evidence_items.summary: This study proposes a methodological framework for analyzing public transit user satisfaction by processing unstructured, voice-derived trip chain data. Traditional survey methods often do not capture the contextual and real time aspects of user experience. To address this limitation, this study employs large language models and natural language processing techniques to analyze trip-related feedback collected from 5,000 public transit users. Sentiment scores were extracted from a station-labeled subset of the data set and applied to a broader corpus to assess satisfaction levels across subway stations in the Seoul Metropolitan Area. Using a combination of sentiment analysis and K-means clustering, this study categorized 102 subway stations into three groups: (1) High Satisfaction Station Group; (2) Low Satisfaction Station Group; and (3) Moderate Satisfaction Station Group. These clusters were the basis for grouping stations, and user feedback on transit experiences was summarized for each station within its respective cluster. This approach enables the identification of low-satisfaction transit stations requiring immediate attention, as well as moderate-satisfaction transit stations where service equity must be addressed. The proposed methodology offers a practical alternative to traditional survey-based assessments by leveraging unstructured public transit users’ data. With further refinement and institutional support, this approach can enhance data-driven, user-centered transit planning and contribute to broader improvements in urban mobility.
evidence_items.title: Large Language Model-Based Sentiment Analysis for Public Transit Satisfaction Using Trip Chain Data

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background Patients increasingly use large language models (LLMs) for health information, yet the evaluation of the quality of fecal incontinence (FI) content from these models is limited. We aimed to evaluate the quality, understandability, and actionability of LLM responses to FI queries. We hypothesized that LLMs would provide variable quality responses with variable understandability and actionability. Methods Search data was extracted from Google Trends’ top five search queries related to FI to create identical prompts used to generate responses from four LLMs: ChatGPT version 4o mini (OpenAI), Perplexity version sonar (Perplexity AI), LLaMA version 3.2 (Meta AI), and Gemini version 2.0 flash (Google). Responses were assessed using DISCERN, Patient Education Materials Assessment Tool (PEMAT), and the Flesch–Kincaid Grade Level (FKGL). Statistical analysis was performed using R version 4.4.2 (R Core Team, 2025). Results Response quality was moderate (median DISCERN 44 out of 80), nominal understandability was median 77% ([7/9] PEMAT) although inter-rater agreement was poor, and actionability was poor (median 40% [2/5] PEMAT). DISCERN scores varied significantly ( p = 0.033). The responses were at the high school to college level using the FKGL score. Readability differed significantly ( p = 0.022). Conclusions LLM responses demonstrated structural clarity using PEMAT criteria but lacked actionability and were above the recommended reading level for consumer health information. Continued evaluation of artificial intelligence is essential before LLMs can be recommended for patient education.
evidence_items.title: Quality, understandability, and actionability of large language model responses to fecal incontinence: a cross-sectional study

evidence_items.summary: Introduction Large language models (LLMs) may enable the extraction of clinically relevant information from unstructured electronic health records, but most previous work focused on identifying diagnoses without preserving their temporal context. We evaluated the ability of an LLM to extract diagnoses and associated dates from longitudinal clinical reports. Methods In an observational study using the Bern Sleep-Wake Registry, diagnostic annotations from 248 patients comprising 2343 clinical entries were analyzed. Six common comorbidity groups, subdivided into 32 hierarchical diagnostic categories, were evaluated. Using gpt-oss-20b, we extracted diagnosis presence, the number of diagnostic instances, and dates per instance. A reference standard was established through independent review by two physicians, with disagreements adjudicated by a third physician. LLM performance was assessed using diagnostic classification and temporal agreement. Direct annotation costs were compared. Results At the patient level, the LLM achieved an overall F1 score of 0.88 for diagnosis presence and 0.96 for the presence of a reported date. For the earliest reported diagnosis date, agreement with the reference standard was 86.73% at the day level. When considering the cumulative set of dates for each diagnosis, date recall was 87.63%, the extra-date rate was 20.88%, and full agreement was achieved in 58.19% of cases. Human annotators showed substantial disagreement in temporal annotation, with a date recall of 75.49%, an extra-date rate of 17.89%, and full agreement in 58.64% of cases. LLM-based extraction reduced direct annotation costs by 94.65%. Conclusions LLMs can extract diagnoses and their dates from heterogeneous clinical text with high agreement with an adjudicated reference standard. These findings support the scalable use of LLMs for longitudinal clinical registries.
evidence_items.title: Bern Sleep-Wake Registry: temporal extraction of comorbidities from unstructured clinical text using a large language model

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Mentalization - the ability to infer others’ beliefs and intentions to guide one’s own choices - is a key cognitive function underlying human social interactions. Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate behaviour consistent with humans on theory-of-mind tasks, yet whether these models can guide adaptive behaviour through mentalization is unknown. Here we use two economic games with cognitive computational modeling to uncover the latent strategies underlying mentalization in LLMs. We tested individual LLM agents across four model families, DeepSeek, GPT-4.1, GPT-5 and Gemini 2.0 Flash (N = 2,099), against opponents of varying sophistication and examined whether a prompting strategy designed to elicit strategic reasoning improved performance. We benchmarked results against human participants (N = 251) as a comparative measure. Across both games, LLMs showed clear behavioural and computational signatures of mentalizing that differed markedly by model provider and size. Strategic prompting generally improved performance by inducing more sophisticated reasoning, yet the extent of the benefit differed across the two tasks. Last, GPT-5 agents flexibly adapted their recursive depth of reasoning to increasingly sophisticated opponents, demonstrating superior performance to human participants. Collectively, we demonstrate different capacities for mentalization across LLMs, and highlight cognitive computational modeling as a formal method for assessing comparative intelligence across humans and machines.
evidence_items.title: Assessing mentalization in humans and large language models

evidence_items.summary: ABSTRACT Simulating human mobility is crucial for urban planning, environmental exposure assessment, and social behavior studies. However, existing methods often rely on rules and assumptions, making it difficult to provide robust results and explicit decision‐making processes when generating plausible daily activity trajectories from sparse location records such as check‐ins. To bridge these gaps, we propose a large language model (LLM)‐based agent framework that innovatively incorporates the Chain‐of‐Thought (CoT) approach and Reinforcement Learning from AI Feedback (RLAIF) mechanisms, namely Daily mobility LLM (DaiLLM). This framework consists of three modules: the Profiler derives user characteristics from historical trajectory data; the Generator simulates movement through the CoT process, which integrates constraints from Profiler outputs; and the Discriminator employs RLAIF to evaluate the similarity between generated results and real data, providing feedback to optimize the results. Experiments demonstrate that: (1) our method improves accuracy by 34.2% compared to traditional approaches in daily activity trajectory generation; (2) the CoT approach enhances activity logic and results in a 26.1% increase through task decomposition and constraint integration; (3) the RLAIF mechanism explicitly provides an optimization process through Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) analysis; and (4) our method excels in transfer learning and long‐term generation across different city contexts. This study provides a robust, transparent, and cost‐effective solution for plausible daily activity trajectory generation from sparse check‐in data, which will establish a new paradigm for mobility behavior analysis in data‐scarce scenarios.
evidence_items.title: DaiLLM: An Agent Framework Based on a Large Language Model and Reinforced by AI to Generate Daily Activity Trajectories

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) show promise in supporting drug recommendations both within and outside clinical settings, but they may also amplify systematic biases affecting equity and cost. We examined the commercial neutrality of LLM-generated product name recommendations among US Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved products containing the same active ingredient. We evaluated product name recommendations from five LLMs using 177,120 synthetic clinical vignettes spanning 123 disease–drug pairs and 1,440 sociodemographic profiles. Each vignette specified a disease and an active ingredient and asked the model to recommend FDA-approved products. Across disease–drug pairs and models, the most frequently recommended product accounted for a mean of 97.5% of first-choice recommendations, and the models showed almost perfect agreement on which products to recommend. LLM-recommended product distributions differed from real-world prescribing patterns and often yielded higher projected acquisition costs. Recommendations inconsistent with regulatory information varied across LLMs and sociodemographic factors. Models more often recommended products with greater online visibility (Google search counts, odds ratio (OR) 1.70; a dedicated Wikipedia page, OR 3.00) and favoured originator products (OR 20.5), whereas products with later FDA approval and those more commonly prescribed in practice were recommended less often (ORs 0.76 and 0.87, respectively). Although modified prompts shifted recommendations in the intended direction, LLMs still favoured a narrow set of products, which could have potential implications for drug costs and pharmaceutical markets. Rigorous evaluation and targeted mitigation are needed before widespread use.
evidence_items.title: Large language models show product name convergence in drug recommendations

evidence_items.summary: Abstract In the legal domain, judgement prediction is an important and challenging problem. In real-life proceedings, judicial decisions depend on the precise presentation of complex case information and, above all, on the argumentative interplay among petitioners, respondents, and judges. However, most existing research work on this judgment prediction primarily focuses on case facts, rather than on argumentative legal reasoning. Furthermore, many such approaches rely on single-agent Large Language Models (LLMs), which are not analogous to the real-life courtroom. To address this limitation, simulating a courtroom conversation becomes essential. Some prior studies explored multiple LLMs (multi-agent) based courtroom simulations, with limited investigation on the quality of argumentation. Motivated by this crucial gap, in this work, we propose simulating courtroom arguments employing a multi-agent conversational system, termed as \naam, specifically tailored to crime-related cases. We consider solely legal cases from the U.S. Supreme Court, evaluating the ability of LLMs in generating courtroom arguments using different in-context learning approaches, including zero-shot, and the variant of few-shot techniques, within a multi-agent setup. Empirically, we find that the quality of arguments improves significantly when using local precedent retrieval based approach employing GPT-4o models. This strategy yields 12$%$ improvement over the zero-shot (baseline) setup. Subsequently, to measure the quality of LLM-based arguments, we propose a new algorithm -- coined as ArguEval. Eventually, to showcase the efficacy of generated arguments, we utilize them in a downstream \texttt{judgment prediction} task, which results in a 14$\%$ performance gain over the zero-shot baseline.
evidence_items.title: ArguGenCourt: Courtroom Argument Generation using Judicial Multi-agent Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Abstract We present an automated framework employing large language models to categorize atomic spectroscopy literature for NIST bibliographic databases. The system processes native PDFs and supplementary materials via instruction-driven reasoning agents to assign structured search keywords encompassing target species, subject codes, and experimental methodologies. Validation against human-curated datasets demonstrates high precision in elemental species identification, while establishing that granular subject code assignment remains the primary source of categorization error.
evidence_items.title: Categorization of scientific publications using large language models as applied to atomic spectroscopy

evidence_items.summary: Multimodal entity alignment identifies equivalent entities referring to the same real-world object across heterogeneous multimodal knowledge graphs and is essential for multi-source knowledge integration. Existing methods often rely on manually labeled seed alignments and multimodal feature similarity, limiting their ability to capture implicit semantic equivalence under heterogeneous attribute and relation expressions. Large language models (LLMs) offer strong semantic understanding and reasoning capabilities for unsupervised alignment, but their direct application remains challenging because of the large entity search space, redundant knowledge graph information, and the stochasticity of LLM inference. To address these challenges, we propose MEA-LLM, an LLM-based fully unsupervised multimodal semantic-enhanced entity alignment method. MEA-LLM first pre-screens candidate entities by jointly exploiting multimodal similarities derived from visual, attribute, and relational information. It then selects discriminative attributes and relations based on degree of freedom, candidate frequency, and discriminability for LLM reasoning. Multiple inference and result aggregation are further employed to improve robustness. Experiments on FB-DB15K and FB-YAGO15K show that MEA-LLM outperforms existing methods across multiple evaluation metrics. Further ablation studies, hyperparameter analyses, experiments with different model-scales, and efficiency evaluations demonstrate the effectiveness of the core components and indicate that MEA-LLM achieves a favorable trade-off between entity alignment performance and inference cost.
evidence_items.title: An Unsupervised Multimodal Semantic-Enhanced Entity Alignment Method Based on Large Language Models

organizations: University of Michigan
evidence_items.summary: Physical exercise lowers blood pressure, but guidelines address broad populations and rarely consider age, comorbidities, medications or baseline severity. No structured, queryable database of exercise interventions for hypertension exists, and manual curation is not scalable. We present PAHD (Physical Activity for Hypertension Database), built with large language models (LLMs). An LLM screened 2,548 PubMed records by title and abstract, then full text, selecting 255 studies. LLMs extracted each study's groups, exercise protocols, patient characteristics and results; two LLMs cross-checked the study structure, and every value carries a verbatim quote. Code standardized and joined the extractions into 17,312 records from 254 studies, one per reported comparison. Against adjudicated benchmarks, screening reached 86.3% recall and 80.6% precision, and extraction recovered 90.1% of blood pressure values with 90.5% precision. A web portal matches patients' hypertension stage and comorbidities to studies. PAHD provides a structured evidence base for personalized exercise interventions on hypertension management.
evidence_items.title: A Knowledge Database of Physical Activity Interventions for Hypertension using Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: This study aims to evaluate the implementation of digital Arabic language learning among students enrolled in an Arabic Language Education Study Program at a state university in Makassar, Indonesia, using the Context, Input, Process, and Product (CIPP) evaluation model. This study employed a qualitative evaluative approach, with the head of the study program, lecturers, and students participating as research participants. Data were collected through observation, in-depth interviews, and document analysis. The data were analyzed using the interactive model developed by Miles, Huberman, and Saldaña, comprising data reduction, data display, and conclusion drawing and verification. The findings indicate that, in the context dimension, the implementation of digital Arabic language learning aligns with the needs of digital transformation and the demands of twenty-first-century education. In the input dimension, digital infrastructure, institutional support, and lecturers’ competencies were generally adequate, although variations in students’ digital literacy remained evident. In the process dimension, digital learning facilitated student interaction, participation, and flexibility in learning. In the product dimension, the implementation contributed to improvements in Arabic language proficiency, learner autonomy, and students’ digital literacy. Overall, the findings indicate that the implementation of digital Arabic language learning was generally effective and warrants further development. This study recommends strengthening technological infrastructure, providing continuous digital literacy training, and optimizing the integration of digital technologies and artificial intelligence into Arabic language learning.
evidence_items.title: EVALUATION OF THE IMPLEMENTATION OF DIGITAL ARABIC LANGUAGE LEARNING USING THE CIPP MODEL AMONG ARABIC LANGUAGE EDUCATION STUDENTS

authors: Marc J. C. van den Homberg
evidence_items.summary: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming disaster risk reduction and management by enhancing prediction, preparedness, response, and recovery. Leveraging techniques such as machine learning, deep learning, and foundation models, AI can analyse diverse datasets, including satellite imagery, sensor networks, social media, and historical disaster records, to improve early warning systems and risk assessments. AI applications range from predictive modelling of floods, earthquakes, landslides, and tropical cyclones to real-time damage assessment using computer vision and drones, and optimised emergency response planning. Additionally, AI supports post-disaster reconstruction and long-term recovery through economic modelling, infrastructure planning, and psychological support. Despite these benefits, challenges such as data scarcity, algorithmic bias, privacy concerns, and infrastructure requirements must be addressed to ensure equitable and effective deployment. Incorporating ethical frameworks, community engagement, and transparency is essential for maximising AI’s potential in building resilient communities and mitigating the social, economical, and environmental impacts of disasters.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Disaster Risk Management

evidence_items.summary: Abstract The environmental comparison of artificial intelligence (AI) systems is context-dependent regarding lifecycle boundaries, the sharing and allocation of infrastructure, the accounting of electricity use and the accounting of water use. A low operational carbon value can coexist with substantial upstream water consumption or a large unallocated hardware burden. This paper develops a lifecycle framework in which primitive resource events are assigned once to workload stages and translated into energy, greenhouse-gas, and water inventories through explicit, versioned factors. The framework separates physical water consumption from scarcity characterization, operational electricity from upstream energy carriers, and attributional reporting from consequential scheduling. We derive conservation under allocation, an exact temporal aggregation bias identity, an identifiability condition for incomplete inventories, a shared-infrastructure allocation model, and a service-volume break-even condition. A constrained minimax routing extension evaluates conflicting operational objectives without collapsing physical units into an unexplained score. A fully specified synthetic study covers three hypothetical regions, 168 hourly intervals, 24 demand profiles, four routing policies, and 10,000 uncertainty draws. For the base case of 3.36 million requests, carbon-only routing reduces serving carbon by approximately 50.5% relative to the reference, but increases serving water consumption by approximately 124.3%. Once fixed lifecycle burdens are included, the corresponding changes are approximately − 4.2% and + 9.6%. Through this specific situation, the minimax policy is redefined, so no enhancement over the minimax reference is claimed. This study does not exhibit accounting accuracy but rather accounting consistency and conditional decision behavior.
evidence_items.title: Lifecycle Intelligence for Carbon Energy Water Footprint Optimization in Artificial Intelligence Systems

evidence_items.summary: ABSTRACT The translation of nanomedicines is frequently bottlenecked by trial‐and‐error optimization. Integrating artificial intelligence (AI) transforms this process into a closed‐loop, experimentally grounded discovery ecosystem. This Review provides a roadmap for this paradigm, demonstrating how AI, high‐throughput testing, and nanoscale design converge to generate clinically translatable nanotherapeutics. We emphasize the necessity of standardized multimodal data—spanning pharmacokinetic, biodistribution, and drug‐release profiles—anchored strictly to validated biological phenomena. Furthermore, we evaluate an algorithmic spectrum, ranging from classical machine learning to physics‐informed neural networks (PINNs) and reinforcement learning (RL), to align models with specific formulation objectives. To bridge computational design and empirical reality, we examine how high‐throughput technologies, such as robotic laboratories and in vivo DNA‐barcoding multiplexing, operationalize the “Design‐Make‐Test‐Analyze” (DMTA) cycle for dynamic model recalibration. Ultimately, this review demonstrates how integrating AI, physical constraints, and automated validation accelerates the rational design of next‐generation nanomedicines.
evidence_items.title: An Integrated Artificial Intelligence Framework for Nanomedicine Engineering

organizations: İZMİR KATİP ÇELEBİ ÜNİVERSİTESİ, TIP FAKÜLTESİ
evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into modern healthcare, supporting diagnostic interpretation, clinical decision-making, workflow optimization, documentation, patient communication, medical education, and outcome prediction. This narrative review examines the current clinical applications and future directions of healthcare AI, with radiology presented as a model specialty because of its standardized workflows, large datasets, and measurable outputs. It discusses the growing roles of generative AI, large language models, multimodal foundation models, patient-facing applications, and AI-assisted medical education, while emphasizing persistent limitations such as hallucinations, bias, limited generalizability, inadequate reporting, and insufficient prospective clinical evidence. Emerging approaches, including digital twins and agentic AI systems, may enable patient-specific simulation, longitudinal monitoring, and multi-step workflow automation; however, their clinical use remains at an early stage. Successful implementation will require external validation, transparent reporting, continuous performance monitoring, institutional governance, and clearly defined human oversight. The future value of AI will therefore depend not on complete autonomy, but on its ability to improve healthcare safely, effectively, equitably, and responsibly within human-supervised clinical systems.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Modern Healthcare: Present and Future

evidence_items.summary: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is now embedded in higher education. Yet educators often adopt it more slowly and cautiously than students, and generic guidance rarely translates into changes in teaching or assessment practice. We designed a short, hands‐on, pedagogy‐first workshop in which life‐science educators work with their own course materials, intended to increase confidence in pedagogically informed AI use and prompt concrete changes to course design, teaching and assessment. However, this is an exploratory feasibility and specification report; therefore, the evaluation was not designed to test that intention. Here we describe the design of a transferable three‐session FEBS Education and Training Academy module, organised around the PICRAT (Passive‐Interactive‐Creative/Replace‐Amplify‐Transform) framework, a four‐element prompt structure and studio‐style application to participants' own teaching artefacts, and evaluate it using matched pre/post surveys, anonymous after‐session feedback and an online follow‐up meeting. Thirty‐four educators from 14 countries attended; 21 completed the pre‐workshop and 13 the post‐workshop survey (12 matched). Among the 12 respondents who completed both surveys, the proportion reporting high confidence rose by the same margin, 4 of 12, in each of the five practical domains. Ten of 13 follow‐up respondents reported implementing at least one idea and while views of AI as beneficial were already positive and changed little, agreement that AI poses significant risks to academic integrity fell. These participant‐reported, uncontrolled findings should be read as evidence of feasibility and perceived usefulness rather than causal impact.
evidence_items.title: Design and evaluation of FEBS Education and Training Academy module – Integrating generative artificial intelligence into life‐science education

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Artificial intelligence is routinely described as a knowledge technology. This paper argues that the description misplaces a boundary Hayek drew in 1945, between “scientific knowledge”—codifiable, statistical, articulable—and “knowledge of the particular circumstances of time and place.” Kiesling (2015) reconstructs part of the latter as the contextual knowledge problem: knowledge that does not exist outside the interaction producing it, as against the complexity problem of aggregating knowledge that exists dispersed but can in principle be codified. The reconstruction is interpretive and identifies a generative subset of Hayek’s category rather than its whole content; much of the remainder is knowledge agents already possess, and AI dissolves a good deal of it. The argument is not that machine systems cannot discover novel alternatives, nor that their search spaces are closed; both are conceded. It is that discovering means does not originate the ultimate ends by reference to which alternatives acquire economic significance, and that current systems receive those ends rather than constituting them. Under a Misesian account of evaluative agency—a premise the paper declares rather than derives—better aggregation, prediction and optimisation therefore cannot by themselves resolve the generative subset, so neither Polanyian tacit knowledge in large language models nor microstructure price discovery by high-frequency traders reaches it. The taxonomy is applied at three levels—the data pipeline, the tacit-knowledge debate, and the institutional conditions of price generation—as three applications of one classification rather than three independent demonstrations. Its products are a set of operational tests, none of which has been run and which are here read against a published Q-learning pricing architecture, and a criterion distinguishing context-preserving from context-suppressing deployment at the level of the market.
evidence_items.title: Data is not knowledge: Hayek’s epistemological challenge to artificial intelligence

organizations: University of Groningen
evidence_items.summary: Abstract Benchmarks – shared prediction tasks with fixed data and a common metric – have driven cumulative progress in many fields but remain rare in the social sciences. We document PreFer (Predicting Fertility in the Netherlands), a data challenge in which participants predicted whether Dutch residents aged 18–45 in 2020 would have a child in 2021–2023, using longitudinal LISS panel surveys or full-population administrative registers. About 150 researchers made 69 valid survey-based and 11 register-based submissions. We describe the challenge design and review how teams handled thousands of features, a small and imbalanced survey sample, missing values and longitudinal data. We then analyse the reproducibility of submissions two years after the challenge. Requiring code and trained models rather than predictions in the survey phase made most submissions reproducible: 67 of 69 saved models reproduced their original scores, while retraining from code reproduced the original F1 score to within 0.03 for 52 submissions. Finally, using feature importance and ablation experiments, we identify which topics contributed to predictive performance. The predictive signal was highly concentrated: in the survey data, fertility intentions with partnership and household information came close to full-model performance; the remaining demographic, economic and attitudinal variables added little. In the register data, which lack intentions, partnership and household characteristics each recovered most of the attainable performance. These analyses inform other data challenges in the social sciences and establish PreFer as a reusable benchmark for cumulative fertility research by providing a reference point against which new predictors, data, and methods can be tested.
evidence_items.title: Building a reusable benchmark for life-outcome prediction: design, modelling approaches, predictors, and reproducibility of the PreFer data challenge

organizations: Independent researcher
evidence_items.summary: Scientific priors speed up Bayesian optimisation in materials discovery, but a prior that steers a small budget toward the materials it favours may miss those it disfavours. We measured this in a benchmark with a registered analysis plan: 7,020 searches (3,000 of them over 3,550 metallic multielement Materials Project structures), for the shear modulus and the specific Young’s modulus, with a historical prior and a composition-only elemental-modulus heuristic, each mixed into expected improvement search with a fixed weight β. Coverage was the recall of the half of the top-5% materials that the prior itself scores lowest. Coverage loss at moderate weight was detected in 4 of 6 prior–objective settings. The elemental heuristic reduced the restricted mean number of acquisitions to a top-1% shear-modulus material by 13.9 at β = 0.25 with no detected loss of coverage, but its shear-modulus form, applied to the specific modulus, lost 44.0% or more of the baseline coverage at every nonzero weight. A weight both beneficial and safe under the registered criterion existed in 3 of 6 settings (2 under a post hoc joint error control), never above β = 0.25, and depended on the safety margin and on curation. At β = 0.5, in 5 of 6 settings the weighted search found more top-5% materials in total but, by its estimates, fewer of those its prior disfavours (a loss detected in 3): the prior redirected the search rather than reducing its yield. Faster discovery alone therefore does not show that a search keeps what its prior disfavours.
evidence_items.title: The efficiency–coverage trade-off of scientific priors in Bayesian search: a registered benchmark on metallic multi-element elasticity data

evidence_items.summary: The local metal- π bond is the microscopic unit from which metal-organic quantum materials are built. We benchmark this bond with both density-functional theory (DFT) and fixed-node diffusion quantum Monte Carlo (DMC), using Slater-Jastrow (SJ) and Slater-Jastrow-backflow (SJB) trial wave functions, to compute binding-energy curves for the first-row metallocenes M ( C 5 H 5 ) 2 with M = Ti, V, Fe, and Co as the metal-carbon distance d is varied. Both DFT and DMC exhibit a distance-controlled crossover in which Fe and Co are favored under compression, while V and Ti form deeper wells near equilibrium and remain more strongly bound at larger separation. Similar V > Ti > Fe > Co ordering at the binding minima persists from DFT through SJ and SJB DMC. DFT-PBE (Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof), however, overbinds all four metallocenes relative to the correlated DMC benchmark by a large amount that is close to uniform across the series but grows mildly from early to late transition metals showing that semilocal mean-field DFT captures the qualitative topology of the crossover but is quantitatively inaccurate. DFT + U with standard literature U values does not reliably correct this overbinding and can substantially reorder the binding-strength ranking across the series, showing that U must be determined self-consistently for this bonding environment rather than adopted from unrelated chemistry.
evidence_items.title: Diffusion quantum Monte Carlo benchmark for metal-ligand binding in first-row metallocenes
