evidence_items.summary: The Poisson–Nernst–Planck (PNP) system governs ion transport in lithium-ion battery electrolytes and presents a canonical stiff coupled PDE challenge: the charge-density prefactor F / ε 0 ≈ 10 16 C V −1 m −3 produces extreme coefficient ratios, the electric double layer imposes sharp boundary layers with a singular-perturbation character, and the Poisson and Nernst–Planck equations are nonlinearly coupled. Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) are appealing here because they require no mesh, differentiate through the physics automatically, and handle forward and inverse problems in one framework. Spectral bias and multi-task loss imbalance, however, have limited their accuracy on stiff PNP systems. We present a systematic, simulation-only benchmark of eleven PINN configurations, organised into four strategy groups (adaptive loss weighting, spectral bias mitigation, spatio-temporal decomposition, and uncertainty-weighted enrichment), on a physically parametrised one-dimensional PNP model for a lithium symmetric cell, implemented entirely within NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo Sym and validated against a finite volume method (FVM) reference solution obtained on a uniform mesh of 500 cells. Root-mean-square errors (RMSE) span 10 − 2 – 10 − 4 across architectures: Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) adaptive loss weighting achieves RMSE = 6.6 × 10 − 4 (anion), 6.2 × 10 − 4 (cation), and 1.1 × 10 − 3 (electric potential). The balanced residual decay rate (BRDR) scheme reaches RMSE values 10% higher than NTK for the concentration fields (24% higher for the electric potential) while reducing mean wall-clock time by 1.9 ± 0.1 h per run, making it the preferable strategy under compute constraints. All configurations were trained for the same 100 000-epoch budget, which is not an equal-compute budget: mean wall time ranges from 13.8 to 47.6 h on one NVIDIA H100, so every comparison reported here is conditional on that protocol.
evidence_items.title: A Systematic Benchmark of Physics-Informed Neural Network Strategies for Stiff Ion Transport in Lithium Symmetric Cells

organizations: Department of Electrical Engineering, Yanbu Industrial College, Yanbu 30436, Saudi Arabia
evidence_items.summary: Co-locating photovoltaic (PV) generation and vehicle-to-grid (V2G) capability with electric vehicle charging stations can offset the network impact of charging. A 24 h planning model on the IEEE 33-bus feeder selects up to three of six candidate buses and sizes each station’s charging, PV and V2G capacity. A hybrid of the grey wolf optimizer (GWO) and the whale optimization algorithm (WOA) that switches to GWO updates when the search stagnates is benchmarked against particle swarm optimization (PSO), GWO, WOA and two random-switching hybrids under equal budgets and common seeds. The best plan places stations at buses 18, 22 and 30 and reduces daily losses by 17.5% and voltage deviation by 26.6% at a 0.8% higher annual cost. These gains are due to the 3 MW of PV, and charging alone would raise losses by 14.8%. Over 1000 random days, loss reduction persists, but the minimum voltage falls below 0.90 p.u. on 8.9% of the days (base feeder: 1.3%). The proposed hybrid outperforms WOA (p=0.003). Against GWO, PSO and two random-switching hybrids, neither a significant difference nor equivalence was established, and the point estimates favor the baselines.
evidence_items.title: Solar Electric Vehicle Charging Stations with Vehicle-to-Grid: A Stagnation-Switched Grey Wolf–Whale Hybrid Benchmark

organizations: Department of Chemistry Al al‐Bayt University  Mafraq Jordan
evidence_items.summary: ABSTRACT Calibration models can improve agreement between calculated and experimental 13 C NMR shifts without necessarily transferring to a new compound. We reanalyzed a literature‐derived finite‐cluster GIAO‐DFT benchmark comprising carbamazepine (CBZ), theophylline (THP), and ibuprofen (IBP) using compound‐blocked validation and added an independent protocol‐heterogeneous external challenge using lamivudine Form II. Uncalibrated predictions, a one‐parameter offset, two‐parameter affine scaling, and a three‐parameter quadratic model were compared. Across the 20 primary sites, raw RMSE was 1.311 ppm. Leave‐one‐compound‐out aggregate RMSE was 1.065 ppm for offset correction, 1.113 ppm for affine scaling, and 1.052 ppm for quadratic calibration; macro‐averaged RMSE was 0.915, 0.986, and 0.916 ppm, respectively. Offset correction was lower than affine scaling in all three internal folds. In the locked lamivudine challenge (eight 13 C sites), however, raw RMSE was 4.174 ppm, and all three transferred calibrations worsened error: 4.643 ppm offset, 4.623 ppm affine, and 4.592 ppm quadratic. Thus the external API does not support generalization of the internally favorable calibration behavior. Because the external calculation used a published Gaussian09 GIAO workflow rather than the historical finite‐cluster protocol, it is an out‐of‐domain robustness challenge rather than like‐for‐like validation. Fbias is interpreted only retrospectively. The results support a bounded conclusion: Calibration rankings in this small benchmark are fragile to API and protocol domain shift and require prospective validation under a harmonized computational workflow.
evidence_items.title:
Compound‐Blocked Calibration Transfer in a Three‐API Finite‐Cluster GIAO‐DFT
                    <sup>13</sup>
                    C NMR Benchmark

organizations: Durham, North Carolina, Duke University, Durham, USA
Duke University, Durham, USA
evidence_items.summary: Wireless researchers prototype algorithms on software-defined radios (SDRs), but streaming raw I/Q samples from a host caps throughput: a 10 Gbps link carries at most 312.5 MSamp/s of 32-bit complex samples. Moving digital signal processing (DSP) into the FPGA fabric removes this bottleneck, yet writing wireless DSP in hardware description language (HDL) is slow, and unguided large language models (LLMs) produce non-deployable or hallucinated circuits. We present a harness engineering workflow that surrounds the model with hardware architecture guidance for common DSP blocks, an AXI4-Stream template project, deterministic numerical and protocol checkpoints, and anti-cheat checks. Benchmarking Codex GPT-5.5, Codex GPT-5.4, and Claude Sonnet-4.6 on OFDM SISO and 2×2 MIMO transceivers, the harness yields valid end-to-end RTL designs in all GPT runs, exposes false passes that the baseline accepts, and maps storage to BRAM instead of registers, at the cost of additional tokens.
evidence_items.title: WiP: Agentic Wireless DSP Generation and Deployment for RFSoC Platforms

organizations: North Carolina Agricultural and Technical State University, Greensboro, USA
evidence_items.summary: Incident response in Internet of Things (IoT) environments is difficult because devices are resource-constrained, visibility is limited, and remediation requires both contextual reasoning and explainable decisions. We present a fully local, autonomous incident-response framework for edge gateways. It combines a compact classifier that routes traffic by confidence, a tool-using language-model agent restricted to vetted mitigation actions, and an Explanation Engine grounded in the agent's recorded observations. Implemented with a 4-bit 3B model, the framework uses approximately 2.1,GB of memory and operates without cloud access. Evaluation on CIC IoT-DIAD 2024 shows that the detector achieves a weighted F1 score of 0.74 while limiting LLM-based triage to 30% of flows. The response agent selects appropriate mitigations in 92.4% of evaluated incidents, and its explanations achieve 0.99 faithfulness to the decision trace. These results demonstrate that autonomous, auditable IoT incident response is feasible within an edge-class resource budget.
evidence_items.title: Agentic AI at the Edge: Self-Explaining Autonomous Framework for IoT Incident Response
Benchmarking Ask Eolas-a medical AI tool for antimicrobial advice available in UK hospitals
Large Language Models and Applied Surgical Anatomy: Evaluation of Anatomical Reasoning in Expert-Derived Plastic Surgery Scenarios.

evidence_items.summary: Mobile electrocardiogram (ECG) capture routes photographed or scanned 12-lead images to an AI model or a clinician, yet missing leads, calibration loss, or photographic degradation can remove diagnosis-critical evidence while the tracing remains visually readable. A condition-aware evidence-sufficiency check is therefore needed to flag unusable captures for recapture or clinician review before diagnosis. Existing ECG multimodal large language model (MLLM) evaluations cannot support this, as they assume every question is answerable. We introduce ECGTrustBench, which evaluates evidence-sufficiency recognition as answerable-versus-insufficient QA over 3,300 image-question pairs, with corruption criteria unanimously approved by three licensed clinicians. Across ECG-specific, medical-domain, general-domain, and proprietary MLLMs, we find a consistent gap between answering and abstaining: ECG-specific models reach up to 77.3% clean accuracy yet abstain on at most 10% of evidence-deficient cases, while proprietary models achieve recognition up to 82%. Overall, current models respond more to visible degradation than to missing diagnostic evidence, highlighting a critical gap for evidence-sufficiency gating.
evidence_items.title: When Not to Diagnose: Evaluating Evidence-Sufficiency Recognition in ECG Multimodal Language Models with ECGTrustBench
Can Language Models Diagnose Sepsis? A Head-to-Head Evaluation Against 353 Physicians

evidence_items.summary: Deploying large language models (LLMs) on edge devices has garnered significant attention due to their inherent privacy and security benefits. However, the enormous parameter scale of modern LLMs poses fundamental challenges for resource-constrained edge devices. Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models emerge as a promising solution by dynamically activating only a subset of experts during inference, and thus enhance computational efficiency. Nevertheless, the runtime uncertainty in expert activation still leads to high memory demands during inference. To address this, prior works concentrate on either compressing or offloading experts, all striving around the tradeoffs among the model precision, memory consumption, and serving throughput, and thus form an “impossible triangle”. To reconciliate the impossible triangle, we propose CFMoE, a Cache-Friendly MoE serving system that holistically integrates optimizations spanning the model architecture, fine-tuning strategy, and inference engine. The key insight behind CFMoE is that the edge-deployed MoE serving system needs to strengthen and leverage the locality of expert routing in order to break through the theoretical caching ceiling caused by the inherent load-balancing constraints in MoE models. Specifically, CFMoE integrates three novel techniques: 1) locality-aware expert routing mechanism, 2) data-aware elastic fine-tuning strategy, and 3) prefill-decoding disaggregated caching management. Evaluation results from state-of-the-art MoE models demonstrate that CFMoE significantly reduces memory usage by 32.9% on average without decreasing serving throughput or degrading model precision.
evidence_items.title: CFMoE: Cache-Friendly Mixture of Experts Model Serving System on Edge Devices

evidence_items.summary: Digital Eye Strain (DES) is a prevalent health issue caused by extended screen usage, improper viewing distances and poor ambient lighting. Current preventative measures rely on static timers and lack the environmental context necessary for personalized intervention. We introduce GUARD-EYE, a context-aware wearable smart-headset system designed to actively monitor and mitigate DES risk factors using the sensor capabilities of modern smart glasses. The system uses a depth sensor, visible light cameras, and edge-based YOLO object detection to dynamically determine viewing distance, ambient lighting, and digital screen usage. We propose a heuristic eye strain risk model that leverages these sensor streams to calculate a real-time fatigue score and trigger audiovisual feedback during extended unsafe conditions. In addition, the system integrates Large Language Model (LLM)-generated contextual insights to deliver more personalized, dynamic behavioral feedback based on viewing data. To compare intervention strategies across diverse scenarios, we introduce a novel LLM-based user simulation framework1. Across three modeled compliance personas, the exploratory simulation produced a lower fatigue burden index for contextual alerts (5.12/10) than for the no-alert baseline (6.74/10), suggesting that context-aware intervention policies warrant further evaluation with human participants.
evidence_items.title: GUARD-EYE: Guiding User Awareness with Real-time Detection for EYe health and Engagement

evidence_items.summary: We present an end-to-end, six-stage modular neural pipeline consisting of speech-to-text transcription, Large Language Model (LLM)-based prompt normalization, diffusion-based motion generation, coordinate conversion, 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) avatar generation, and 3DGS rendering. We then empirically expose where and why such a system falls short of real-time operation, paving the way toward interactive, language-driven 3D avatars. Our objective and subjective evaluations demonstrate that our pipeline achieves: (i) correct coordinate alignment across all considered raw text inputs, (ii) a mean semantic similarity between raw and normalized prompts of 0.698, (iii) a text-to-motion alignment Mean Opinion Score (MOS) of 3.78/5.00 from N = 24 subjects, (iv) an end-to-end latency dominated by the 3DGS generator (> 80%), and (v) a 4× bandwidth reduction by reducing the frame rate from 20 to 5 FPS. Our publicly available implementation establishes a practical baseline and highlights key latency and bandwidth optimization vectors to guide future research on interactive, language-driven 3D human avatars.
evidence_items.title: Modular Neural Pipelines for Text-to-3DGS Avatar Generation: System Implementation and Preliminary Optimization

evidence_items.summary: We introduce Activity-Centric Timeline (ACT) Description, a task that generates natural-language summaries of daily routines from Internet of Things (IoT) sensing data. Traditional human activity recognition (HAR) pipelines typically output sequences of activity labels that are inefficient for non-experts to interpret. We present FACT (Foundation Models for Activity-Centric Timeline Description), a hierarchical framework that combines cross-modal signal distribution alignment, foundation-model-based construction of structured activity representations, and instruction-guided description generation. FACT leverages publicly available audio recordings to reduce the need for labeled vibration data and learns semantically meaningful activity representations that enable large language models to generate coherent, temporally grounded, and sensor-faithful descriptions of daily routines. Evaluated on two real-world residential deployments, we show that FACT generates semantically faithful activity descriptions despite imperfect activity predictions. Generated summaries achieve Semantic Textual Similarity (STS) scores above 0.861 while attaining ROUGE-1 F1 scores of 0.710 and 0.627 across the two deployments. These results demonstrate that foundation models and LLM reasoning can translate privacy-preserving sensor data into coherent, interpretable routine summaries for remote care.
evidence_items.title: Only Speaking FACTs: Foundation Models for Activity-Centric Timeline Description
DELAD - an initiative for facilitating sharing of corpora of speech disorders: Progress and survey-based insights.

evidence_items.summary: On-device fine-tuning of Large Language Models (LLMs) is becoming increasingly important for personalized AI assistants and adaptive agents. However, standard backpropagation imposes substantial training-state memory overheads that often exceed the stringent resource budgets of mobile platforms. To address this, Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization leverages forward-only probing instead of backpropagation, drastically reducing memory footprints and offering a compelling alternative for on-device adaptation. Nonetheless, scaling ZO fine-tuning to billion-scale trainable parameter spaces remains challenging, as the cost of recovering reliable update directions scales poorly with dimensionality under mobile constraints. In this paper, we present Prism, a mobile-native infrastructure for practical billion-scale on-device ZO fine-tuning. Prism re-architects the ZO loop around a scalable probing substrate, bringing both per-step training latency and memory overhead closer to the inference footprint. We implement Prism end to end on commodity smartphones and evaluate it across diverse tasks and multiple model scales. Prism achieves accuracy comparable to that of state-of-the-art ZO fine-tuning baselines while reducing per-step latency by 53.4%-76.3% and peak memory by 10.6%-13.8% relative to the best baseline in each setting. These results demonstrate the practical feasibility of billion-scale on-device ZO fine-tuning for LLMs under real mobile constraints. We will release our code to support future research.
evidence_items.title: Prism: Efficient Zeroth-Order Fine-Tuning for On-Device LLMs

evidence_items.summary: 5G operational logs are highly structured procedural traces, yet most text-generation approaches treat them as isolated messages rather than multi-step protocol flows. We study multi-step summarization of verified 5G procedure logs, where the goal is to generate coherent natural-language summaries over short same-procedure windows. We propose a protocol-aware hybrid encoder-decoder that fuses per-step text, categorical protocol metadata, and parsed telecom entities, contextualizes step sequences with a local Transformer, and decodes summaries with T5. We evaluate the model across increasing context sizes and compare against non-pretrained variants and a step-level CLIPCap baseline. Beyond ROUGE, we report structured telecom fidelity metrics for entities, procedures, statuses, and procedure-status tuples. Results show that protocol-aware pretraining yields larger gains as contextual scope grows, and that structured evaluation captures factual improvements not visible from lexical overlap alone.
evidence_items.title: Protocol-Aware Multi-Step Summarization of 5G Logs
Morality: a battle royale—the performance of evaluative procedures in symmetric interactions

evidence_items.summary: Operational RAN observability is reported every 5 to 15 minutes, averaging over as many as 1.8 million slots. Resolution is only half the problem: the quantities that explain a physical-layer fault, such as the beamforming weights the DU computed and the elements each layer actually drove, are not counted at all. Neither limit will cope with 6G integrated sensing, non-terrestrial networks, and ever-larger MIMO arrays. The 7.2x fronthaul split puts a standardized, tappable boundary in the middle of every modern base station; we argue it is the right place to obtain real-time observability, and that the analysis must run at the far edge, because the evidence is transient: it crosses the wire once, cannot be averaged down without losing the fault, and is not recoverable afterwards at any resolution. From passive captures, with no vendor-supplied instrumentation and no cooperation from either the DU or the radio supplier, we recover DU-side scheduling behavior and radio-side execution, including the per-beam and per-layer beamforming weights carried on the C-plane, separating measured quantities from those conditioned on an array hypothesis. On that extraction we ground an eleven-agent platform in which a language model only interprets measurements. Across three independent capture labs covering 4T4R, 32T32R, and 64T64R radios, a fourth lab read over the M-plane, and a dataset of 87 distinct captures, one unmodified code path recovered per-layer weights and revealed three faults nobody was looking for, two of them on the DU side, including a pair of effectively un-beamformed layers for which no alarm currently exists. A separate root-cause diagnosis was confirmed by the repair that followed.
evidence_items.title: Real-Time RAN Observability at the Far Edge: AI on the Fronthaul
Usability and Physician Acceptance of AI in Chest Radiography: An Evaluation of the MeDeep Platform Using SUS and ATRAI-14
Patient-level consequences of local updates to retinal AI for diabetic retinopathy screening: a retrospective two-cohort evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) support is becoming a critical design requirement for next-generation radio access networks (RAN), with AI-RAN emerging as a leading architecture to integrate AI workloads alongside RAN functionalities. While accelerator-based platforms are widely pursued for high-demand AI-RAN applications, CPU-based Distributed Unit (DU) nodes remain a practical and cost-effective deployment point. This raises a central question: Can AI workloads share a CPU-based DU host while preserving real-time RAN operation? To answer this, we develop SlotScope, a slot-aligned, multi-layer monitoring framework that jointly captures perslot RAN events, processing time, CPU-pipeline counters, and platform state. We validate SlotScope on an over-the-air 5G NR testbed running an OpenAirInterface (OAI) DU with a commercial radio unit (RU), serving as a proof-of-concept CPU-resident AI-RAN node. Evaluating across AI-for-RAN, AI-on-RAN, and AI-and-RAN workloads, SlotScope reveals that CPU-resident feasibility is workload-dependent, with each failure traceable to a distinct limiting mechanism that no single monitoring layer alone could expose.
evidence_items.title: SlotScope: Slot-Aligned Multi-Layer Observability for CPU-Resident AI-RAN Workload Assessment

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) is transitioning from a predictive flow-simulation technique into a central enabling technology for the design, intensification, scale-up, and digitalization of catalytic reactors. This review critically synthesizes advances reported across fixed-bed, packed-bed, fluidized-bed, trickle-bed, slurry bubble-column, monolithic, membrane, and microreactor systems, spanning chemical, petrochemical, environmental, and energy applications. Rather than treating reactor configurations and numerical methods independently, the review establishes a multiscale framework linking hydrodynamics, heterogeneous reaction kinetics, porous-media transport, heat and mass transfer, radiation, catalyst-scale phenomena, and reactor-scale performance. Particular emphasis is placed on the evolving integration of Large Eddy Simulation, Direct Numerical Simulation, Population Balance Models, artificial intelligence, Physics-Informed Neural Networks, digital twins, and high-performance computing. Their capabilities are critically compared in resolving conversion, selectivity, pressure drop, thermal gradients, species transport, catalyst utilization, and multiphase interactions, with explicit consideration of the trade-offs among predictive fidelity, computational cost, scalability, and industrial relevance. The influence of turbulence closure, mesh resolution, reaction-mechanism complexity, reactor geometry, boundary conditions, parameter uncertainty, and experimental validation on model credibility is systematically assessed. Key unresolved barriers include multiscale coupling, catalyst deactivation, numerical stiffness, uncertainty propagation, computational expense, and reliable scale-up from laboratory reactors to industrial systems. Emerging opportunities in AI-assisted CFD, GPU-accelerated simulation, uncertainty-aware modelling, autonomous optimization, and continuously updated digital twins are critically evaluated. The review ultimately proposes a pathway toward physics-informed, data-augmented, and decision-oriented CFD frameworks capable of accelerating the development of safer, more efficient, flexible, and sustainable catalytic reactor systems.
evidence_items.title: Advanced computational fluid dynamics for catalytic reactor design, multiphysics modelling, optimization, and digital transformation

evidence_items.summary: This paper examines how artificial intelligence (AI) can strengthen applied learning in the social sciences by transforming raw information into analyzable material that students actively interpret, evaluate, and convert into disciplinary knowledge. It argues that AI, when guided by theoretical rigor and ethical awareness, enhances critical pedagogy by supporting qualitative interpretation, computational analysis, simulation based inquiry, and independent reasoning. Rather than replacing instruction, AI functions as an analytical scaffold that students interrogate, correct, and contextualize, enabling deeper engagement with social structures, patterned behavior, and institutional dynamics.
evidence_items.title: Beyond the Algorithm: Integrating AI into Applied Learning Pedagogy—A Critical Inquiry

evidence_items.summary: An acceptable standard of care in medical practice, including histopathology, is both a professional and legal requirement, yet its definition is increasingly challenged by rapid technological advances, including molecular testing, digital pathology and artificial intelligence, alongside evolving diagnostic thresholds. Although the interpretative nature of histopathology and its inherent diagnostic variability are well recognised, the implications of this variability for medicolegal assessment remain insufficiently conceptualised. Using breast pathology as a model, this review examines the medicolegal challenges of retrospective diagnostic assessment, in which subspecialist experts may be influenced by hindsight and knowledge of clinical outcomes, creating unrealistic expectations for the original reporting pathologist. We synthesise existing pathological, professional, and legal principles into a structured conceptual approach for evaluating the reasonableness of histopathological diagnoses. This approach integrates adherence to professional guidance with the "reasonable pathologist" peer standard and is informed by three key principles: reasonable competence within the relevant professional role, the diagnostic context at the time of reporting, and recognised diagnostic variability. Within this framework, we describe a conceptual contextual diagnostic standard that shifts the focus from identifying a single retrospectively optimal diagnosis to recognising a range of diagnostically reasonable interpretations supported by a responsible body of similarly competent practitioners working under comparable conditions. By aligning medicolegal assessment with the realities of contemporary pathology practice, this conceptual pathology-based framework may support more consistent expert opinion, facilitate defensible clinical decision-making, and provide a structured basis for evaluating histopathological performance.
evidence_items.title: Contextual diagnostic framework for evaluating histopathology grey zones: a proposal with medicolegal implications using breast pathology as a model.

evidence_items.summary:
This study examines how anthropomorphic cues that make AI agency socially salient influence employee work engagement in mandatory, performance-oriented human–AI collaboration. It distinguishes AI agency from AI anthropomorphism, tests affective and evaluative motivational mechanisms and identifies perceived AI threat as a boundary condition grounded in the Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) model.
 
 
 
 Across two pilot studies and two main experiments (total N = 501), we used immersive workplace role-playing scenarios to test a dual-pathway model. Integrating social response theory with the JD-R model, this research tests a dual-pathway model in which anthropomorphic design influences work engagement through emotional bonding and acquisitive impression management motive (IMM), whereas perceived artificial intelligence threat operates as a hindrance demand that weakens these resource pathways.
 
 
 
 Anthropomorphic AI enhanced work engagement through two motivational routes: an affective route via emotional bonding and an evaluative route via IMM. However, perceived AI threat significantly attenuated these benefits. When threat was high, the positive effects of anthropomorphism on emotional bonding, IMM and work engagement became non-significant, suggesting that replacement-related threat drains the psychological capacity needed for anthropomorphic cues to function as job resources.
 
 
 
 This research contributes to workplace AI and information systems (IS) scholarship by clarifying how anthropomorphic cues make AI agency socially salient without equating anthropomorphism with agency. It extends prior work on anthropomorphic AI and engagement by identifying an evaluative pathway – performing for AI – alongside the affective pathway of bonding with AI. It also offers a contingency-based explanation for the anthropomorphism paradox by showing that the benefits of humanlike design depend on the surrounding AI-threat climate.
evidence_items.title: Beyond Human–AI interaction: exploring the influence of AI anthropomorphism on work engagement

evidence_items.summary: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools such as ChatGPT are increasingly used by students in higher education, offering opportunities to support learning, creativity, and efficiency. At the same time, their rapid adoption raises significant concerns related to academic integrity, ethical engagement, data privacy, and uncritical reliance on AI-generated outputs. While institutional policies and educator-focused frameworks are emerging, practical, student-facing guidance remains limited. This article presents development of Using GenAI Tools – Practical Guide for Students, a 16-point practical guide designed to support students in the responsible and reflective use of text-based generative AI tools in academic contexts. The guide was developed through a design-informed, practical-based and iterative process involving literature, policy and practice inputs, classroom use, student feedback, conference-based feedback, academic review, and successive refinement across multiple teaching trimesters. The Technology Acceptance Model and Constructivist Learning Theory informed the guide’s design logic, shaping elements that support perceived usefulness, ease of use, ethical decision-making, critical evaluation, and active engagement with learning. Rather than evaluating learning outcomes or performance gains, the article focuses on the development and rationale of a student-centred guidance artefact that complements institutional academic integrity policies. The resulting guide offers accessible and actionable support for students navigating ethical boundaries of GenAI use, while positioning AI as a supportive tool rather than a substitute for independent thinking or academic responsibility. Finally, it contributes a practice-oriented resource to ongoing discussions on academic integrity, student agency, and responsible GenAI use in AI-enabled higher education.
evidence_items.title: Developing a practical student guide for responsible and reflective use of GenAI in higher education

evidence_items.summary: The next failure mode for mobile GUI agents is not a bad answer in a chat window; it is a bad tap on a phone. In high-stakes app workflows, one tap can submit a form, upload identity, disclose private data, accept terms, change account state, or authorize payment. This paper presents GuardedMobile, a lightweight runtime verifier that mediates proposed mobile GUI actions before app execution. We introduce MobileRiskBench-WiP, a trace-based benchmark of 52 workflows, including 12 ambiguous stress cases with misleading button labels and weak confirmation screens. Across three LLM-like agents and action-noise levels of 0.00, 0.10, and 0.20, Full GuardedMobile-Stress reduces unsafe workflow rate by about 95% and risk-weighted failure by about 95%, while retaining 86.5% task completion. The result is preliminary: stress tests show a safety-completion tradeoff, including clarification requests, delay, false positives, and residual unsafe actions.
evidence_items.title: WiP: GuardedMobile: Runtime Verification for LLM-Based Mobile GUI Agents in High-Stakes App Workflows

evidence_items.summary:
This article examines how employment-based initial teacher education programs can serve as a sustainable model for school–university partnerships by analysing agency redistribution as the mechanism through which more equitable and sustainable partnership conditions are produced. Drawing on the Master of Teaching Secondary Internship (MTSI) program at the University of Melbourne, Australia, it argues that locating selection authority with schools and professional choice with intern candidates restructures the foundational dynamics of school–university collaboration.
 
 
 
 The article employs a conceptual and descriptive case study drawing on program-level enrolment, completion and retention data; de-identified analytics from its UniConnected partnership platform (ethics approval HREC 27923); documentary materials and reflective accounts from program leaders writing as insider practitioners.
 
 
 
 Devolving intern selection to school principals repositions schools as active agents and candidates as visible emerging professionals. This redistribution functions as an equity mechanism, reducing mismatches that allocation-based models generate in under-resourced schools. Equity-centred design in turn supports sustainability: the MTSI program has achieved a 94% completion rate against a national postgraduate Initial Teacher Education (ITE) benchmark of 74%.
 
 
 
 The article offers a replicable framework built on three principles: formal vesting of selection authority in schools, enabling infrastructure designed for mutual discovery rather than administrative allocation and university oversight repositioned as quality assurance rather than gatekeeping.
 
 
 
 The article proposes that the transition from placement to partnership restructures agency dynamics and demonstrates empirically that equity and sustainability are mutually reinforcing rather than competing design priorities.
evidence_items.title: From placement to partnership: agency, equity and sustainable school–university relationships in employment-based initial teacher education

evidence_items.summary: AI-assisted auscultation based on phonocardiogram (PCG) recordings is moving from the resting clinic to mobile, connected settings where users are often recorded after activity, yet murmur classifiers are trained primarily on resting data and routinely mistake exercise-induced physiological murmurs (EM) for pathological murmurs (PM), driving false alarms. We study this exertion-induced shift through a unified three-class (no-murmur/EM/PM) formulation that joins CirCor PCG recordings with a clinician-annotated post-exercise cohort under a strict subject-level five-fold split. Benchmarking a broad set of pretrained audio encoders, PCG-specific models, and from-scratch temporal networks, we find that pretrained representations are strongest overall, while the proposed M2D-based ExerMurmur modules achieve the best accuracy (0.9275), improving PM recall while retaining high EM recall. We then explore an exertion-conditioned adapter with a prototype objective, reporting a reproducible majority-class collapse under naive training, with EM recall falling to zero, that a staged, identity-preserving recipe repairs.
evidence_items.title: WIP:ExerMurmur: Exertion-Aware Phonocardiogram Classification for Mobile Auscultation
Comprehensive evaluation of multi-method bias correction for cmip6 climate models and future scenario simulation of extreme climate events: a case study of Jiangsu Province, China
Evaluation of electromagnetic field effects on the viability and structure of Candida albicans and Streptococcus mutans biofilms

evidence_items.summary: Energy infrastructure systems, e.g. EV charging networks, smart buildings, must make real-time decisions to satisfy time-varying, context-dependent human demand. Yet existing methods fall short: edge controllers cannot interpret human-demand contexts, whereas LLM agents that excel at fusing such human information are unreliable and latencyprone for direct physical control. We propose Human-Aware Agentic Operation (HAAO), a hybrid framework that involves these two reasoning modes: at the upper level, in-context prompting leverages a black-box LLM agent to fuse community context and predict human demand in a structured, machine-readable form; at the lower level, a lightweight model maps this human context and system states to physical control actions. The performance of HAAO is evaluated on the EV charging power management problem.
evidence_items.title: Harnessing Agent Capabilities to Integrate Human Demands into Energy Infrastructure Operations

evidence_items.summary: Recent advances in LLMs have enabled mobile agents that can automate user tasks through natural language interaction with app interfaces. However, current agents execute tasks as sequences of basic UI actions (taps, swipes), incurring extra latency, token cost, and accumulating error risks. Motivated by this, we propose AMAS, an Android Macro Action System that constructs reusable, system-grounded macro actions by identifying system-level application entry transitions that directly jump to task-relevant, app-specific screens. Results show that AMAS reduces agent's average LLM calls by 23.22%, LLM latency by 26.38%, and token cost by 21.9%, while having a 6.0% gain on success rate. Further coverage analysis shows that AMAS constructs 184 stable and distinct macro actions across the 20 benchmark apps, averaging 9.2 per app. At the task level, AMAS provides every task with at least one macro action, and 54.3% of tasks coverage. These results demonstrate that system-level macro actions can provide broad coverage while improving both the efficiency and reliability of LLM-based mobile agents.
evidence_items.title: WIP: AMAS: An Android Macro Action System for Efficient LLM Mobile Agents

evidence_items.summary: Antimicrobial resistance is a global public health concern, and appropriate antimicrobial use in food-producing animal medicine requires accurate bacteriological diagnosis. However, the effectiveness of bacteriological training and the reliability of in-house antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) in food-animal practice remain unclear. We assessed preliminary organism identification accuracy and the impact of a bacteriological training program among bovine veterinarians affiliated with NOSAI Hokkaido, Japan, and evaluated disk diffusion AST variability using the same Escherichia coli isolate. Preliminary identification accuracy increased from 37% (35/94) before training to 91% (86/94) immediately afterward. Pre-training accuracy was significantly higher among frequent testers than among participants who performed no routine bacteriological testing, whereas post-training accuracy was high across all three testing-frequency groups. In the AST assessment, inhibition zone diameters varied substantially across all six antimicrobial disks, and discordant susceptible/resistant (S/R) interpretations occurred in more than 50% of participants for two agents. Multivariable generalized estimating equation analyses showed that smear technique was significantly associated with discordant S/R interpretations, whereas agar medium was not significantly associated with discordance after adjustment. The association between inoculum quantity and discordance could not be reliably established because only two participants were classified in the appropriate-inoculum category. These findings demonstrate the immediate benefit of structured practical training for improving preliminary organism identification and highlight the need to standardize field-based AST, particularly smear technique. Wider adoption of the simplified disk diffusion procedures described in the national mastitis guidebook may improve AST consistency in clinical practice.
evidence_items.title: Educational impact of a bacteriological training program and field assessment of antimicrobial susceptibility testing among bovine veterinarians in Japan.

evidence_items.summary: Modern scheduling tools manage fixed events but do not automatically adapt as a user's life changes—for example, when a user starts a scheduled activity later than planned, disrupting the rest of the day. Horae bridges this gap with a behavior-aware scheduler that adapts to evolving routines. Horae processes mobile sensor data directly on the user's device, learns what is normal for that person, and recommends simple schedule changes that better reflect changes in their life. In blinded evaluations, an AI reviewer preferred Horae's suggestions in 71.8% of cases. Human raters also preferred Horae, selecting its suggestions 57.3% of the time, compared with 36.5% for suggestions based only on existing calendar events and 6.3% for leaving the schedule unchanged. We demonstrate Horae's end-to-end workflow live; a recorded video is available at: Demo Link.
evidence_items.title: Demo: Can AI Agents Adapt to Your Daily Life? Horae, a Behavior-Aware Scheduler Grounded in Mobile Sensing

evidence_items.summary: In the near future, communication networks will move into space, particularly low Earth orbit (LEO). Given the closed nature and high cost of commercial satellite deployments, it's vital that researchers have access to open platforms that allow them to develop and evaluate innovations in LEO Satellite Networks (LSNs). In this demonstration we present an ecosystem of tools developed to make both tasks easier. It includes SatGym, a flexible, framework compliant environment for training RL agents; SERENADE, a large-scale, realistic satellite network emulator; and SatGym-Server, an HPC bridge application that enables LSN controllers (including RL agents) to interact with SERENADE in a fully distributed way. Together these tools allow researchers to develop and evaluate large-scale, decentralized LSN orchestration controllers in real time with realistic traffic generation and orbital dynamics.

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) can serve as helpful assistants, yet they can equally function as harm amplifiers that enable malicious users to achieve harmful outcomes beyond their capabilities through extended interactions. This risk manifests along two axes, i.e., democratizing domain expertise that allows novices to produce specialized harmful content, and scaling harmful operations at volumes that manual effort cannot match. Existing works, however, often overlook how LLMs compound harm across multi-turn conversations. We introduce HarmAmp, a new benchmark for multi-turn harm amplification scenarios spanning twelve risk categories. Each scenario is grounded in real-world threats and satisfies rigorous criteria, i.e., substantive amplification, operational specificity, and multi-turn necessity. We further propose TrajSafe, a proactive monitor that anticipates harmful trajectories and intervenes through actions such as probing users' genuine intents and steering the models towards safer completion. Our extensive experiments demonstrate that TrajSafe significantly reduces the harmfulness incurred in multi-turn interactions while preserving a low over-refusal rate and the target model's general capabilities. Our work offers a promising paradigm to alleviate the nuanced safety risks in LLM interactions.
evidence_items.title: Investigating and Alleviating Harm Amplification in LLM Interactions

evidence_items.summary: A controversial test for Large Language Models concerns the ability to discern possible from impossible language. While some evidence attests to the models sensitivity to what crosses the limits of grammatically impossible language, this evidence has been contested on the grounds of the soundness of the testing material. We use model-internal representations as a direct means of investigating the way Large Language Models represent the grammatical-ungrammatical distinction. In a novel benchmark, we elicit sum log probabilities from 8 models and compute minimal-pair surprisal differences, juxtaposing probabilities assigned to grammatical sentences to probabilities assigned to (i) lower frequency grammatical sentences, (ii) ungrammatical sentences, (iii) semantically odd sentences, and (iv) pragmatically odd sentences. The prediction is that if string-probabilities can function as proxies for the limits of grammar, the ungrammatical condition will stand out among the conditions that involve linguistic violations, showing a spike in the surprisal rates. Our results do not reveal a unique surprisal signature for ungrammatical prompts: across models, we observe comparable surprisal for the pragmatically odd condition, and the semantically odd condition consistently shows even higher surprisal. We thus demonstrate that probabilities do not constitute reliable proxies for grammaticality, showing that probability differences alone cannot be used to infer model-internal representations of syntactic knowledge. Consequently, claims about models being able to distinguish possible from impossible language need verification through a different methodology.
evidence_items.title: Large Language Model probabilities cannot reliably distinguish between possible and impossible language

evidence_items.summary: This article presents two corpora of English and Czech texts generated by large language models (LLMs). The motivation is to create a resource for comparing human-written texts with LLM-generated text linguistically. Emphasis was placed on ensuring these resources are multi-genre and diverse in terms of topics, authors, and text types, while maintaining comparability with existing human-created corpora. These generated corpora replicate reference human corpora: BE21 by Paul Baker, which is a modern version of the original Brown Corpus, and the Koditex corpus that also follows the Brown Corpus tradition but in Czech. The new corpora were generated using models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Alphabet, Meta, and DeepSeek, ranging from GPT-3 (davinci-002) to GPT−4.5, and are tagged according to the Universal Dependencies standard (i.e., they are tokenized, lemmatized, and morphologically and syntactically annotated). The subcorpus size varies by model used (the English part contains, on average, 864k tokens per model and 27 M tokens altogether; the Czech part contains on average 768k tokens per model, 21.5M tokens altogether). The corpora are freely available for download under the CC BY 4.0 license (the annotated data are under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license) and are also accessible through the search interface of the Czech National Corpus.
evidence_items.title: AI Brown and AI Koditex: LLM-generated corpora comparable to human-written corpora of English and Czech texts

evidence_items.summary: Codes of professional ethics guide and restrict specialists, who increasingly work with assistants built on large language models. Such an assistant can breach the user's code, or help the user breach it, without the user noticing. Evaluations reporting broad categories of harm cannot show how often this happens or which provision is breached. TenetBench pairs 3,433 requests conflicting with clauses of fifteen Russian-language professional codes with benign twins that differ only in the legitimacy of what is asked. An automated pipeline generates the tasks from the text of a code, so the corpus grows with every code added and a provision yields new tasks on every run. It also produced tasks and human-validated verdicts from two English codes of other jurisdictions. In human validation of the frozen pipeline, specialists rated 0.995 of the conflicting tasks plausible, and the model judge agreed with the adjudicated label at Gwet's AC1 of at least 0.894 on 1,860 elements. We evaluated fourteen model and reasoning-mode combinations on whether they produce the conflicting text, decline or warn. Eleven of the fourteen produce conflicting content on most such requests, mostly without a warning, and nearly three warnings in four accompany conflicting content. The models that conform more do so by declining while still serving the legitimate twin, and enabling reasoning halved the refusals of two models. We hope the dataset and pipeline will help evaluate how language models observe professional norms and let diagnostic datasets be built for particular professions and organisations.
evidence_items.title: TenetBench: A Clause-Anchored Russian Corpus for Evaluating Language Models against Professional Codes of Ethics
