evidence_items.summary: While Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) excel at zero-shot reasoning, their spatial capabilities are primarily evaluated through static, passive observation. In complex, human-centric scenes, occlusion often hides crucial geometric evidence, and passive benchmarks force models to guess rather than recognize their own visual uncertainty. To bridge this gap, we introduce SATE-Bench, a novel interactive benchmark comprising 316 real-world scenes and 2,525 multi-turn QA pairs to evaluate visual self-awareness and active exocentric view-exploration. It combines a Passive multi-view control with an Active exploration setting, where models start from a severely occluded view and must iteratively query adjacent viewpoints until they gather enough evidence to fully ``sate'' the question, scored by a step-penalized efficiency reward. Evaluating state-of-the-art MLLMs reveals that they terminate exploration prematurely while reporting high confidence, and struggle with fine-grained 3D geometric tasks; matched-view controls further attribute the Active--Passive gap primarily to insufficient evidence acquisition. Moreover, fine-tuning with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) shows that rewarding view-seeking increases active exploration but lowers overall accuracy, as models over-explore and fail to fuse expanding multi-view contexts across turns. These findings indicate that scaling passive multi-view perception does not intrinsically yield active spatial reasoning, highlighting the need for models that know where to look, how to integrate what they see, and when to stop. Code and data are available at https://gtc-gh.github.io/SATE-Bench/
evidence_items.title: Humans in Space: Can MLLMs Construct Human-Centric Spatial Understanding via Active Exocentric Exploration?

evidence_items.summary: Hallucination detection is increasingly important for evaluating and deploying large language models. However, existing methods are often compared across benchmarks that define and measure hallucination in substantially different ways, making reported scores difficult to interpret across settings. We study hallucination detection as a benchmark-conditioned measurement problem and organize existing benchmarks along three axes: provenance, which describes how model outputs and evidence conditions are obtained; typology, which captures the factuality and faithfulness failures represented by benchmark labels; and granularity, which specifies the unit at which hallucinations are annotated, predicted, and evaluated. Using this framework, we analyze how benchmark construction, annotation, and evaluation choices shape the underlying prediction task, and relate detector mechanisms and assumptions to the settings in which their performance is measured. We also examine span-level evaluation, where variation in annotation boundaries can substantially affect reported results, and propose Span Coverage F1 as a complementary containment-based metric. Our analysis clarifies what detector scores capture, highlights limitations of cross-benchmark comparisons, and motivates more explicit evaluation of generalization across benchmark conditions.
evidence_items.title: Mycelium: A Meta-Study of Hallucination Detection Across Provenance, Typology, and Granularities

evidence_items.summary: Learning visual design is essential for prompt enhancement (PE) to turn underspecified user requests into coherent visual specifications for text-to-image (T2I) generation. Existing methods preserve user intent and improve overall visual appeal, with less explicit emphasis on fine-grained design dimensions. To address this gap, we introduce Qwen-Image-PE, which learns visual design through two-stage training. Supervised fine-tuning with Caption-Based Reverse Distillation (CRD) uses dense captions of well-designed images as design supervision. Reinforcement learning with Groupwise Design Reward (GDR) jointly compares all candidate images for the same request to refine lighting, composition, layout, and detail. On Qwen-Image-Bench with Qwen-Image-2.1, Qwen-Image-PE-397B improves over original requests by 7.81 points, while Qwen-Image-PE-9B outperforms all evaluated PE baselines. Further evaluations show gains in visual design, aesthetics, image quality, and human preference. We find that PE scales along three axes: training data, model size, and information density, with sufficient information density as a prerequisite for effective enhancement. Moreover, we demonstrate that Qwen-Image-PE generalizes to four additional T2I backbones, even surpassing native prompt enhancers on HunyuanImage-2.1 and FLUX 3 Image Klein. We release Qwen-Image-PE-9B at https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen-Image-2.1-PE-T2I.
evidence_items.title: Qwen-Image-PE: Learning Visual Design for Text-to-Image Prompt Enhancement

evidence_items.summary: The life-cycle of robotics foundation models crucially depends on data labels. Outcome reward labels are needed for monitoring real-world deployments. Process reward labels are needed during RL post-training. Timestamped captions are needed for filtering and balancing pretraining data. We present Flora, an industrial-quality data engine used for training GR00T models, that simultaneously covers these capabilities. Flora achieves SOTA scores on the captioning benchmark WGO-Bench and reward benchmarks RoboReward and Robometer. On internal benchmarks it is competitive with GPT-6 Astra while beating other frontier models. The model is substantially cheaper than API-based alternatives, roughly 125 times cheaper than GPT-6 Astra. Florais battle tested at scale, labeling 200,000 hours of data per day across 512 GB300s. By open-sourcing our data engine, we enable researchers to scale custom robotics datasets and explore emerging applications such as physical auto-research and human-to-robot transfer.
evidence_items.title: FLORA: An Open Model Suite for Scaling Robotics Data Engines

evidence_items.summary: Open multimodal reasoning models have benefited from large-scale reasoning supervision, yet reliable post-training remains challenging due to uneven data quality, inefficient supervision construction, imbalanced difficulty, and cross-domain interference. We introduce MMVistaReason (MVR), an open-data post-training recipe with three components: (1) broader capability coverage across complementary Analytical and Real-World reasoning groups, emphasizing structured reasoning versus visual perception and spatial grounding; (2) efficient SFT and RL data construction, standardizing heterogeneous open data through staged cleaning and annotation, combining difficulty-aware cascaded teacher distillation with answer-likelihood-based trajectory selection to construct MVR-SFT-528K, and applying scale-specific frontier filtering for MVR-RL-63K; and (3) specialize-then-integrate training, which trains complementary RL experts and consolidates their capabilities through multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD). Our analyses reveal a capacity-dependent interaction between supervision difficulty, trajectory quality, and model capacity: smaller students benefit more from selected supervision, while larger students are robust to trajectory variation and mixed-domain interference. Mixed-domain RL introduces benchmark-level negative transfer, whereas MOPD provides consistent capability integration, with the preferred KL direction varying across model scales. Across 15 multimodal benchmarks, MVR-4B achieves an average score of 72.8, outperforming Qwen3.5-9B (Instruct) and MMFineReason-8B while using about 70% fewer samples than MMFineReason. Scaling to 9B improves the average to 74.4, surpassing Qwen3.5-35B-A3B (Instruct). Overall, MMVistaReason demonstrates that systematic open-data construction and capacity-aware post-training provide a practical and scalable path toward reliable multimodal reasoning.
evidence_items.title: MMVistaReason: Toward Open-Data and Post-Training Recipes for Multimodal Reasoning

evidence_items.summary: The growth of time-series datasets and foundation models has made dataset comparison a central part of time-series workflows. Assessing source-target transfer before model adaptation requires similarity estimates that can summarize transfer-related dataset relationships without exhaustive source-target evaluation over every candidate pair. Many metrics have been proposed for measuring similarity between time-series datasets, but they capture different dataset relationships and vary in how well they align with downstream utility across tasks. We evaluate this gap by measuring the correlation between source-target similarity scores and downstream forecasting errors in out-of-distribution and transfer-learning settings. We propose Domain-Integrated Similarity Cost (DISC), a learnable aggregation framework that uses calibration transfer observations to select, weight, and combine similarity metrics for different downstream tasks. By integrating complementary metric values, DISC better distinguishes source-target dataset differences that matter for downstream behavior. After calibration, DISC scores source-target pairs using only their similarity-metric values and yields higher alignment than single-metric references on the reported split. These results show that time-series dataset similarity is task-dependent, and that learned metric integration provides a stronger proxy for downstream transfer behavior than manually selecting one similarity metric.
evidence_items.title: DISC: Domain-Integrated Similarity Cost for Time-Series Dataset

evidence_items.summary: The rapid growth of microdramas has increased demand for high-quality script production. Long-form microdrama script generation with LLMs requires both diverse plot progression and long-range narrative coherence. Our observations reveal that candidate continuations increasingly concentrate on fewer narrative mechanisms as generation progresses, while conventional retrieval may reinforce trope reuse and overlook historical information essential to future plots. To address these challenges, we propose DraMaze, a multi-agent pipeline that explores diverse causal paths through trope memory-guided evolutionary tree search and mutation. It further constructs a Backward Narrative Dependency Tree to organize, retain, and retrieve historical memories based on future narrative goals. We also introduce MiDramaBench, a bilingual benchmark for evaluating script logic and creative quality across different script lengths, together with causal-pattern metrics for narrative repetition and diversity. Experiments show consistent improvements across three backbone LLMs. For 60-episode scripts of up to 60k words, DraMaze reduces causal-pattern repetition by 32.1% and achieves a Logic score of 82.5, outperforming the best-performing baseline by 8.5 points.
evidence_items.title: DraMaze: A Multi-Agent Pipeline with Future-Aware Memory for Diverse Microdrama Script Generation

evidence_items.summary: World Models (WMs) can support Multimodal Agents (MAs) through simulated experience, while Agent trajectories can inform World Model refinement. Evaluating this interaction requires separate evidence about action selection and state evolution. We introduce Dual Exam, which tests Agents under fixed environment response mechanisms and World Models under fixed action interventions across physical, digital, social, and scientific domains. The Agent track compares 10 configurations on 1,088 items in 15 reporting categories. The World Model track contains 400 cases across eight scenarios; 15 configurations have full coverage and one covers six scenarios. GPT 6 Astra leads the case-weighted Agent Index at 31.3, and GPT-Image-2 leads the full-coverage WM Overall at 21.7. These scores use different tasks and metrics and are not directly comparable. A 150-case pilot of one coupled pairing records zero task successes and motivates component-level diagnosis. Results reveal uneven task performance and failures to preserve task-relevant state. Their value for predicting coupled success or sustained reciprocal learning remains to be established.
evidence_items.title: Dual Exam: Controlled Evaluation of Multimodal Agents and World Models

evidence_items.summary: Fine-grained multimodal intelligence requires models to both understand a designated region and localize it from language. Existing methods learn these directions with separate objectives and task-specific annotations. We present Generalized CycleGRPO, the first unified reinforcement learning framework coupling region understanding and localization across spatial, temporal, and spatio-temporal domains. Given a region, a multimodal large language model generates candidate descriptions and then localizes each description to reconstruct the input region. Reconstruction overlap provides a verifiable reward for captioning, while individual localization rewards improve the inverse mapping. A common region-space formulation extends this cycle from image masks and boxes to video intervals and timestamped spatial evidence, without reference captions or an external language-model judge during reinforcement learning. In videos, the cycle encourages descriptions that distinguish a target event from similar recurrences. We introduce DOVE (Distinctive Occurrence-level Video-caption Evaluation), a human-verified contrastive benchmark for this temporal distinctiveness. CycleGRPO improves SAMTok's overall gIoU from 57.5% to 68.2% on GroundingSuite and average gIoU from 71.2% to 78.7% on GRES. For temporal tasks, it achieves 51.9% tIoU on Charades and 33.3% Temporal Evidence Coverage on DOVE, compared with 45.6% and 14.8% for the Qwen3-VL initialization. These results establish region-text cycle consistency as a general self-evaluation principle for multimodal understanding and localization. Models, code, and DOVE are available at https://devinxzhang.github.io/Generalized-CycleGRPO-Page/.
evidence_items.title: Generalized CycleGRPO for Fine-Grained Multimodal Understanding and Grounding

evidence_items.summary: Existing reasoning evaluations typically provide task-relevant information to models as available premises, rarely examining concurrently how models discover evidence autonomously and how information presentation within narratives guides or obscures judgment. This paper proposes the WORTH Benchmark: models read original mystery narratives without clue annotations, autonomously select key clue sentences, identify case participants, and explain their reasoning process. The narrative materials are designed by professional authors such that evidence facilitating reasoning coexists with narrative arrangements that delay the revelation of truth. We report a pilot experiment under full-story conditions across two episodes, conducting a total of 70 formal runs on models, of which 67 runs are content-scorable. Scoring separately records hits on author-designated key clue sentences and participant selections; natural language explanations are used for case diagnosis and are not scored independently. The results show that clue hits and participant judgments are not synchronized; across 37 content-scorable runs in Episode 02, 31 runs simultaneously selected the same set of incorrect participants, while adjacent suspicion-oriented and exoneration-oriented sentences were selected 25 times and 0 times, respectively. These phenomena illustrate the diagnostic value of component-wise analysis and suggest that not-fully-cooperative informational relationships may influence evidence selection and judgment. This study only implements full-story conditions for two episodes, and does not establish stable model rankings or infer general mechanisms on this basis; human player records have not yet been cleaned, and this version does not report human-model comparisons.
evidence_items.title: WORTH Benchmark: Evidence Discovery under Not-Fully-Cooperative Information -- A Two-Episode Pilot

evidence_items.summary: Generative reward models (GenRMs) generate natural language rationales to justify preference judgments, yet a correct verdict does not guarantee a sound justification. Existing approaches often rely on reference explanations to supervise rationales, but obtaining such references can be costly and does not necessarily establish whether generated rationales support the resulting verdict. To address these limitations, we propose DeCert, a framework that evaluates the validity and verdict consistency of generated rationales without requiring reference explanations. Crucially, DeCert translates these assessments into preference supervision that accounts for both verdict correctness and justification quality. In particular, when multiple sampled judgments share the same correct verdict, differences in certificate quality enable DeCert to construct rationale preference pairs that distinguish stronger from weaker justifications. Extensive empirical studies across two model families and multiple in- and out-of-distribution benchmarks demonstrate that DeCert consistently outperforms strong generative judge baselines while improving rationale quality. Moreover, DeCert effectively mitigates positional bias, improving position-consistent accuracy by up to 14.8 points. These results highlight the importance of supervising not only which verdict is correct, but also how that verdict is justified.
evidence_items.title: Judging the Justification: Decision Certificate Supervision for Generative Reward Models

evidence_items.summary: Language models can make personalized recommendations from rich item content, user history, and feedback. However, evaluating many candidates with full-text inputs incurs substantial online computation and limits serving throughput. We introduce DuoLM, a framework for fast and effective personalized recommendation that integrates a compact recommendation model with an efficient serving runtime. An encoder LLM learns compact item representations for offline reuse, while a personalized ranker LLM combines them with user history and feedback for recommendation. We train both models end to end with recommendation supervision and teacher distillation. The runtime further accelerates inference through virtual token IDs for embedding access, shared history computation, and CUDA Graph replay. Benchmark results show that our framework achieves recommendation quality comparable to that of the expert teacher model. On a single H100, it delivers approximately 26,400 candidate scores per second, about 60times the throughput of the teacher served with vLLM and automatic prefix caching.
evidence_items.title: DuoLM: Fast and Effective Personalized Recommendation with Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Music source separation (MSS) has been conventionally addressed by discriminative methods. Recently, flow matching has emerged as a strong generative paradigm for modeling complex data distributions, with successful applications across diverse domains. These advances motivate us to systematically investigate flow matching for MSS in a four-source (Vocals, Bass, Drums, Other) setting in full-band stereo. Specifically, we investigate prediction targets, flow paths, single-source versus multi-source modeling, and mixture consistency constraints. Beyond the signal-level metrics commonly used for MSS, such as signal-to-distortion ratio, we further evaluate MSS methods using embedding-based metrics, as well as a listening test, providing a comprehensive benchmark. On MUSDB18-HQ, our proposed model exhibits competitive performance in both objective and subjective tests, highlighting the potential of flow matching for generative MSS. Demo: https://ik4sumii.github.io/FLOMSS/
evidence_items.title: FLOMSS: Generative Music Source Separation by Flow Matching

evidence_items.summary: Native NVFP4 promises to accelerate reinforcement learning (RL) for large language models (LLMs), but achieving stable learning across separate training and sampling engines remains challenging. We show that matching model weights and numerical formats is insufficient to ensure consistent policy evaluation, highlighting the importance of cross-engine numerical execution. We introduce miniTE, a lightweight framework that combines execution diagnostics, cross-engine numerical alignment, and efficient native W4A4 (4-bit weights and activations) GEMM computation for LLM RL. It improves numerical execution consistency without modifying the RL objective, while reducing implementation overhead to realize the benefits of native low-bit computation. Long-horizon RL experiments on Qwen3-30B-A3B demonstrate stable training and benchmark performance close to BF16, outperforming naive Transformer Engine (TE) NVFP4 in evaluation quality. On single NVIDIA B300 GPU node, the optimized learner reaches 33,540 tokens/s, yielding 1.39x and 1.47x the throughput of BF16 and TE NVFP4, respectively, for complete learner updates. We released the framework, kernels, diagnostics, and training configurations to make native low-bit RL easier.
evidence_items.title: miniTE: Diagnosing and Bridging the Execution Gap in Native NVFP4 Reinforcement Learning

organizations: Xinyang University
evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) can convert long documents into structured research variables. Auditability becomes difficult when evidence selection and model scoring are not stored. We study an inspectable scoring workflow that converts archived annual-report Evidence Packs into a five-dimension digital-transformation disclosure score. The design combines report selection, PDF-to-text normalization, bounded paragraph retrieval, and DeepSeek rubric scoring through a strict JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) interface; the original canonical prompt/run binding is not available. We evaluate three measurement questions and one secondary utility check: reproducible Evidence Pack construction, LLM–human agreement on shared Evidence Packs, ordinal error/confusion diagnostics, and non-causal panel-use stress tests. The evaluation panel contains 476 firm-year observations from 64 firms for 2013–2024. The post-validation score shows high internal coherence for the additive rubric (Cronbach’s α = 0.893; first principal component explains 0.704 of standardized dimensional variance), substantial within-firm variation (mean within-firm standard deviation (SD) 2.901; 92.19% non-zero), and strong LLM–human agreement on shared Evidence Packs (total-score Spearman 0.910, Pearson 0.921, mean absolute error (MAE) 1.273; dimension-level weighted kappa 0.665–0.823). Human–Human total-score reliability, measured by the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC), is ICC(2,1) = 0.811. Baseline comparisons show lower error than frozen lexicon-count and firm-grouped term frequency–inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) Ridge alternatives (MAE = 1.273 vs . 6.387 and 2.737). A 96-record rule-based retrieval audit shows high mean dimension coverage (0.936) but incomplete heuristic paragraph recall@30 (micro recall = 0.419); four audited zero-hit packs are false empty (4.17%). The main reliability claim is therefore bounded to shared archived evidence.
evidence_items.title: Auditable large language model scoring of annual-report evidence packs: human calibration, baselines, and reproducibility checks

organizations: Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai
evidence_items.summary: Human body contains endogenous metabolites, nutrients and xenobiotics chemicals. These chemicals can be detected in a biospecimen using high-resolution mass spectrometry instruments, yielding metabolomic and exposomic datasets. Mass spectral libraries are critical components of these workflows to annotate experimental data with chemical information. In this data descriptor, we report mass spectral libraries for human-relevant small molecules, that are generated using Google Gemini large-language model. Using an optimized chain-of-thought prompt and instructions, we have generated mass spectra for each compound at high/medium/low energy fragmentation level. Each spectrum was reported in the NIST MSP text format for easy to use by metabolomics software. These libraries cover 91,231 unique 2D structures from the Blood Exposome Database and the Metabolomics Workbench data repository. Technical validation was shown by comparing the Gemini-generated spectra against NIST 23 mass spectral database, which demonstrated 55% accuracy. LLMs represent a useful and accessible tool for expanding in-silico spectral libraries to annotate compounds in the HRMS data for human biospecimens and may accelerate the compound annotation in metabolomics and exposomics.
evidence_items.title: In-silico Tandem Mass Spectral Libraries for the Blood Exposome and Metabolomics Workbench Databases: Application of Gemini Large Language Model
Artificial intelligence in the physician’s seat: a scenario-based evaluation of scientific accuracy, quality, and readability

organizations: ERZİNCAN BİNALİ YILDIRIM ÜNİVERSİTESİ
evidence_items.summary: Accurate prediction of the in-cylinder pressure trace does not necessarily preserve pressure-derived combustion descriptors. This study uses a synthetic spark-ignition benchmark to examine whether explicit supervision of these descriptors changes surrogate accuracy. Six neural-network variants share a 5382-parameter architecture and training budget, with cumulative supervision of pressure derivatives, apparent heat release, peak descriptors, combustion phasing and gross indicated work. The benchmark comprises 960 operating points divided into training, validation, interpolation and simultaneous speed–load extrapolation sets, plus a closure-shift test with altered combustion and wall-heat-transfer relations. At the specified 1° output resolution, validation-selected A4 reduces interpolation CA50 mean absolute error from 0.0938° to 0.0688° and maximum pressure-rise-rate (MPRR) error from 0.0506 to 0.0303 bar/°, corresponding to improvements of 26.6% and 40.1%. Pressure RMSE increases from 0.0980 to 0.1031 bar, and gross IMEP error increases from 0.0296 to 0.0529 bar. A4 retains a lower MPRR error during speed–load extrapolation, with higher pressure and work errors, while all models deteriorate under the closure shift. The 1° MPRR discretisation discrepancy of 0.01702 bar/° is comparable in magnitude to the 0.0203 bar/° model improvement. These results establish a redistribution of approximation error within the prescribed benchmark. The fixed geometry, nominal fuel and simplified single-zone generator, together with the absence of experimental validation, preclude interpreting the reported gains as demonstrated improvements on real engines.
evidence_items.title: Derivative and Combustion Metric Supervised Cylinder Pressure Surrogates for Spark-Ignition Engines: A Synthetic Benchmark Study

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Automated regression testing is essential for maintaining rapid, high-quality delivery in Agile and Scrum organizations. Many teams, including Hacon (a Siemens company), face a persistent gap: validated test specifications accumulate faster than they are automated, limiting regression coverage and increasing manual work. This paper reports an exploratory industrial case study of the Hacon Test Automation Copilot, an agentic AI system that generates system-level regression test scripts from validated specifications using retrieval-augmented generation and a multi-agent workflow. Integrated with Hacon’s CI pipelines, the Copilot operates asynchronously as a “silent AI teammate”, producing candidate scripts for human review. Mixed-method evaluation shows the AI accelerates script authoring and increases throughput, with 30–50% code reuse. However, human review remains necessary for maintainability and correct domain interpretation. Clear specifications, explicit governance, and ongoing human–AI collaboration are critical. We conclude with lessons for scaling regression automation and enabling effective human–AI teaming in Agile settings.
evidence_items.title: Human–AI Collaboration for Scaling Agile Regression Testing: An Agentic-AI Teammate from Manual to Automated Testing

evidence_items.summary: Automated accessibility checkers can identify WCAG violations but cannot resolve them, leaving remediation as a manual burden for developers. Large language models (LLMs) have been proposed as a means of generating code-level fixes, yet their effectiveness on unmodified production code remains largely untested. This poster evaluates GPT-5.5 and LLaMA-3.3 on remediating WCAG 2.2 violations naturally occurring across ten real-world websites spanning seven domains, using four prompting strategies: Zero-Shot, Few-Shot, In-Context Learning, and Chain-of-Thought. This poster showcases that LLaMA outperforms GPT overall (45.58% vs. 37.6%), with CoT yielding the highest accuracy for LLaMA and Few-Shot for GPT. While a combined-model approach raises the fix rate to 49.26%, both models fail on semantically demanding violations like missing image alt text, revealing a fundamental grounding limitation. We translate these findings into concrete recommendations for practitioners building LLM-assisted accessibility tools and for researchers designing future evaluations.
evidence_items.title: Evaluating Large Language Models for Web Accessibility Remediation in Real-World Websites

evidence_items.summary: Digital accessibility barriers are easier to prevent during design than to remediate after implementation, yet accessibility is often taught and practiced as a downstream concern. Despite growing attention in computing and design education, accessibility efforts continue to emphasize code-level auditing, remediation, and compliance checking, with less attention to early design decisions. The shift-left principle seeks to address this gap by embedding accessibility from the initial UX design phase, but its adoption remains limited. To explore how AI can support this shift, we developed a Figma plugin that uses a multimodal large language model (LLM) to evaluate UI frames against WCAG criteria and provide contextual, design-stage feedback. In a three-week deployment, 89 practicing professionals and computing or design students used the plugin alongside existing tools (Stark and Axe for Designers) and reported their perceptions, experiences, and self-reported abilities through pre- and post-use surveys. Overall, 92.1% reported identifying accessibility issues earlier, 96.6% reported productivity gains, and participants rated recommendation likelihood (M=4.25/5) and generated specification accuracy (M=4.08/5) highly. Findings also suggest that contextual AI feedback can help learners identify and reason about accessibility issues earlier in the design process. We conclude with practical takeaways for integrating AI-supported tools into accessibility education.
evidence_items.title: Designing and Evaluating an AI-Powered Figma Plugin for Accessibility Education

evidence_items.summary: As large language model (LLM)-based voice agents increasingly enter high-risk domains such as medical recommendation, voice personality is becoming a key social cue for trust. Yet research has largely focused on sighted users, leaving how blind users interpret these cues unclear. To address this gap, we conducted a two-part exploratory study with blind participants. We first created four theory-inspired voice probes varying intended warmth and competence, and ran a participatory co-design workshop (N=6) supported by tactile toolkits. This approach enabled participants to directly experience, evaluate, and articulate their perceptions. Our findings show how the two features (acoustic and linguistic) relate to perceived warmth and competence, which jointly shape trust judgments. To further examine these insights in a more realistic interaction context, we conducted a follow-up within-subject study (N = 11). Across both studies, blind users consistently prioritized competence over warmth in medical decision-making. Together, these findings contribute design knowledge and methods for building trustworthy and accessible voice agents in risk-sensitive contexts.
evidence_items.title: Exploring How Warmth and Competence Shape Trust in Medical Voice Agents with Blind Users

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in settings that affect disabled people, but little is known about how these systems represent disability stereotypes in the Chinese social context. We compare the three-dimensional stereotype profiles of six disability groups in China across a non-disabled public sample (N = 176), a self-identified disability community sample (N = 51), and four LLMs (ChatGPT 5.4, Claude 4.6 Sonnet, Qwen3-Max, and DeepSeek-Chat V3.2; 50 independent application programming interface (API) calls for each model, temperature, and disability group; 2,400 valid responses). The main human materials and LLM prompts were in Mandarin Chinese. A later English-prompt robustness set used the same models, temperatures, and disability groups and produced a similar profile. Three results are central. First, humans and models preserve the same broad hierarchy: physical and sensory disabilities are rated more positively than intellectual and psychiatric disability (human-human profile r = .987; human-LLM r = .82 to .94 when temperatures are pooled). Second, the models rate courage above the human baseline (model-level difference +0.38 to +0.76) and show much less within-condition variability than either human sample (mean cell standard deviation (SD) 0.02-0.09 vs. 0.90 and 0.94). Third, the closest human reference varies by model: the two U.S.-built models are closer to the non-disabled public sample, whereas the two China-built models are slightly closer to the disability community sample. Because we evaluated only four commercial models, we treat this model-origin pattern as descriptive, not causal. In this setting, LLMs preserve the structure of disability stigma while raising courage ratings and narrowing observed response variability.
evidence_items.title: Preserved Hierarchy, Inflated Courage: How Four LLMs Re-inscribe Chinese Disability Stereotypes Across Public and Community Perspectives

evidence_items.summary: Chronic hepatitis B (CHB) burdens the healthcare system, affecting millions of individuals worldwide with a potential progression to complications such as cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). The World Health Organization launched the chronic viral hepatitis elimination plan which aimed to eliminate chronic hepatitis B virus by 2030, yet the goal has seemed to be far from reach with the remaining few years owing to different hurdles ranging from screening strategy and diagnosis to risk stratification for antiviral treatment and HCC surveillance. To refine the management of CHB, previous studies focused on identifying the at-risk populations and predictors for adverse outcomes using conventional statistical methods. With the emerging role of artificial intelligence (AI), there is further room to improve different aspects of screening and management. For instance, generative AI, such as large language models (LLMs), has been proven to have the ability to answer different clinical questions, assisting patients' and physicians' decision on various clinical scenarios. Different machine learning and deep learning models have also been developed to assess for liver fibrosis, as well as to aid segmentation of liver structures and detection of focal liver lesions through various imaging modalities. While different AI models have shown superior performance compared to those developed through traditional statistical models, the lack of standardized datasets in training cohorts and the unresolved concerns of hallucination of false information in LLMs pose challenges on applying AI in the current management of CHB, in which further studies are required to adopt AI into daily clinical practice.
evidence_items.title: Clinical Application of Artificial Intelligence in the Management of Chronic Hepatitis B.

evidence_items.summary: Sidewalk images are increasingly used to support route planning for people facing mobility challenges, but interpreting them one by one remains a burden. While recent work has explored automatic extraction of accessibility information from such images, two gaps remain: whether large language models (LLMs) can accurately describe sidewalk problems, and whether these descriptions reflect the perspectives across mobility groups. To address these gaps, we evaluated LLM-generated sidewalk image descriptions from the perspectives of perceived accuracy and user-centered relevance. We compared four conditions combining generation format (monologue or dialogue) and role setting (generic or participant-matched role), based on evaluations by 12 participants, including manual wheelchair users, cane users, and stroller users. The results showed that, in the evaluated pipeline, dialogue-based generation did not clearly improve perceived accuracy, whereas participant-matched role assignment improved user-centered relevance. We also found that, without explicit role assignment, the evaluated LLM tended to adopt a wheelchair-user perspective as the implicit default, with additional checks suggesting a similar but model-dependent bias in other LLMs. Based on these findings, we derive design implications for sidewalk image description systems that better accommodate needs across mobility groups.
evidence_items.title: Can Dialogue and Role Improve LLM Sidewalk Image Descriptions Across Mobility Groups?

evidence_items.summary: Abstract The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) and text and data mining (TDM) technologies has become a crucial factor in supporting linguistic diversity of smaller languages, such as Estonian. However, the growing reliance on large-scale data processing raises significant legal and ethical challenges, particularly concerning the lawful use of copyrighted materials to train AI systems. While the European Union has introduced regulatory instruments such as the AI Act and the Copyright Directive to address these concerns, the intersection of AI development, TDM, and intellectual property rights remains insufficiently resolved. This research aims to explore how AI-driven text and data mining can both comply with European copyright law and actively contribute to the preservation and wider use of the Estonian language. The authors investigate this research topic from the perspective of the Estonian language, enmeshed within Estonian cultural norms and parameters. The analysis examines the legal and economic appropriateness of enabling the training of generative AI-based large language models (LLMs) in the Estonian language as a means of promoting the language and assuring its appropriate use in digital environments, thereby contributing to its long-term relevance. Methodologically, the study combines a comparative analysis of EU, US, and Asian legal frameworks with a theoretical evaluation of existing models for balancing innovation and rights protection. The article seeks to provide concrete recommendations for developing AI and data mining practices that enhance linguistic innovation while safeguarding creators’ rights, thereby contributing to Estonia’s digital and cultural resilience within the EU’s evolving AI ecosystem.
evidence_items.title: Regulating LLM training under EU copyright law and its linguistic implications for smaller languages such as Estonian

evidence_items.summary: Abstract This article examines the relationship between data protection law and copyright law in the regulation of scientific research and the development of artificial intelligence (AI) in the European Union (EU). It argues that the coexistence of purpose-based and status-based regulatory models creates a fragmented legal environment for AI training and undermines the coherence of EU innovation policy. Data protection law adopts a purpose-oriented framework centred on scientific research and the public interest, whereas copyright law conditions research-related uses on institutional status and lawful access under the Digital Single Market (DSM) Directive. Through a doctrinal analysis of EU legislation, case law, and Estonian implementing law, the article demonstrates how this asymmetry generates legal uncertainty where AI training depends simultaneously on access to personal data and copyright-protected works. It further argues that the absence of a public-interest-oriented framework in copyright law limits its capacity to support scientific progress and technological innovation, particularly in smaller linguistic communities that rely on access to national-language datasets for AI development.
evidence_items.title: Regulatory asymmetries in EU scientific research law: data protection, copyright, and AI development

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Educational artificial intelligence (AI) does not become high-risk under the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act 2024 merely because it is used in schools. Its classification depends on the function it performs within the educational process: whether it supports learning formatively, or whether it evaluates learning outcomes in ways that affect a student’s educational trajectory. This distinction is especially unstable in adaptive generative AI systems, where the same interactional features that make a tool pedagogically useful may, if repurposed or institutionally relied upon, move it towards the assessment logic of Annex III, point 3(b) of the AI Act. This paper uses Estonia’s AI Leap initiative as an early test case for that boundary. It develops four claims. First, the boundary between formative tutoring and high-risk assessment is conditional and dynamic, rather than inherent in the technology itself. Second, the profiling rule in Article 6(3) of the AI Act is best understood as an anti-derogation trigger: it does not independently bring a system within Annex III, but once an educational AI system falls within Annex III, profiling prevents reliance on the derogation from high-risk classification. Third, the initiative exposes a value-chain asymmetry characteristic of public-sector educational deployments built on third-party general-purpose AI models, in which downstream actors may acquire compliance responsibilities without full technical control. Fourth, Section 20¹ amendment to the Basic Schools and Upper Secondary Schools Act (Estonia) 2010 provides an unusually concrete national-law basis for educational AI processing, but it cannot by itself resolve the data-protection problems created by open-input generative systems, especially the incidental capture of special-category and third-party data. The paper concludes that the initiative’s regulatory significance lies less in its present classification than in the governance conditions needed to prevent functional drift and mitigate the data-protection risks created by open-ended student inputs.
evidence_items.title: Educational AI at the boundary of high risk: Estonia’s AI Leap as a stress test for the EU AI Act and the GDPR

evidence_items.summary: Fully autonomous ride-hailing services (FARS) promise new independence for blind and low-vision (BLV) travelers, yet research remains largely anticipatory. Surveys, proxies, and staged enactments dominate, leaving the lived experience of deployed, commercial FARS nearly unexamined. We conducted a qualitative interview study with five BLV riders who frequently use human-operated ride-hailing and have completed multiple Waymo trips, benchmarking FARS against human-driven rides. Data comprised semi-structured Zoom interviews of 75 minutes, transcribed and analyzed via reflexive thematic analysis. Four themes emerged. Riders described recovered autonomy and ownership, comparative trust with a privacy inversion favoring corporate over human-driver recording, pickup and drop-off as critical failure points around an otherwise friction-free ride, and design pathways toward an assisted FARS model. We reframe driverless ride-hailing as restructuring rather than removing the assistance relationship, relocating support from driver to system. These findings motivate multimodal, embodied assistance for accessibility researchers, designers, and developers.
evidence_items.title: It’s Our Ride, We’re Just Out of the Driver’s Seat: Perceptions of and Challenges with Fully Autonomous Vehicles Among BLV Waymo Riders

evidence_items.summary:
INTRODUCTION
Tobacco use and recreational nicotine consumption remain among the leading preventable causes of morbidity and mortality worldwide, including in Hungary. The World Health Organization Framework Convention on Tobacco Control and related international recommendations identify healthcare institutions as key actors in tobacco control. To support the implementation of comprehensive tobacco- and nicotine-free healthcare services, the Global Network for Tobacco Free Healthcare Services (GNTH) has developed an evidence-based framework consisting of 8 standards and a structured institutional self-audit tool. However, no Hungarian-language version of this methodology has previously been available.


OBJECTIVE
This study aims to present the Hungarian linguistic and cultural adaptation process of the English version of the self-audit tool developed by the GNTH and the Spanish implementation guide.


METHOD
Linguistic and cultural adaptation of the English-language GNTH self-audit tool and the Spanish implementation guide were conducted. The adaptation process considered the Hungarian legal, policy and healthcare system context. Content validation was supported by expert review, while practical applicability was assessed through pilot testing in a tertiary healthcare institution. The adaptation followed an iterative process involving consultations with representatives of the GNTH Board.


RESULTS
The adaptation process resulted in the development of the complete Hungarian GNTH audit package, including the institutional self-audit questionnaire, scoring template, and a detailed implementation guide tailored to the characteristics of the Hungarian healthcare system. The final tool enables objective assessment of tobacco- and nicotine-free institutional performance based on 8 GNTH standards, 48 assessment criteria, and 192 scoring specifications. The Hungarian adaptation was formally reviewed and acknowledged by the GNTH Executive Board.


CONCLUSION
The Hungarian GNTH self-audit tool represents a novel quality improvement and management instrument for healthcare organizations. Its implementation may facilitate the transition from passive regulatory compliance towards a proactive, systems-based and data-driven institutional approach to tobacco and nicotine control. The methodology also provides a foundation for benchmarking, continuous quality improvement, and the future development of a national professional network supporting tobacco-free healthcare services. Orv Hetil. 2026; 167(43): 1739-1748.
evidence_items.title: [On the way to tobacco- and nicotine-free healthcare institutions].

evidence_items.summary: Improving the fidelity of computational eukaryotic models will require an enormous amount of high quality and reproducible data from biological experiments. In this study we present and demonstrate a modular 12-channel micro-chemostat system. This micro-chemostat is designed for use by Genesis, a Robot Scientist developed to automate scientific research in yeast systems biology. We performed bioreactor characterization experiments to evaluate the performance of the micro-chemostat system. We also cultivated the Saccharomyces cerevisiae reference strain, BY4741, at three different dilution rates (0.1, 0.2, and 0.3 h-1) and under two aeration conditions (microaerobic and aerobic), resulting in six different conditions. The bioreactor performance fulfilled our requirements, and enabled substrate-limited continuous cultivation of yeast. Furthermore, the empirical results from the biological experiments were consistent with the literature, suggesting that results obtained from our system are comparable to those reported for other platforms in the field. Based on the evidence presented in this study, we conclude that the 12-channel micro-chemostat system is a suitable platform for yeast systems biology research. The modular design of the micro-chemostat system enables future scaling to hundreds or thousands of concurrent chemostats and facilitates integration with autonomous agents for automated optimization and improvement of eukaryotic model systems.
evidence_items.title: A Modular Micro-Chemostat System for High-Throughput Continuous Cultivations.

evidence_items.summary: Spider venom-derived peptides have emerged as promising therapeutic agents due to their high specificity and ability to modulate cellular and immunological pathways. LW-9, a peptide isolated from Phoneutria nigriventer venom, was identified as a potential immunomodulatory molecule with antitumor activity. This study evaluated the therapeutic effects of LW-9 in a murine breast cancer model using EO771 cells. Treatment with LW-9 significantly delayed tumour progression, with enhanced efficacy observed when combined with the chemotherapeutic agent doxorubicin. The therapeutic dose of LW-9 (1 μg/kg) showed a favourable safety profile, with no significant alterations in hepatic or renal biochemical markers, including AST, ALT, creatinine, and urea. In addition, LW-9 improved animal well-being, as indicated by increased food intake and maintenance of body weight compared with doxorubicin-treated controls. Immunological analyses demonstrated that LW-9, particularly in combination with doxorubicin, promoted substantial remodelling of the tumour microenvironment. Flow cytometry revealed reduced PD-L1 expression and increased frequencies of CD3+ and CD3+/GITR+ T cells, indicating enhanced antitumor immune activation. Immunohistochemical analysis confirmed increased lymphocytic infiltration within tumour tissue. Tumours maintained a stable ER-negative, PR-positive, HER2-negative, and EGFR-positive phenotype across all groups, suggesting that LW-9-mediated antitumor activity occurs independently of classical molecular subtype alterations. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that LW-9 enhances chemotherapy efficacy by modulating the tumour immune microenvironment, supporting its potential as a novel immunoadjuvant strategy for breast cancer therapy.
evidence_items.title: Immunomodulatory Peptide LW-9 Enhances Doxorubicin Efficacy by Downregulating PD-L1 and Promoting Intratumoral T-Cell Responses in Murine Breast Cancer.

authors: Fábio de Oliveira da Silva Ribeiro
evidence_items.summary: Prostate cancer (PCa) is the second most common cancer in men worldwide, and chemotherapeutic treatment may exhibit limited efficacy owing to side effects and hypersensitivity. Cabazitaxel (CTX) is an antineoplastic agent used to treat prostate cancer; however, it has low selectivity and adverse effects that limit its adherence and efficacy. In this context, transferrin (Tf)-functionalized polymeric nanoparticles have emerged as a potential targeted therapy directed toward the Tf receptor (TfR), which is overexpressed in prostate cancer cells. In this study, cabazitaxel was encapsulated in polycaprolactone (PCL) polymeric nanoparticles functionalized with transferrin (Tf), and its in vitro activity was evaluated in PCa cell lines. Therefore, a study was conducted to determine the optimal preparation conditions in terms of formulation characteristics. The nanoparticles were produced by nanoprecipitation using acetone as the solvent in the presence of the surfactant Poloxamer 188. Transferrin was covalently bound to the PEG-PCL-maleimide moiety on the nanoparticle surface. The transferrin-functionalized nanoparticles had an average particle size of 123.9 nm ± 1.13, a polydispersity index (PDI) of 0.168 ± 0.11, a zeta potential of -11.43 mV ± 1.89, and an encapsulation efficiency (EE%) of 79.6% ± 6.8. In electrophoresis, free transferrin exhibited a band near 80 kDa, with a corresponding band observed in the elution of the functionalized nanoparticles, indicating protein attachment to the nanoparticles. Circular dichroism analysis, together with fluorescence spectroscopy, demonstrated the preservation of protein structural integrity after conjugation. Microscopy techniques (SEM and AFM) revealed the spherical morphology of the nanoparticles, and AFM further confirmed successful conjugation through changes in the surface roughness of the functionalized nanoparticles. The in vitro release study demonstrated that both non-functionalized and transferrin-functionalized PCL-based nanoparticles provided a sustained release of cabazitaxel over 192 h, confirming the potential of these systems for prolonged drug delivery. In cell culture assays, the high cell viability observed in the L929 cell line demonstrated the safety of the developed systems, whereas the marked reduction in viability in DU145 and PC3 cell lines demonstrated the effect of encapsulation on cytotoxicity of the developed systems. Functionalization with transferrin (Tf) significantly increased the in vitro toxicity and cellular internalization. The percentage of cellular internalization was higher in the PC3 cell line than in the DU145 cell line, corroborating the literature reporting higher TfR expression in this lineage. Encapsulation and functionalization demonstrated potential as active drug-targeting vectors, as they increased cytotoxicity compared to free drugs. This finding represents an important advancement in the development of a formulation and approach capable of enhancing therapeutic efficacy while reducing the systemic side effects of the drug.
evidence_items.title: Transferrin functionalization enhances prostate cancer cell uptake and cytotoxicity of cabazitaxel-loaded polymeric nanoparticles.

evidence_items.summary:
AIMS
To evaluate the impact of semaglutide initiation for weight management on the use of concomitant medications commonly prescribed for obesity-related comorbidities.


MATERIALS AND METHODS
We conducted a nationwide interrupted time series study using data from Danish registers, including adults initiating semaglutide for weight management between 12/2022 and 12/2024. Monthly prescriptions for 10 medication classes were analysed in the 24 months before and 12 months after initiation. Effects at 12 months were expressed as rate ratios (RRs) comparing observed values with expected values based on pre-initiation trends.


RESULTS
Among 189 392 semaglutide initiators (68% women; median age 50 years), prescription volumes at 12 months declined and were lower than projected from pre-initiation trends for antiasthmatics (RR: 0.82, 95% confidence interval 0.79-0.86), topical corticosteroids (0.91, 0.87-0.96), antipsoriatics (0.91, 0.83-1.00), analgesics (0.93, 0.90-0.96), antidepressants (0.93, 0.89-0.98) and topical antifungal formulations (0.92, 0.86-0.99). Antihypertensive prescriptions continued to rise after semaglutide initiation, but more slowly than projected (0.92, 0.89-0.95). Glucose-lowering medications declined (0.87, 0.82-0.92), mainly non-insulin agents, but a similar reduction was observed in the negative control cohort. Anxiolytic use increased (1.16, 1.08-1.24) and remained elevated at 2 years. Changes in lipid-modifying agents and medications for gastric acid disorders were small or transient.


CONCLUSIONS
Semaglutide initiation for weight management was associated with reduced use of several concomitant medications for obesity-related comorbidities, while anxiolytic use increased. Changes in other therapeutic classes were limited. These findings suggest that semaglutide treatment may influence overall medication use and support continued monitoring of prescribing patterns during therapy.
evidence_items.title: Impact of Semaglutide Introduction on the Use of Concomitant Medications: An Interrupted Time Series.

evidence_items.summary: AI systems built around large models increasingly use experience and feedback to make persistent changes to models, prompts, memories, tools, and workflows. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) extends this process to inductive biases and to the mechanisms that govern future updates, which can themselves be revised and reused across improvement cycles. Yet self-modification alone does not guarantee trustworthy improvement. Reported gains may reflect flawed evaluations, previously acquired capabilities may deteriorate, and compliance with behavioral constraints may weaken. Compromised artifacts or sensitive information may also persist in successor systems. Changes to improvement mechanisms may invalidate earlier verification results and make human oversight less effective. This survey presents an operational definition and process framework for RSI and organizes the requirements for trustworthy RSI into four interconnected themes: genuine and sustained improvement; behavioral constraints, alignment, and fairness; system security and privacy; and transparency and controllability. We examine these themes from three perspectives: Improvement Validity, Constraint Preservation, and Effective Oversight. This analysis covers improvement diagnosis, proposal generation, proposal evaluation, and update implementation (S1--S4), including the recursive application of these stages to improvement mechanisms (RI). We review risks, safeguards, and evaluation evidence for individual updates, effects inherited by successor systems, and revisions to improvement mechanisms, while distinguishing direct RSI findings from evidence in related systems. Finally, we examine evaluation settings, identify requirements for independent and longitudinal assessment, and discuss applications and open research problems.
evidence_items.title: Trustworthy Recursive Self-Improvement in the Era of Large Models: Foundation, Risks, Evaluation and Open Challenges

evidence_items.summary: Behavior cloning for robotic manipulation is highly sensitive to the coverage of its training data, yet collecting diverse successful demonstrations remains costly. We study reinforcement learning (RL) not as a deployable controller, but as a data generator for downstream visuomotor imitation learning. Our key premise is that multiple successful solution modes cover a broader range of successful trajectories than repeatedly collecting a single narrow solution. We introduce DiscoDemo, which trains a privileged latent-conditioned RL generator with a parallel reverse curriculum and a success-gated diversity objective to discover diverse solutions while preserving task success. The trained generator produces multiple successful closed-loop behaviors, which are safety-filtered and exported as a static dataset for downstream imitation learning. Across four manipulation tasks, DiscoDemo produces broader successful-state coverage and improves downstream visuomotor policies in both simulation and the real world. Averaged across tasks, downstream success increases to 62% from 40% for the strongest baseline in simulation, and to 78% from 39% on the real robot, respectively. These results suggest that successful solution diversity improves imitation learning for a pretrained flow-matching VLA and remains complementary to corrective data collection. Project page: https://davian-robotics.github.io/DiscoDemo
evidence_items.title: DiscoDemo: Discovering Efficient and Diverse Robot Demonstrations for Imitation Learning

evidence_items.summary: Many language-model pipelines end in a closed-set decision, such as selecting a tool. Prompting a large language model for it is slow and order-sensitive. We ask how small an encoder for such decisions can be and whether it should read the options jointly or separately. In a three-seed study at 32 million parameters, per-option scoring beats joint scoring on a held-out sample of a 37-benchmark decision suite by 5.8 points of chance-corrected skill at matched optimizer steps and by 2.8 at approximately matched training compute; two external benchmarks agree, though not significantly on their unseen tasks. Crossing reader with initialisation shows that the advantage requires a reranker initialisation, whose query-candidate pair input matches per-option reading; from the raw encoder the two readers are indistinguishable. Per-option scoring needs 5 to 13 times more encoder passes: at most twice the median latency, but more than four times the mean. Of six released joint encoders (17 million to 1 billion parameters), the 68- and 150-million-parameter models exceed a 435-million-parameter DeBERTa-v3 zero-shot classifier by 4.9 and 5.9 accuracy points on 209 overlap-audited System1-Arena tasks and are at least on par with it on the 145 tasks unseen in training. The smallest answers a median request in 14 milliseconds on 16 processor threads, against 728 for the classifier. Reordering options changes 12 to 23% of the joint models' answers (per-option scoring: none). Up to 68 million parameters, they lead their size range on a public leaderboard's private, mainly in-distribution tests.
evidence_items.title: Joint or Per-Option? Compact Encoders for Closed-Set Decisions from 17 Million to 1 Billion Parameters

evidence_items.summary: Large-scale AI training increasingly relies on massive video datasets with random temporal sampling patterns. However, existing video storage paradigms are optimized for sequential playback and employ sophisticated inter-frame reference structures to maximize compression efficiency. When applied to the random-sampling workloads of AI training, these paradigms face substantial decoding-efficiency bottlenecks. Workarounds such as independent JPEG frames and short groups of pictures (GOPs) reduce decoding work at the cost of larger storage and transfer volumes. In this paper, we identify two sources of decode amplification: sequential reconstruction of unrelated frames and reconstruction of the reference chains required by sampled targets. We address both sources by co-designing the decoding schedule and video reference structure. Dependency-aware sparse decoding reconstructs only requested frames and their required references, skipping unrelated reconstruction without transcoding the source videos. Optional offline Dependency-Decoupled Random Access (DDRA) encoding further reduces reference reconstruction by restricting each interior frame to two bounding intra-coded anchors. Together, sparse decoding and DDRA retain inter-frame prediction while bounding reconstruction to at most three frames per requested target, independent of the intra period. Experiments on a large-scale robotics corpus show that, at comparable reconstruction quality, our method achieves 1.45times the loading throughput of LeRobot v3 with 58.7% less media payload.
evidence_items.title: Rethinking Video Storage for AI Training: Breaking Cross-Frame Dependencies for Efficient Random Access
